name: Ultra-high-power (UHP) CW InP lasers and external-laser-source (ELS/ELSFP) modules for CPO/NPO
definition: IN: InP CW-DFB laser chips at roughly 200-400+ mW per emitter qualified for external light sources, plus the pluggable ELS/ELSFP modules that package them (8 emitters per module in Nvidia's design, PM-fiber pigtails, isolators, TEC/control) and feed silicon-photonics optical engines in CPO/NPO switches and, from ~2028, XPU optical I/O. OUT: 50-100 mW CW chips mounted inside SiPh pluggables (slower sibling), EMLs, VCSELs, 980 nm pump lasers, the optical engines/PICs themselves.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> scale-out / scale-up networking -> optical interconnect -> co-packaged / near-packaged optics (CPO/NPO) -> external light source -> UHP InP CW-DFB laser chips + ELS/ELSFP modules
also_serves_megatrends: AI scale-out switching (Nvidia Spectrum-X/Quantum-X Photonics, Broadcom TH6-Davisson)
AI scale-up optical I/O for XPUs (Nvidia Feynman NVLink-CPO, Marvell/Celestial AI) from 2028
Silicon-photonics pluggables moving to 400 mW-class CW lasers for 1.6T/3.2T (shares fab capacity)
size_2026_usd: $0.08-0.3B (own estimate; Lumentum alone guided ~$50M CPO revenue for CQ4-2026)
size_2030_usd: $2-6B (own estimate; derived from third-party CPO/NPO forecasts of $9.3B (Morgan Stanley base) to >$39B (TrendForce) times a 10-20% laser/ELS share of CPO optics value)
volume_vs_price: ~90%+ volume. ELS units go from ~0.2-0.4M (2026) to ~2-3M (2027) and much higher once scale-up CPO starts in 2028. Per-laser ASP likely deflates 10-15%/yr after 2027 as Coherent, Sumitomo, Lumentum Greensboro and Chinese capacity arrive, but value per port rises because vendors sell full ELS modules (Lumentum: 2-2.5x the revenue content of bare lasers) and per-emitter power climbs (200 -> 400 mW) for 400G lanes. Today's pricing is LTA/prepayment-backed shortage pricing; the durable part is volume.
math: Top-down 2026: Nvidia CPO switches ~15-20k (GF Securities est.) x 16-18 ELS per switch (Nvidia: 16 per single-ASIC Spectrum-X, 18 in Quantum-X Q3450) = 0.24-0.36M ELS x 8 emitters = 2-3M UHP lasers. At $500-1,000 per ELS module (own est.; consistent with Lumentum's 2-2.5x module uplift over ~$25-50 lasers and a secondhand Mizuho $10-20k laser content per switch, unverified) = $120-360M if fully shipped; haircut for evaluation units/yield -> $80-300M. 2027: ~100k Nvidia CPO switches (GF Securities) plus Broadcom; Morgan Stanley's 6-7M optical engines / 32 engines per switch (Citi SN6810 model) = ~200k switch-equivalents -> ~2-3M ELS x $500-900 = $1.0-2.5B. 2030: CPO/NPO $9-39B x 10-20% laser/ELS share = $1-8B, central $2-6B. Supplier check: Lumentum CQ4-26 ~$50M (~$200M annualized) plus a multi-hundred-million UHP purchase order shipping 1H CY2027.
catalyst_timing: 2H26: Nvidia Spectrum-X Photonics capacity expands; Lumentum 'meaningful revenue exiting CY2026'; Coherent CPO ramp from FQ2-FY27 (Oct-Dec 2026). 1H27: Lumentum multi-hundred-million UHP PO ships; first ELS module order delivers 2H CY27. 2027-28: CPO switch volume ramp (TrendForce). 2028: Nvidia Feynman NVLink-CPO / Kyber CPO variant; Lumentum Greensboro UHP fab contributes; Marvell Celestial AI revenue from 2H FY2028.
key_suppliers: Lumentum (LITE, Nasdaq; Japan InP fabs, Caswell UK, Greensboro NC from 2028) est. 40-55% of merchant UHP/ELS 2026-27; Coherent (COHR, NYSE; Sherman TX 6-inch InP, 400 mW CW sampling) est. 15-25%; Sumitomo Electric (5802.T) est. 10-20%; Broadcom (AVGO) captive CW lasers for its own CPO est. 10-20%; followers Mitsubishi Electric (6503.T), Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI), Yuanjie Semiconductor (688498.SS, CPO/NPO lasers sampling). ELS module assembly also at Fabrinet (FN) and TFC Optical (300394.SZ). All shares are own estimates (unverified). Geography: Japan, US, UK, China.
supply_tightness: Very tight. Lumentum says it is far behind on high-power laser shipments as CPO/NPO demand outpaces capacity; its InP fabs are fully allocated and the Greensboro conversion is not material until early 2028. High-current UHP reliability is hard (Everbright), qualification runs ~12-24 months (own estimate), and Nvidia's $2B investments with capacity-access rights in each of Lumentum and Coherent (Mar-2026) pre-empt capacity. Suppliers are signing prepayments, take-or-pay and capacity reservations, so pricing power is high through 2027.
substitution_risk: Medium for 2028-30: (1) brighter lasers feeding more lanes cut unit counts; (2) lasers integrated on the PIC (heterogeneous III-V, quantum-dot) could remove the external source, more likely after 2030; (3) microLED/VCSEL NPO for short scale-up links (TrendForce microLED CPO ~$848M by 2030); (4) copper stays dominant in-rack through at least 2028 (TrendForce), and NPO designs with in-module lasers could take some ELS demand.
cyclicality_risk: High timing risk. CPO volume has slipped before (TrendForce: volume ramp 2027-28; some analysts 2028-29; Morgan Stanley sees only 6-7M engines in 2027 vs 20-30M expected), so LTAs/POs placed now could turn into double orders if engine yields stay low. From 2028, Coherent 6-inch, Lumentum Greensboro, Sumitomo and Chinese entrants (Yuanjie's RMB4.27B laser park) raise oversupply risk.
faster_sub_niche: This is already the faster child of 'InP CW-DFB laser chips'. Split: (a) 50-100 mW CW chips inside SiPh pluggables, ~$1.5-2.5B in 2026 (own est.), growing ~25-40% CAGR (Yuanjie H1-26 revenue RMB925M, +351%; Q3 guide RMB650-700M); (b) UHP/ELS for CPO/NPO at 60-150%, analyzed here. Within (b), finished ELS/ELSFP modules grow faster than bare UHP chips because a module carries 2-2.5x the laser revenue.

evidence.source: Lumentum Q4 FY2026 results (8-K Ex.99.1) and call coverage

The leverage is real because each CPO switch removes pluggable lasers but adds a concentrated, high-ASP ELS bill; whoever ships qualified 200-400 mW InP emitters in 2027 earns shortage-era margins. The 2026 base is small and the 2027 number depends on CPO engine yields at TSMC/SPIL. Watch for a slip of Nvidia's Spectrum-X Photonics ramp past mid-2027, which would push the inflection into 2028 and lower the 2026->2030 CAGR toward ~60%. The Mizuho $10-20k per-switch figure and the supplier mapping for ELS assembly rest on secondary sources (unverified).

name: Merchant optical circuit switches (OCS) for AI clusters
definition: IN: OCS systems sold by merchant vendors (MEMS-mirror, liquid-crystal/DLC, piezo beam-steering), including the MEMS arrays, 2D collimator arrays and control, used for reconfigurable AI cluster fabrics (TPU-style scale-out today, GPU rack-to-rack scale-up from 2028). OUT: value of Google's internally built OCS (Apollo/Palomar), telecom ROADM/WSS, OCS-compatible transceivers and circulators (adjacent niches).
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> scale-out / scale-up networking -> optical switching layer (spine / reconfigurable fabric) -> optical circuit switches -> merchant OCS systems (MEMS mirror arrays + collimator arrays)
also_serves_megatrends: Google TPU scale-out (only volume application today)
GPU scale-up rack-to-rack domains (Nvidia Rubin Ultra NVL576, significant volume from 2028)
Other hyperscaler XPU clusters seeking power savings and failure-domain reconfiguration
size_2026_usd: Merchant $0.35-0.65B (own estimate, mostly Lumentum); total market including captive Google value up to ~$2.8B (own inference from Cignal's >$8B 2030 at >30% CAGR; unverified)
size_2030_usd: Total >$8B (Cignal AI, third-party estimate); merchant $3-6B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: ~85-95% volume (ports shipped). Price per port (~$500 on a $150k 300x300 unit, third-party estimate) likely falls ~5-10%/yr, offset partly by higher-radix and scale-up variants. Merchant growth also comes from share shift: Google is moving from in-house OCS to third-party vendors.
math: Bottom-up 2026 merchant: Lumentum CY26 OCS ~$0.3-0.45B (OCS shipments doubled FQ3->FQ4-FY26; first >$100M quarter guided for Jul-Sep 2026; CQ4 likely $120-160M, own est.) + Coherent $0.03-0.15B (unverified) + Polatis/DiCon/Chinese <$0.05B = $0.35-0.65B. Units: $100M per quarter / ~$150k per 300x300 switch = ~650-700 switches = ~200k ports per quarter. 2030: Cignal total >$8B x merchant share rising from ~25-40% to 50-75% = $4-6B; haircut for port-price decline and Cignal's own low conviction on 2028+ XPU volumes -> $3-6B. CAGR (3/0.65)^(1/4)=47% to (6/0.35)^(1/4)=103%.
catalyst_timing: Jul-Sep 2026: Lumentum's first >$100M OCS quarter. FY2027 (to Jun-2027): Coherent guides significant OCS growth against a $4B addressable market. 2026-27: Google TPU builds (Alphabet 2026 capex $195-205B) and shift to third-party OCS. 2028: Nvidia Rubin Ultra NVL576 integrates OCS (Cignal) -> second demand leg.
key_suppliers: Lumentum (LITE; R300 300x300 MEMS OCS, in-house MEMS) est. 60-80% of merchant 2026 (Cignal Dec-2025: could be ~half of the total market); Coherent (COHR; DLC-based OCS) est. 10-25%; Huber+Suhner Polatis (HUBN.SW, piezo) small; DiCon (private, Taiwan) small; Sai MicroElectronics (300456.SZ; Beijing MEMS-OCS in small-batch trial) emerging; Silex Microsystems (MEMS foundry for Google OCS mirrors, now deconsolidated from Sai). Captive: Google. Shares own estimates.
supply_tightness: Tight. Lumentum calls OCS its biggest ramp, 'gated by the supply chain', 'on a tightrope', and holds a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar purchase agreement plus >$400M orders (Chinese press, single source). Few qualified vendors; MEMS mirror-array yield and 2D collimator alignment are the constraints; qualification at Google-scale customers takes 1-2+ years (own estimate).
substitution_risk: Medium: higher-radix electrical switches (102.4T Tomahawk 6) reduce the need for optical reconfiguration; Google could re-insource; Nvidia may use CPO-based electrical scale-up without OCS; silicon-photonic or LC switches could undercut MEMS on price.
cyclicality_risk: High customer concentration (Google), so TPU deployment timing makes revenue lumpy; LTAs can create double ordering; Chinese MEMS-OCS entrants could pressure pricing after 2028.
faster_sub_niche: GPU scale-up OCS (rack-to-rack, Nvidia NVL576-class) is the fastest child but inflects in 2028 (listed as too early). Within 2026-2028 the faster dynamic is merchant share gain at Google, so the merchant segment is analyzed rather than the total market.

name: Silicon-photonics PIC foundry wafers (merchant 200/300 mm)
definition: IN: merchant foundry fabrication of silicon-photonics PIC wafers (waveguides, Mach-Zehnder and micro-ring modulators, Ge photodetectors; also SiPh+BiCMOS platforms sold as photonics wafers) for pluggable DR/FR transceivers, LPO/LRO, CPO/NPO optical engines and other photonics. OUT: captive internal SiPh output (e.g., Intel internal use), 3D stacking/packaging services (COUPE SoIC step), stand-alone EIC/driver wafers, InP and TFLN devices.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> networking -> optical interconnect -> SiPh transceivers and CPO optical engines -> PIC die -> merchant SiPh foundry wafers
also_serves_megatrends: AI scale-out pluggables (EML -> SiPh shift at 1.6T)
Photonic quantum computing (e.g., PsiQuantum on GlobalFoundries) and FMCW LiDAR/sensing
size_2026_usd: $1.35-2.1B (own estimate from supplier disclosures)
volume_vs_price: ~75-85% volume (wafer starts, 300 mm migration), ~15-25% ASP/mix (200G/400G-per-lane PICs, micro-rings, CPO-grade wafers, prepayment-backed pricing). Price per wafer is more likely flat to up through 2027, then at risk once TSMC, Tower Japan 300 mm and Samsung capacity lands in 2028.
math: 2026 bottom-up: Tower SiPh ~$0.75-0.85B (Q2 annualized >$680M rising to a $1B run-rate in Q4; quarters ~$150/170/210/250M, own est.) + GlobalFoundries ~$0.4-0.45B (>$200M in 2025, 'more than double' in 2026) + TSMC PIC wafers $0.1-0.4B (10-15k wafers/month in 2H26 per Commercial Times estimates x unverified $2-4k/wafer) + ST/Samsung/China $0.1-0.4B (unverified) = $1.35-2.1B. 2030: Tower $3-4.5B ($1.3B contracted for 2027, 'even higher' 2028, 4x Japan 300 mm by late 2028) + GF $1.5-2.5B ($1B run-rate by end-2028) + TSMC $1.5-3B (25k+ wpm x 12 x $3-6k plus mix) + others $0.5-1.5B = $6.5-11.5B. Demand check: TrendForce 800G+ transceivers ~63M in 2026; 1.6T ~22M with 70% SiPh (CMBI); LightCounting SiPh share 30% (2025) -> 60% (2030). Capacity check: TSMC alone ~194M PICs/yr at 25k wpm x 648 dies, so supply is ample by 2028-29 and later pricing risk is real.
catalyst_timing: Q4-2026: Tower $1B SiPh run-rate; TSMC COUPE volume production and 200G micro-ring modulator in 2026. 2027: Tower $1.3B contracted SiPh revenue ($290M prepayments); TrendForce expects SiPh >50% of the transceiver market by 2027. Q4-2027: Tower Japan 300 mm Track 1 ready; late-2028: Track 2 quadruples Japan 300 mm output. End-2028: GF $1B SiPh run-rate. 2028: scale-up CPO adds a second demand leg.
key_suppliers: Tower Semiconductor (TSEM, Nasdaq/TASE; Israel, US, Japan) est. 45-55% of merchant 2026; GlobalFoundries (GFS; incl. Advanced Micro Foundry, Singapore) est. 20-30%; TSMC (2330.TW/TSM) est. 10-20% and rising fastest; STMicroelectronics (STM; PIC100 300 mm, Crolles) est. 5-10%; Samsung Foundry (005930.KS) entering; China (SMIC, CUMEC, SITRI) small. Shares own estimates.
supply_tightness: Tight through 2027: Tower collected $290M of capacity-reservation prepayments and is still qualifying added capacity; GF frames 2026 as supply-ramp-limited; TSMC capacity is reportedly going 500 -> 25k wpm. New SiPh capacity needs ~12-24 months for tool install plus customer qualification (own estimate). Loosening risk from 2028.
substitution_risk: Low to medium. InP EML keeps longer-reach and some 1.6T share (CMBI: 30% EML at 1.6T); TFLN may take 400G/lane modulators but is likely bonded onto SiPh platforms rather than replacing them; VCSEL/microLED for very short reach. CPO and LPO both still use SiPh PICs, so the platform shift is a tailwind.
cyclicality_risk: Medium-high after 2027: a simultaneous capacity race (TSMC ~50x, Tower 4x Japan 300 mm, GF with $300M US support, Samsung entry, Chinese fabs) could overshoot 2028-29 demand; module makers' 2026 double ordering is partly hedged by prepayments.
faster_sub_niche: 300 mm CPO-grade PIC wafers (micro-ring, COUPE-type, mainly TSMC) should grow faster than 200 mm pluggable PICs, but supplier disclosure does not allow sizing it separately (unverified), so the merchant SiPh foundry total is kept as the unit of analysis.

name: Indium phosphide (InP) single-crystal substrates (merchant)
definition: IN: merchant semi-insulating and n-type InP substrates (2, 3, 4-inch; emerging 6-inch) sold to laser, EML, CW, UHP and photodetector makers. OUT: InP epitaxial wafers (separate merchant step: LandMark, IQE, IntelliEPI), InP devices/chips, indium metal, captive substrate output where it exists (unverified).
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> networking -> optical interconnect -> laser and photodetector chips (EML, CW-DFB, UHP, PD) -> InP epitaxy -> InP substrates
also_serves_megatrends: AI optical interconnect (EML, CW, UHP lasers, PDs)
Defense/space mmWave and THz InP HBT/HEMT electronics
size_2026_usd: $0.4-0.65B (own estimate; bottom-up from AXT disclosures and share estimates; generic market-research figures range $0.22-1.8B and are unreliable)
volume_vs_price: 2026-27 growth is ~40-50% price/mix (four consecutive hikes; China 3-inch +78% end-2025 to Jun-2026; Q4-2026 hike >10%). 2028-30 should be volume-driven (wafer area ~4-6x 2026) with blended ASP falling 10-35% as JX, Sumitomo, AXT and Chinese capacity lands. Over 2026-2030, volume is more than 100% of growth and price is a drag after 2027, so the shortage-price slice is not durable.
math: AXT 2026 InP: Q1 $13.6M + Q2 $30.7M + Q3 ~$45-50M (inside ~$66M of permitted Q3 revenue) + Q4 ~$55-60M (~$60M per quarter InP capacity by YE26) = ~$145-165M. AXT share 25-36% per secondary sources (one outlier 12%) -> merchant market $0.4-0.65B. Unit cross-check: 0.6-0.75M wafers effective capacity (single source) x blended $500-900 per 3-inch-equivalent (China 3-inch ~RMB3,200 = ~$450; export and 4-inch higher; own est.) = $0.3-0.7B. 2030: area supply ~4-6x (JX 7-10x FY25 by FY30; Sumitomo 3.1x FY24 by FY28; AXT ~2x+ by 2027; Yunnan Germanium 150k -> 450k 4-inch-eq by 2H27) x ASP -10% to -35% = $1.2-2.2B.
catalyst_timing: Q4-2026: >10% price hike (largest on record). 2026-2031: AXT LTAs (Lumentum minimum capacity commitments to Dec-2031, Coherent prepayment, Casela 2027 offtake). FY2028: Sumitomo 3.1x capacity complete. 2H27: Yunnan Germanium 450k-wafer capacity. By FY2030: JX 7-10x. Ongoing: China export-permit flow (indium compounds remain controlled; excluded from the Nov-2025 truce per secondary source). 2027-28: 6-inch InP ramps at Coherent.
key_suppliers: Sumitomo Electric (5802.T, Japan) est. 35-45%; AXT / Beijing Tongmei (AXTI, Nasdaq; production in China) est. 25-36%; JX Advanced Metals (5016.T, Japan) est. 10-15%; Chinese others est. 10-15%: Yunnan Germanium / Yunnan Xinyao (002428.SZ), Vital Advanced Materials (private), others. Shares from secondary sources and own estimates; they conflict (42/36/13 in one retail source).
supply_tightness: Severe through 2027. Single-source estimate of 2026 demand at 2.6-3.0M wafers vs 0.6-0.75M effective capacity (unverified); AXT and Sumitomo backlogs each >$100M; crystal-growth (VGF/VB) yield limits; expansion cycles 18-36 months; 6-inch is much harder than 3/4-inch; customers paying deposits (Lumentum $43.5M + $43.5M, Coherent $22.3M); export permits restrict AXT's China-made supply to non-China customers (North America ~1% of AXT Q1 revenue).
substitution_risk: Medium: SiPh needs fewer InP lasers per Gb/s than EML (one CW laser feeds 4-8 lanes); larger wafers (6-inch) and InP-on-GaAs/Si templates (Fraunhofer 150 mm InP-on-GaAs) cut substrate area per die; GaAs VCSEL/microLED for very short reach. Demand per Tb/s falls even as total volume rises.
cyclicality_risk: High. A classic overbuild setup: JX 7-10x, Sumitomo 3.1x, AXT 2x+, Yunnan Germanium 3x and other Chinese entrants all land in 2027-2029 as customers stockpile under export-control fears. A price reversal in 2028-29 is likely, and part of 2026 demand is safety stock.
faster_sub_niche: 4-inch and 6-inch substrates grow faster than 2/3-inch (6-inch rises from near zero as Coherent and others move to 6-inch InP fabs), but 6-inch output is partly captive and unsized (unverified). The merchant total is kept; note that the price-driven share of 2026-27 growth is the least durable part.

name: Wafer-level and optical-engine opto-electrical (OE) test and burn-in equipment for SiPh PICs and CPO
definition: IN: production test and burn-in tools built for photonic devices at wafer/die/engine level: double-sided OE wafer probers and optical probe cards, PIC wafer-level burn-in (e.g., Aehr FOX-XP), CPO optical-engine test (Insertion 3) and system/module optical-I/O test cells (Insertion 4-O/E), high-power sockets and alignment software. OUT: module-level BERT/oscilloscope instruments, general logic ATE, laser-die burn-in/LIV testers for pluggable supply chains (larger, slower, more cyclical sibling).
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> networking -> optical interconnect manufacturing -> photonic device production test -> SiPh/CPO wafer-level and engine-level OE test and burn-in
also_serves_megatrends: AI optics capacity build (SiPh pluggables and CPO)
FMCW LiDAR / photonic sensing and quantum photonics wafers
size_2026_usd: $0.15-0.35B (own estimate; FormFactor CPO >$20M, Chroma CPO starting, Aehr SiPh tens of $M, MPI/ficonTEC/Keysight/Teradyne unverified)
volume_vs_price: ~70% volume (tester count tracks PIC wafers and engines), ~30% content/price (more channels per PIC, double-sided probing, burn-in added per wafer, sub-second alignment software). Equipment demand follows capacity additions rather than unit shipments, so growth is lumpy.
math: Tester-hours: TSMC alone at 25k wpm x 648 dies = ~194M PICs/yr; at ~100 s per full PIC test (TrendForce) = ~5.4M tester-hours = ~620 tester-years at 100% utilization, or ~1,000 test cells at 60% utilization; at $0.5-1.5M per cell = $0.5-1.5B of installed base for TSMC-linked PICs alone, before Tower/GF wafers, CPO engine test (Insertion 3/4) and wafer burn-in. Spread over 2026-2029 builds plus replacement and engine test -> ~$1-2.5B/yr by 2030 (own estimate). Supplier anchors: FormFactor CPO >$20M in 2026; Citi sees Chroma photonics revenue NT$7.7B (2026) -> NT$25.4B (2027), which includes transceiver test (so an upper bound for the CPO-specific slice).
catalyst_timing: 2H26: TSMC COUPE ramp; Chroma ships Insertion 4-O tools and runs an Nvidia CPO pilot; FormFactor raises CPO outlook. 1H27: Aehr follow-on SiPh burn-in systems ship. 2027: TrendForce calls 2027 the pivotal year for converging CPO test architectures. 2028: scale-up CPO and TSMC 25k wpm drive the next tool wave.
key_suppliers: FormFactor (FORM, US; OE probe systems), Chroma ATE (2360.TW; CPO Insertion 3/4 test), MPI Corp (6223.TWO; CPO tools qualified at 3-4 customers), Aehr Test Systems (AEHR; SiPh wafer-level burn-in), ficonTEC (private, Germany), Keysight (KEYS), Teradyne (TER, via Quantifi Photonics), Advantest (6857.T), Hon Precision (Taiwan), Lianxun Instruments (688808.SS). Shares unverified; Taiwan vendors are closest to TSMC COUPE.
supply_tightness: Moderate. TrendForce says dynamic optical wafer burn-in and high-power module sockets are still missing and test/DFT standards lag; PIC test still exceeds 100 s, so throughput is the bottleneck. Few vendors have nm-level optical probing qualified at TSMC/Nvidia, but tool capacity can scale faster than InP fabs, so pricing power is moderate.
substitution_risk: Medium: faster parallel optical probing and on-chip monitors (design-for-test) cut tester counts; fabs may skip Insertion 2 in early ramps (DigiTimes); TSMC/Nvidia may build in-house test cells.
cyclicality_risk: High. This is capex equipment: CPO timing slips or a 2028 capacity overshoot would cut orders sharply, and the 2027 spike (Citi: Chroma photonics ~3x) is unlikely to repeat every year.
faster_sub_niche: Split: (a) laser-die burn-in/LIV and module test for pluggables, ~$1-2B in 2026 (Lianxun H1-26 revenue RMB1.53B, +209%; Chroma photonics), growth likely 10-25% after the 2026-27 build with high cyclicality; (b) SiPh/CPO wafer- and engine-level OE test and burn-in, analyzed here, at 35-80%.

name: 800G / 1.6T ZR/ZR+ coherent pluggables for AI scale-across DCI
definition: IN: 800ZR/800ZR+ and, from 2027-28, 1600ZR/ZR+ coherent DWDM pluggable modules (QSFP-DD/OSFP) used by hyperscalers for IP-over-DWDM data-center interconnect and multi-site AI 'scale-across' links (~100-1,000+ km). OUT: 400ZR (maturing), chassis transponders (e.g., WL6e line cards), open line systems/amplifiers, intra-DC IMDD optics.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> networking -> optical interconnect -> inter-DC / scale-across links -> coherent DWDM pluggables -> 800G/1.6T ZR/ZR+ modules
also_serves_megatrends: Cloud DCI and regional/sovereign data-center clusters
size_2026_usd: $1.1-1.5B (third-party estimate: Cignal 800ZR+ ~$1B in 2026 plus 800ZR)
size_2030_usd: $3.5-5.5B (own estimate within Cignal's $7.5B 2030 WDM pluggable total)
volume_vs_price: ~70-80% volume (units from ~0.2-0.25M in 2026 to ~0.8-1.2M by 2030, own est.), ~20-30% mix (800G -> 1.6T, high-power ZR+, L-band). Price per bit falls ~15-20%/yr; module ASP roughly flat with generation upgrades.
math: 2026: ~200-250k units (Cignal: >200k, STALE 2025) x ~$4-6k ASP (own est.) = $0.8-1.5B, consistent with Cignal's 800ZR+ ~$1B. 2030: Cignal WDM pluggables $7.5B, of which cloud/colo $6.1B; 800G/1.6T ZR+ class at ~55-75% of cloud = $3.4-4.6B; plus telco use -> $3.5-5.5B. Supplier check: Ciena coherent pluggable revenue (incl. WL6 Nano 800ZR) roughly doubled YoY in FQ3-26.
catalyst_timing: 2026: 800ZR+ large-scale rollout (Meta first, other hyperscalers following); Cisco-Acacia and Arycs begin shipping mid-2026. 2027: 1600ZRx arrives (OIF 1600ZR IA released). 2028-30: 1600ZRx becomes the largest module category (Cignal). Lumentum pump lasers (amplified scale-across lines) up ~4x over the next several quarters.
key_suppliers: Ciena (CIEN; WL6 Nano), Cisco/Acacia (CSCO), Marvell (MRVL; COLORZ and coherent DSPs), Coherent (COHR), Nokia/Infinera (NOK; ICE-X), Lumentum (LITE), Arycs (new), Chinese module makers (Innolight 300308.SZ, others). Coherent DSP supply concentrated in Marvell, Acacia, Ciena, Nokia. Shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Moderately tight: coherent DSPs at 3 nm from four sources, narrow-linewidth tunable lasers and coherent modulators (InP/SiPh/TFLN) constrained; Ciena says backlog conversion ($8.5B backlog) is limited by component supply and FY27 growth of >=30% is 'contingent upon component supply'.
substitution_risk: Low to medium: 800G LR/ER IMDD for <40 km; chassis transponders still win >1,000 km; 'coherent-lite' could take campus links; hollow-core fiber changes latency, not modules.
cyclicality_risk: Medium: hyperscaler capex timing and concentration (Meta first), Chinese module price competition, and 800G-to-1.6T generation air pockets in 2027-28.
faster_sub_niche: 800ZR+ (high-power, Open ROADM-compatible) grows fastest in 2026-27 (~$100M -> ~$1B), then 1600ZR/ZR+ in 2028-30. A related bottleneck, 980 nm pump lasers for scale-across amplifiers (Lumentum sold out, ~4x shipment growth expected), could grow faster still but its size is unverified.

name: CPO fiber-to-chip connectivity (FAU harnesses, detachable PIC connectors, ELS PM jumpers, internal shuffles)
definition: IN: passive precision fiber subassemblies specific to CPO/NPO: fiber array units and FAU harnesses bonded to SiPh optical engines, detachable PIC connectors (Senko MPC, US Conec/3M EBO, Corning detachable FAU), polarization-maintaining jumpers between ELS and engines, internal fiber shuffles/cassettes and front-plate high-density connectors. OUT: FAUs inside pluggable transceivers (mature), structured cabling and MPO trunks, bare fiber.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> networking -> optical interconnect -> CPO/NPO switches -> optical engine packaging -> fiber-to-chip connectivity subassemblies
also_serves_megatrends: XPU scale-up optical I/O from 2028 (much higher fiber counts per rack)
size_2026_usd: $0.05-0.15B (own estimate; emerging, near the $50M emerging threshold)
volume_vs_price: ~85-90% volume (switches and later XPUs shipped); content per system rises with fiber count (more engines, more lanes per engine, PM fibers per ELS). Per-unit ASP falls as yields improve; FAU alignment/reliability yield is the near-term price support.
math: Per Nvidia SN6810-class switch: 32 optical engines (Citi model) x 1 FAU harness at $80-200 + 16 ELS x PM jumpers at $30-60 + internal shuffle/cassettes and front-plate connectors at $1-3k = ~$4-10k per switch (own estimate, unverified). 2026: 15-20k switches -> $0.06-0.2B (haircut -> $0.05-0.15B). 2027: ~100-200k switch-equivalents (GF Securities; Morgan Stanley engine estimate) -> $0.4-1.0B. 2030: CPO at ~35% of AI DC optical modules (TrendForce) plus scale-up -> $1-3B.
catalyst_timing: 3Q26: FOCI 1.6T CPO FAU mass production. 2H26: Nvidia Spectrum-X Photonics ramp; TFC CPO FAU/ELS products in stable delivery. 2027-28: FOCI-planned large-scale ramp with an international customer; CPO volume ramp. 2028+: scale-up CPO multiplies fiber counts.
key_suppliers: Corning (GLW, US; harnesses for Broadcom Bailly, Nvidia SiPh ecosystem partner), TFC Optical (300394.SZ, China; FAU/ELS for CPO), FOCI Fiber Optic Communications (3363.TWO, Taiwan; TSMC-linked FAU), Browave (3163.TWO, Taiwan), Senko (private, Japan), US Conec (private, US), Sumitomo Electric (5802.T), Fujikura (5803.T). Shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Moderate to tight: sub-micron FAU alignment and reflow-compatible detachable interfaces have few qualified suppliers; Corning says demand for high-density optical products exceeds its capacity and is spending ~$2B of 2026 capex on Optical Communications; TrendForce names optical engine yield and thermals as bottlenecks.
substitution_risk: Medium: alternative coupling (grating/edge couplers with glass waveguides, expanded-beam) may shift value between vendors; vertical integration by engine makers (TSMC, Nvidia partners) could capture FAU assembly; microLED/copper for short reach.
cyclicality_risk: High timing risk tied to CPO yields and ramp; Chinese suppliers (TFC and others) under US tariff/export scrutiny, which could reshuffle sourcing.
faster_sub_niche: Detachable PIC connectors and PM-fiber ELS jumpers likely grow faster than fixed FAU harnesses, because serviceability pushes designs toward detachable interfaces, but no sizing data exists (unverified).

name: AC-to-800 VDC (and +/-400 VDC) power-conversion equipment for AI racks: row-level power sidecars/power racks, centralised rectifiers, later SSTs (excluding battery/supercap storage and on-tray DC-DC)
definition: IN: equipment that converts facility AC (480/415 VAC or MV) to an 800 VDC or +/-400 VDC bus feeding AI racks: row-level 'sidecar' power racks (rectifier sections only), centralised MV/LV-to-DC rectifier skids, MV solid-state transformers sold for DC use, and the DC protection/distribution sold with them. OUT: BBU/supercap storage inside sidecars (scored as C2), PSUs inside 48/50 V power shelves, on-tray 800->12 V DC-DC converters, the power semis inside (counted in the system price).
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> power delivery -> facility power distribution -> DC distribution architecture (800 VDC / +/-400 VDC) -> AC-to-DC conversion equipment (sidecars/power racks -> centralised rectifiers -> SSTs)
size_2026_usd: $0.1-0.35B (own estimate; Delta's 800V + +/-400V power cabinets are <1% of its 2026 revenue per institutional investors, plus first shipments from Vertiv, Eaton, Lite-On, ABB)
size_2030_usd: $4-9B (own estimate built on Citi's 25+ GW/yr of new 800 VDC capacity in 2030 x $0.15-0.35M per MW for conversion)
cagr_2026_2030: 80-180% (central ~120%; very wide because the 2026 base is tiny)
volume_vs_price: Almost all volume and adoption. 800 VDC goes from ~0 to 16% of new capacity in 2027 and 79% in 2030 (Citi). ASP per MW should fall 30-50% from 2027 to 2030 as sidecars (~$400-500K each, ~$0.5M/MW including storage per SemiAnalysis) give way to centralised rectifiers and SSTs, and as Chinese vendors (Sungrow, Kehua, Megmeet) qualify. Early pricing is a first-of-kind premium, not shortage pricing.
math: Top-down 2030: 25 GW/yr new 800 VDC capacity (Citi) x $0.15-0.35M/MW for conversion only = $3.8-8.8B. The per-MW figure is my estimate: the SemiAnalysis sidecar runs ~$0.5M/MW including BBU/supercaps; I assume conversion is 40-60% of that, then a 30-50% cost-down by 2030. Cross-checks: SemiAnalysis sees ~39 GW of 800 VDC-covered increments by 2030 (different scope, upside). Industrial Securities' 2030 'off-cabinet power' TAM of RMB271B (~$38B, incl. SST RMB176B) looks like an aggressive ceiling. Bottom-up 2026: Delta 2026 revenue ~NT$650-750B x <1% = <NT$7B (~$0.2B), plus <$0.1B from all other vendors = $0.1-0.35B. CAGR: (3.8/0.35)^0.25-1 = 81%; (8.8/0.15)^0.25-1 = 177%.
catalyst_timing: Delta: +/-400V shipping in 2026, 800V in mass production Q3 2026 with small Q4 2026 shipments and main contribution in 2027 (Apr-30-2026 call). Vertiv 800 VDC portfolio available H2 2026. Lite-On MW-class 800 VDC cabinets in volume from Q1 2027 (press). NVIDIA Kyber / Rubin Ultra in 2H27. TrendForce sees large-scale adoption in 2028. Citi: sidecar retrofits peak 2027-28, SST-native builds from 2029. Downside: market rumours of mass adoption slipping to 2028; KGI says VR200 does not need HVDC.
key_suppliers: Delta Electronics (2308.TW): leader, est. 35-50% of 2026-27 NVIDIA-ecosystem DC power-rack shipments (own estimate, unverified; KGI puts Delta at 60-65% of AI server PSUs). Vertiv (VRT), Eaton (ETN; MV SST reportedly 2 MW at >97% efficiency), Lite-On (2301.TW), Schneider Electric (SU.PA), ABB (ABBN.SW), Siemens (SIE.DE), Flex (FLEX). China: Sungrow (300274.SZ; 3 MW MV-to-800 VDC SST launched July 2026), Kehua Data (002335.SZ), Megmeet (002851.SZ), Zhongheng (002364.SZ). Start-ups: DG Matrix (raised $60M), Amperesand, Heron Power. Device suppliers: Infineon, onsemi, ST, Wolfspeed, Navitas.
supply_tightness: Moderate. The bottleneck is qualification (NVIDIA MGX/OCP reference designs, UL/IEC DC safety, hyperscaler site acceptance) and DC protection gear (solid-state/hybrid DC breakers), not semiconductors: SiC is in oversupply. Few vendors are qualified for 2026-27 programmes (Delta, Vertiv, Lite-On, Eaton). Lead times unverified.
substitution_risk: Medium-high. (1) +/-400 VDC (Mt Diablo / OCP, Google/Meta/Microsoft) versus 800 VDC: this niche is defined to include both, so the risk is mix, not loss. (2) AC + 50 V busbar may last longer (VR200 does not require HVDC). (3) Sidecars may be skipped for centralised rectifiers or SSTs, which shifts share to grid-equipment majors (ABB, Siemens, Hitachi Energy, Eaton) away from Taiwanese rack-power ODMs.
cyclicality_risk: Tied to AI capex timing; the architecture change is one-way, but first-generation sidecar volumes may be lumpy (peak 2027-28, then cannibalised by SSTs). Chinese capacity (Sungrow, Kehua and others) could compress pricing after 2028.
faster_sub_niche: MV solid-state transformers are the fastest piece (Citi: 901 MVA in 2027 to 37,152 MVA in 2030, roughly 240% CAGR 2027-30). Volume inflects only in 2029, so they are listed under too_early and the analysis keeps the whole AC-to-800 VDC conversion niche.

name: High-voltage (+/-400 V / 800 V) lithium-ion BBU modules for AI power racks and sidecars (sub-niche of rack-level BBU)
definition: IN: Li-ion battery backup modules plus BMS, built into +/-400 VDC or 800 VDC power racks or row-level sidecars, that provide ride-through (seconds to minutes) and help smooth GPU load. OUT: 48/50 V ORv3-style BBU shelves (parent market, slower); central facility UPS batteries; facility-scale BESS; supercapacitor/LIC shelves.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> power delivery -> rack power -> rack/row energy storage -> lithium-ion BBU -> high-voltage (400/800 V) BBU modules
also_serves_megatrends: grid/C&I BESS (same high-rate cells and BMS)
size_2026_usd: HV BBU: <$0.1B, emerging (own estimate; mass production only from 2H26). Parent rack-BBU market (all voltages): $0.9-1.5B (own estimate from supplier revenues).
size_2030_usd: HV BBU: $0.75-4B (own estimate). Parent rack-BBU: $3-6B (own estimate).
cagr_2026_2030: HV BBU: 70-150%+ from a near-zero base. Parent rack-BBU: 20-40%.
volume_vs_price: Mostly volume: BBU replaces central UPS in 800 VDC racks (AES-KY: 'irreversible'). Content per pack rises (5.5 kW in 2025 -> 12 kW in 2026 -> ~22 kW in 2027), and kWh per MW rises with longer hold-up and load-smoothing duty. $/kWh falls with cell prices, so ASP per MW is roughly flat to up. The parent 48 V market is already decelerating: AES-KY 9M-2026 revenue is +26% vs +59% in 2025, which points to price competition.
math: Parent 2026, supplier sum: AES-KY 2026E revenue ~NT$19-20B (9M = NT$14.57B) x 75-80% BBU = NT$14.5-16B (~$0.45-0.5B). Dynapack BBU >NT$5B (~$0.16B). Delta, Lite-On, Simplo and Chinese pack makers ~$0.3-0.8B. Total ~$0.9-1.5B. HV 2030 top-down: 25 GW/yr new 800 VDC capacity (Citi) x 60-90% BBU attach x $50-180K/MW = $0.75-4B. The $/MW figure is my estimate: 30 s-5 min hold-up is ~8-80 kWh/MW, at ~$1,000-2,500/kWh for module + BMS + enclosure; unverified. CAGR from a $0.05-0.1B 2026 base is >70%.
catalyst_timing: AES-KY: 400/800 VDC HV BBU mass production from 2H26 to early 2027, with HVDC lines expanded in 2026 for 2H26-2027 demand. Dynapack HV BBU in volume from 2027 (Q4 2026 at the earliest). Lite-On BBU customers go from 2 to 3. 800 VDC scale-up follows Rubin Ultra/Kyber in 2H27-2028.
key_suppliers: AES-KY (6781.TW): co-developer with Delta and a US CSP, leader in HV, est. 30-40% of 2025-26 rack-BBU modules (own estimate). Dynapack (3211.TW) ~10-15%. Simplo (6121.TW). Delta (2308.TW) and Lite-On (2301.TW) integrate BBUs into power racks. Vertiv and Eaton integrate their own storage in sidecars. Cells: Murata (6981.T), Samsung SDI (006400.KS), LG Energy Solution (373220.KS), Panasonic (6752.T), EVE (300014.SZ). Shares are unverified.
supply_tightness: Moderate. Hyperscaler qualification is 12-18 months, and high-rate cell qualification (UL 9540A, thermal-runaway propagation) limits the field to a handful of Taiwanese pack makers. Cell supply itself is ample (global Li-ion overcapacity). AES-KY 2026 capex was guided +20-30% with large HVDC line expansion.
substitution_risk: Medium. (1) Storage may be centralised at row/facility level in Vertiv, Eaton or Schneider sidecars with their own batteries, bypassing Taiwanese BBU makers. (2) Facility BESS plus a grid-forming UPS could replace rack ride-through. (3) LIC/supercaps handle millisecond-scale smoothing but not minutes of hold-up.
cyclicality_risk: Chinese pack makers and cell-price deflation could compress margins. Revenue is tied to AI rack builds. HV timing depends on 800 VDC adoption (see C1).
faster_sub_niche: This entry is already the faster split. 48/50 V shelf BBUs (the bulk of 2026's $0.9-1.5B) grow more slowly, ~15-30%, and AES-KY's 2026 growth has slowed to ~26%.

name: Vertical (backside) power-delivery modules for AI accelerator core rails
definition: IN: integrated power modules (power stages + inductors/magnetics + caps in one module) mounted on the PCB directly under or behind the GPU/ASIC package to deliver core current vertically, at 48 V-input or 12 V-input (e.g., MPS 48 V vertical modules, Infineon TDM2454xx, Vicor VPD, Delta/Cyntec VPD on Infineon silicon, Flex VPD). OUT: discrete lateral multiphase VR (controllers, DrMOS, TLVR inductors), in-package IVRs, PSUs and intermediate bus converters.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> power delivery -> board/package power -> accelerator core voltage regulation -> integrated power modules -> vertical (backside) power-delivery modules
also_serves_megatrends: high-end server CPUs and switch ASICs
size_2026_usd: $0.3-0.8B for vertical modules (own estimate, low confidence). All integrated modules (lateral + vertical): ~$0.6-1.5B (own estimate). Total AI accelerator power ICs + modules: $4-7B (own estimate; MPS Enterprise Data alone >= $1.6B in 2026).
volume_vs_price: Roughly half content, half units. Core current per package roughly doubles: Rubin ~1.8-2.3 kW at ~0.7-0.8 V is ~2,500-3,000 A; Rubin Ultra / 3 kW-class AMD parts are ~4,000-5,000 A. Lateral PDN losses push the 3 kW+ class to vertical, and accelerator units roughly double 2026-2030. Module $/A falls ~5-10%/yr.
math: Units x attach x content. 2026: ~10-15M accelerator packages (own estimate) x 8-15% vertical attach x $250-500 per package = $0.2-1.1B, taken as $0.3-0.8B. 2030: ~20-30M packages x 45-65% attach x $400-800 = $3.6-15B; I use $3-8B conservatively for price-down and IVR substitution. Content uses ~$0.12-0.25 per amp of module capacity (e.g., a 280 A quad-phase module at ~$35-60), own estimate, unverified. Supplier cross-check: MPS Enterprise Data $701.8M (2025) -> >= $1.61B (2026, +130% floor), and MPS says module content is a growing share. Vicor advanced products $94.2M in Q2 2026 (+45% q/q). Infineon AI data-centre power ~EUR1.5B (FY26) -> ~EUR2.5B (FY27), including PSU devices.
catalyst_timing: Shipping now: MPS 48 V vertical power to 'more than a couple' of customers (Q2 2026 call). Vicor second-generation VPD demos to OEMs and hyperscalers in 2026. Rubin Ultra (~3.6 kW) mass production 2H27; AMD validating VPD for 3 kW-class parts. Feynman and next-generation TPU/Trainium in 2028.
key_suppliers: MPS (MPWR): likely leader in GPU modules, est. 30-45% of AI module dollars (own estimate). Infineon (IFX.DE) 15-25%; ships PCB-VPD modules since 2024, bought C2i. Vicor (VICR) 5-10%; needs a second fab for its $2.5B target. Delta/Cyntec (2308.TW) on Infineon OptiMOS. Renesas (6723.T), TI (TXN), Flex (FLEX), AOS (AOSL), Empower Semiconductor (private). Murata (6981.T) starts DC power-module mass production in 2026. Magnetics: TDK (6762.T), Murata, Cyntec, Chilisin/Yageo (2327.TW). Shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Tight on qualification, not wafers. Each accelerator platform needs a 12-24 month co-design (PCB stack-up, embedded caps, thermals under the socket), so 2-4 suppliers per platform. MPS expanded foundry capacity (GlobalFoundries deal) and raised its capacity goal beyond $6B. Vicor is fab-constrained. Pricing power is evident in margins (Vicor GM ~58%).
substitution_risk: Medium. (1) Discrete lateral VR (DrMOS + TLVR) stays on many ASICs below ~2 kW. (2) In-package IVRs (TSMC/Empower style) could take the last-mm stage after 2028. (3) 800 V architectures could change the intermediate bus (800 -> 12/6 V) and how much current must be delivered vertically.
cyclicality_risk: High near-term. MPS's +130% Enterprise Data growth floor likely includes channel and inventory build for the VR200 ramp (double-ordering risk). Supplier share swings per platform are large (MPS lost and regained NVIDIA share in 2024-25).
faster_sub_niche: Split: vertical modules (this entry, ~45-90%) vs discrete lateral power stages + controllers + TLVR inductors (~20-30%, under price pressure). Kept vertical.

name: SOFC power systems for data-centre behind-the-meter prime power
definition: IN: solid-oxide fuel cell systems (stacks + balance of plant, installation, service) sold for data-centre prime or bridge power, in system sales, PPAs or leases. OUT: SOFC for non-DC commercial and industrial use, utilities and microgrids (same factories; counted only in notes); PEM/MCFC backup; SOEC electrolysers.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> power delivery -> power generation (BTM) -> fuel cells -> solid-oxide fuel cell systems for DC prime power
also_serves_megatrends: C&I and utility distributed generation (AEP 1 GW deal)
hydrogen economy (SOEC with same cell technology)
size_2026_usd: $2.5-3.5B DC-related (own estimate: ~65-85% of Bloom's guided $3.9-4.2B 2026 revenue). Total SOFC ~$4.0-4.3B (company guidance plus small Doosan/Ceres licensees).
volume_vs_price: ~85-90% volume (MW shipped); ASP per kW flat to slightly down as Bloom cuts cost. Margin expansion (non-GAAP GM 34.3% in Q2 2026, +6 pts y/y) suggests time-to-power pricing power, not shortage pricing.
math: 2026: guidance $3.9-4.2B x ~85-88% product + install = $3.3-3.7B; x 65-85% DC share (own estimate) = $2.2-3.1B, plus DC service, so ~$2.5-3.5B. Implied 2026 shipments ~1.0-1.2 GW at ~$2,800-3,800/kW product ASP (own estimate; Bloom does not disclose $/kW). 2030: 4-6 GW/yr (Fremont can host ~5 GW run-rate per the 10-K; RBC sees demand >4 GW in 2028) x $2,600-3,200/kW x 70-80% DC share, plus service = $7-15B. Consensus 2027 revenue ~$6.8B (+65%) is consistent. CAGR (10/3)^0.25-1 = 35%.
catalyst_timing: Fremont 1 -> 2 GW by end-2026, fully used in 2027. Each further +1 GW takes 6-9 months and $100-150M capex (10-K). RBC (Apr 2026): air permit received to scale towards 5 GW. Oracle MSA up to 2.8 GW (1.2 GW contracted); Brookfield financing framework ($5B, reportedly expanded); AEP. 2029-30 risk: grid interconnection and frame CCGTs catch up.
key_suppliers: Bloom Energy (BE): ~90%+ of DC fuel-cell deployments (company claims a 'high-90s' DC share among fuel cells). Doosan Fuel Cell (336260.KS): 50 MW/yr SOFC plant on a Ceres licence. Ceres Power (CWR.L): licensor to Doosan, Delta and Shell. Mitsubishi Heavy (7011.T): small. Effectively a single-supplier niche.
supply_tightness: Factory capacity is not binding: Bloom says capacity is not a constraint, and it adds U.S. capacity in 'copy exact' increments ahead of orders. Possible material bottleneck in scandium oxide: Hunterbrook claims 5 GW/yr needs ~220 t vs ~240 t global supply; Bloom says it has visibility for 25 GW/yr and is not China-dependent (contested, unresolved). The real moat is that hyperscalers have validated a single vendor, plus permitting ease (low NOx).
substitution_risk: High medium-term. Gas recips (~$1,500/kW installed) and aeroderivatives are cheaper per kW. The grid catches up after 2028-29 (Wood Mackenzie: gas-equipment lead times start falling by 2027). Nuclear PPAs come after 2030. Customers can mix technologies on a site.
cyclicality_risk: BTM 'bridge' demand is front-loaded (2025-2028) and financing-dependent (Brookfield). The July 2026 short report (supply-chain claims) shows how sensitive the stock is to execution. A single-vendor niche means company-specific risk equals niche risk.

name: High-capacitance, low-voltage MLCCs for AI server/accelerator power-delivery networks
definition: IN: MLCCs of roughly 10-100+ uF (focus 47 uF+) in 0201-1210, X5R/X6S/X7R at 2.5-6.3 V (plus some 16-25 V for 12/48 V rails), sold into AI accelerator boards, AI server motherboards, switch trays and AI PSUs/power modules. OUT: general-purpose/consumer MLCCs, automotive high-voltage MLCCs, tantalum/polymer and silicon capacitors.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> power delivery -> board/package power -> passives for the power-delivery network -> MLCCs -> high-capacitance low-voltage MLCCs (47 uF-class)
size_2026_usd: $1.0-2.5B (own estimate, low confidence)
volume_vs_price: 2026-27: an estimated 30-40% of revenue growth is price and mix: Taiyo Yuden list +6-13% (Apr 2026), SEMCO +30% to its China channel (Aug 2026), Huaqiangbei spot for AI high-cap +50-60%, and AI-server MLCC ASP is 8-10x generic. That part is shortage pricing and not durable. 2028-30: mostly volume. MLCCs per rack go ~320K (GB300) -> ~570-600K (VR200), the 47 uF+ share rises from <20% to >30%, and Morgan Stanley sees 47 uF+ cloud-AI units going ~4B (2025) -> 40B+ (2027). Expect price normalisation once Murata Izumo and SEMCO capacity land (2027+).
math: Units x ASP: 47 uF+ cloud-AI demand ~15-20B units (2026, interpolated) -> 40B+ (2027) per Morgan Stanley, x ~$0.02-0.06 average (own estimate; per-rack value / count ≈ $0.007-0.02 average across all MLCC values) = $0.3-1.2B for 47 uF+. Adding other high-end AI MLCCs gives $1.0-2.5B in 2026. Rack cross-check: ~60-70K NVL72-equivalent racks x $1.5-4.7K (Morgan Stanley GB300, two versions) = $0.1-0.33B for NVIDIA rack-scale only. ASIC servers (TPU/Trainium/MTIA; TrendForce calls them the main driver), HGX, PSUs and switches are several times that. Supplier cross-check: SEMCO alone signed ~KRW745B (~$0.54B) of AI-server MLCC supply contracts covering through 2027. 2030: per-rack content 2.5-3x GB300 x ~2x AI server units, less 20-30% price normalisation = $3-7B.
catalyst_timing: VR200 ramp 2H26-2027 (MLCC value per rack +166-182% vs GB300). TrendForce flags structural shortage in 2H26. Murata Izumo full capacity 2027. Murata adds ~JPY80B of MLCC capex over FY26-27. SEMCO long-term contracts cover through 2027. Rubin Ultra/Kyber (2H27-2028) raises content again.
key_suppliers: Murata (6981.T): est. 40-50% of high-end AI MLCC (own estimate). Samsung Electro-Mechanics (009150.KS): ~25-35%. Taiyo Yuden (6976.T): ~10-15%. TDK (6762.T) and Kyocera-AVX (6971.T): small. Yageo (2327.TW), Walsin (2492.TW), Fenghua (000636.SZ) and Three-Circle (300408.SZ) lag at the highest capacitance. Guosen describes some high-end specs as close to a Murata-SEMCO duopoly. Shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Very tight. Book-to-bill: Murata 1.30, SEMCO 1.31, Taiyo Yuden 1.25 (post-pandemic highs); Murata's 1.27 orders/backlog exceeds the 2018 shortage peak of 1.25. High-cap X6S lead times stretched from ~8 to ~20 weeks. SEMCO utilisation was 91% in Q1 2026 (off-season) vs 98% in Q3 2025. High-cap needs in-house nano BaTiO3 powder and thin-layer stacking, which takes multi-year know-how; new entrants cannot qualify quickly.
substitution_risk: Low-medium. Silicon capacitors and in-package/embedded caps take some decoupling close to the die. Vertical power modules with embedded capacitor layers (Infineon TDM2454xx) move some MLCC content into modules, though still largely MLCC-based. Polymer caps serve bulk.
cyclicality_risk: High. MLCC is a classic shortage -> double-ordering -> crash market (2018 -> 2019). Huaqiangbei quotes 'updating every 30 minutes' signals speculative channel stocking. Expect a price reset when 2027 capacity lands, even if AI unit volume keeps growing.
faster_sub_niche: 47 uF+ / X6S parts in 0402-0603 grow fastest (10x units 2025 -> 2027 per Morgan Stanley); the 10-22 uF tier grows more slowly. This entry is centred on the faster tier. The general MLCC market is roughly flat in real terms.

name: Liquid-cooling quick disconnects for AI racks (UQD, blind-mate UQB, MQD)
definition: IN: dripless quick-disconnect couplings used at compute/switch tray-to-manifold connections (UQD/UQB, incl. blind-mate), on in-tray cold-plate loops (MQD) and at rack-to-CDU interfaces, for AI racks. OUT: manifolds, hoses, cold plates, CDUs; industrial/hydraulic couplings.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> thermal -> direct-to-chip liquid cooling -> rack-level fluid distribution -> quick-disconnect couplings (UQD/UQB/MQD)
also_serves_megatrends: liquid-cooled power electronics (EV fast chargers, BESS PCS)
liquid-cooled 800 VDC power racks and busbars
size_2026_usd: $0.8-1.5B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: Volume plus pairs per rack, offset by price. Pairs per rack roughly doubled GB200 -> GB300 (~126 -> ~250 per an industry estimate; ~198 -> ~342 in a Chinese consultancy model). VR moves to larger bore (Dash 04 -> Dash 08) and Kyber to blind-mate. But ASP per pair falls ~30% (the consultancy model assumes RMB500 -> RMB350) as Taiwanese and Chinese suppliers enter the RVL. Net value per rack is roughly flat to +20%; growth is mainly rack volume and ASIC liquid-cooling attach.
math: 2026: ~60-70K NVL72-equivalent racks (own estimate, from TrendForce's $710B 2027 NVL72 value at +214%, implying ~$226B in 2026, at ~$3.3-3.8M per rack) x $12-17K QD content per rack (consultancy: 342 pairs x RMB350 ≈ $16.6K; a relayed JPM figure of ~512 QDs ≈ $10.2K for Trainium3, unverified) = $0.7-1.2B. Adding ASIC/HGX/CDU-side QDs ($0.1-0.3B) gives $0.8-1.5B. Cross-checks: a Chinese consultancy put UQD at RMB6.44B (~$0.9B) for 2026 [STALE]; Fositek's server products (QD + rails) were ~NT$4.4B in H1 2026. 2030: racks x2.2-3 (TrendForce +50% in 2027, then +10-20%/yr) x pairs/rack x1.2-1.4 x ASP x0.6-0.75 = x1.6-3.2, i.e. $1.8-4B.
catalyst_timing: VR200 ramp 2H26-2027: rack coolant flow nearly doubles vs GB300 (Kuo) and Morgan Stanley attributes VR cooling content growth to more manifolds and QDs. Kyber blind-mate in 2H27. Liquid-cooling penetration of AI chips goes 33% (2025) -> 53% (2026) -> ~60% (2027) (TrendForce). Fositek adds ~50% QD capacity in Q4 2026.
key_suppliers: Western incumbents: Staubli (private, CH), CPC/Dover (DOV), Parker Hannifin (PH), Danfoss (private), Eaton (ETN), CEJN (private); a secondary estimate gives the top five ~63-73% combined. Taiwan: Fositek (6805.TW, NVIDIA UQD-certified, GB300 first-batch), Lotes (3533.TW), AVC (3017.TW, Vietnam QD/manifold capacity), Auras (3324.TW). China: Envicool (002837.SZ, UQD in NVIDIA MGX ecosystem), Yonggui (300351.SZ), AVIC Jonhon (002179.SZ). Shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Easing. NVIDIA's RVL qualification (leak, pressure-cycle, flow) was the 2024-25 bottleneck, when ~7 suppliers were qualified and two Chinese vendors were capacity-limited. In 2026 capacity is expanding fast: Fositek ~3M pieces/month, +50% in Q4 (analyst estimate); Staubli's Duncan, SC line (Nov 2025); AVC Vietnam. Pricing power is eroding.
substitution_risk: Low for the function: every liquid-cooled tray needs dripless couplings. Medium for specific designs: blind-mate UQB and fewer, larger couplings could reduce pair counts per rack. Micro-channel lids change cold-plate loops but not tray QDs.
cyclicality_risk: Medium-high. Capacity is being added faster than demand (Fositek +50%, AVC, Chinese entrants), so ASP per pair should keep falling. Double-ordering around VR200 transitions is possible.
faster_sub_niche: Blind-mate UQB and large-bore (Dash 08+) couplings for VR/Kyber and rack-to-CDU grow faster (~30-40%) than standard UQD/MQD, which face Chinese price erosion. Data are too thin to size separately.

name: Gas reciprocating gensets (approx. 2-20 MW units) for data-centre prime/bridge power
definition: IN: natural-gas reciprocating engine generator sets (high- and medium-speed, fast-response) and their packaging, sold for behind-the-meter prime or bridge power at data centres, as direct sales or via IPPs/packagers (e.g., VoltaGrid). OUT: diesel standby gensets, gas turbines (aeroderivative/frame), recips for oil and gas, utility peaking or marine; O&M is noted but not sized.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> power delivery -> power generation (BTM) -> modular gas generation -> large-bore gas reciprocating gensets for DC prime/bridge power
also_serves_megatrends: grid balancing for renewables (Wartsila balancing orders)
size_2026_usd: $2-4.5B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: 2025-26 growth carries a price/lead-time premium: Cat's segment profit rose 30% on volume and better pricing, and new large-recip orders deliver late 2027 at the earliest. 2027-30 growth is volume as OEMs add capacity: Cat ~3x 2024 large-recip capacity by 2030, Wartsila 2.2x 2025 output by Q1 2029, Rolls-Royce mtu plant 3 by 2028, Cummins new 130 L gas platform. Pricing likely flat to down once lead times ease (Wood Mackenzie: from 2027).
math: 2026: ~3-5 GW of DC gas-recip deliveries (own estimate). Order evidence: Cat 2 GW Monarch + 1.5 GW Joule (636 x G3520K); INNIO 1.5 GW VoltaGrid (300 engines, delivery by 2028) + 1.1 GW; Wartsila 1.2 GW firm DC orders in Q2 2026 alone. x ~$0.6-0.9M/MW for equipment + package (own estimate; Thunder Said uses ~$1,500/kW installed) = $1.8-4.5B. 2030: 6-12 GW/yr globally (Enverus: 29.6 GW of US gas BTM by 2030, 61% recips/small GT/fuel cells; Jefferies: equipment availability of 19/49/76 GW by 2028/29/30) x $0.55-0.8M/MW = $3.3-9.6B. CAGR (6/3)^0.25-1 = 19%.
catalyst_timing: Cat capacity investment 2027-2029 (payback by end-2030); 10 MW gas platform restart adds 1.5 GW, shipping from Q4 2026. INNIO VoltaGrid deliveries through 2028. Wartsila STH expansion fully commissioned Q1 2029. Rolls-Royce plant 3 done in 2028. Risk: permitting (New Mexico pipeline block on the Stargate 2.45 GW site; NJ air-permit issues).
key_suppliers: Caterpillar (CAT): est. 40-50% of DC gas-recip MW (own estimate). INNIO Jenbacher (private) ~15-25%. Wartsila (WRT1V.HE) ~10-15%. Rolls-Royce Power Systems/mtu (RR.L), Cummins (CMI), Everllence/MAN (VW), Bergen Engines, Kawasaki (7012.T), MHI (7011.T). Packagers/IPPs: VoltaGrid, Aggreko, APR. Shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Tight through 2027. New large-recip orders land late 2027 at the earliest, mostly 2028 (Evercore ISI via press). Rolls-Royce factories 'at capacity limits'. Cummins says growth is capped by large-genset capacity. Cat's backlog is $72.1B (+92% y/y), 59% deliverable within 12 months. Qualification barrier is moderate: fast-response gas engines need DC load-acceptance validation.
substitution_risk: High. SOFC (Bloom) on permitting and emissions; aeroderivatives as their slots free up; grid interconnection after 2028-29; nuclear post-2030. Recips win on lead time (~24 months to COD) and modularity (overbuild ~1.1x vs ~1.5x for frames, per Enverus).
cyclicality_risk: High. Bridge demand is front-loaded; OEMs are tripling capacity just as grid and turbine supply catches up (2028-30), which is classic overbuild risk. Cat says it can redirect capacity to oil and gas and other markets, which limits OEM damage but not niche revenue.
faster_sub_niche: Fast-response large-bore units (>2.5 MW: G3520K, J620/J624, W34SG, mtu 4000 L64) for prime power grow faster than DC diesel standby (~15-20%). Within BTM gas, recips should outgrow aeroderivatives, whose capacity is more constrained and whose growth is more price-driven.

name: HBM logic base dies made on foundry logic nodes (HBM4/HBM4E/HBM5, incl. custom cHBM base dies)
definition: IN: the bottom interface/logic die of HBM4, HBM4E and HBM5 stacks when it is made on a foundry logic process. Nodes: TSMC N12FFC+/N5/N3P/N2 and Samsung Foundry SF4/SF2, with Intel Foundry possible later. These dies are sold as wafers or dies to SK hynix and Micron, or made captively at Samsung. Also IN: the design/NRE layer for custom base dies (controller, PHY, near-memory logic) supplied by ASIC houses. Measured as base-die value at the foundry level plus custom-design revenue. OUT: DRAM core dies; HBM3E-and-earlier base dies made on DRAM processes; interposers and LSI bridges; the stack revenue the DRAM makers earn.
value_chain_path: AI accelerators -> memory subsystem -> HBM stack -> HBM4-generation base (logic) die -> foundry-made base die (standard N12 -> custom N3P/N2)
also_serves_megatrends: leading-edge foundry utilisation (N3/N2 demand beyond compute dies)
size_2026_usd: $0.3-1.0B (own estimate; foundry-level die value. About 65-80% is external TSMC revenue; the rest is Samsung captive)
size_2030_usd: $5-16B (own estimate); the external, non-captive share is about $3-12B
volume_vs_price: About 75-80% volume/adoption and 20-25% content/ASP. Units rise roughly 8-10x for two reasons. (a) The share of HBM stacks with a foundry-made base die goes from ~15-25% in 2026 (only the HBM4 ramp; Micron's HBM4 base die is still in-house) to ~95% by 2030, when all HBM4E/HBM5 use logic processes. (b) HBM stack count roughly doubles or triples (Rubin Ultra-class packages carry 16 stacks vs 8). ASP per base die rises ~1.5-2x as N12 gives way to custom N3P/N2 dies. This is not shortage pricing: it comes from node migration and customisation, so it is durable. The main pricing risk is TSMC cost pressure, the reason SK hynix is reportedly weighing Intel.
math: TOP-DOWN 2026: TrendForce puts HBM at ~9% of DRAM bits -> ~3.2-3.6 EB (own conversion). Divided by a ~34 GB average stack -> ~95-105M stacks. HBM4 is ~20-30% of those -> 20-32M stacks. Foundry-made share 70-85% (SK hynix uses TSMC N12, Samsung uses its own SF4, Micron makes HBM4 base dies in-house) -> 15-27M dies. Die value: ~100-120 mm2 on N12, wafer ~$4-5k, ~450 good dies -> ~$10-15 raw. Add KGD test and margin, and anchor on Herald's estimate that the base die costs 3-4x a 1b core die -> $20-35 per die (own). Result: 15-27M x $20-35 = $0.3-0.95B. 2030: TrendForce puts HBM at 13% of DRAM bits in 2027; growing 25-35%/yr after that gives 11-14 EB. Divided by 48-64 GB average stacks -> 175-290M stacks; x95% foundry base -> 165-275M dies. Blended $30-60 per die: a mix of standard N5/N12 and custom N3P/N2. N3-class wafers cost ~$18-22k and yield ~400-500 good dies, i.e. $36-55 per die before the custom premium. Result: $5-16.5B. CAGR: (5/1.0)^0.25-1 = 50% at the low end; central (9/0.6)^0.25-1 = 97%; stated as 50-110%. CROSS-CHECK: 165-275M dies / ~450 per wafer = 0.37-0.6M wafers/yr (30-50k wpm), a few percent of TSMC leading-edge output, so plausible.
catalyst_timing: 2H26: HBM4 with TSMC N12 base die ramps on Nvidia Rubin. 2027: HBM4E standard and custom base dies on TSMC N3P (Micron moves to TSMC; TSMC C-HBM4E); Rubin Ultra doubles stacks per package. 2028: Intel Foundry possible as a second source for SK hynix HBM4E base dies. 2029-30: HBM5 base dies carry more logic (near-memory compute) on N3/N2.
key_suppliers: TSMC (2330.TW / TSM): est. 65-80% of 2026 foundry base dies and the only external source at scale. Samsung Foundry (005930.KS): est. 20-30%, captive for Samsung HBM4 on SF4. Intel Foundry (INTC): 0% today, reportedly evaluated by SK hynix for HBM4E. Buyers: SK hynix (000660.KS), Micron (MU). Custom base-die design: GUC (3443.TW), Alchip (3661.TW), Marvell (MRVL), Broadcom (AVGO), MediaTek (2454.TW). HBM4 PHY/controller IP: Synopsys (SNPS), Cadence (CDNS). Shares are own estimates.
supply_tightness: TSMC is effectively the only external source. Base dies compete for N5/N3 wafers with GPUs, ASICs and CPUs. Qualification is tied to each HBM qualification at each GPU/ASIC customer (6-12 months). SK hynix reportedly evaluating Intel because of TSMC cost pressure (Aug 2026) shows TSMC has pricing power. Herald: TSMC HBM4 base die costs 3-4x a 1b DRAM core die, with the gap widening for HBM4E.
substitution_risk: Medium-low through 2030. (1) DRAM makers could keep standard base dies on in-house CMOS, as Micron did for HBM4; this shrinks the external market. (2) Samsung's captive base die moves share, not niche size. (3) After 2030, memory-on-logic 3D stacking or moving controller functions into the accelerator die (UCIe-style custom HBM) could simplify or remove the base die.
cyclicality_risk: Follows HBM unit volume. An HBM oversupply or price reset in 2028-29 would slow stack growth but not the per-stack content trend. Foundry overbuild at N3/N2 is unlikely. Double-ordering risk is lower than for equipment because dies are built to HBM build plans.
faster_sub_niche: Custom base dies (cHBM on N3P/N2 with integrated controller/PHY or near-memory logic). Near zero in 2026, first volume with HBM4E in 2027 (Micron+TSMC, TSMC C-HBM4E); own estimate 40-60% of base-die value by 2030. Standard N12 HBM4 base dies plateau once HBM4E arrives.

evidence.claim: TSMC makes HBM4 base dies on N12 rather than a DRAM process, cutting operating voltage from 1.1 V to 0.8 V. TSMC's custom C-HBM4E moves the base die to N3P and integrates the memory controller (custom PHY).
evidence.label: reported fact

evidence.claim: SK hynix reportedly weighing Intel for HBM4E base dies amid TSMC cost pressure. Herald Business estimates TSMC HBM4 base dies cost 3-4x SK hynix's 1b DRAM core dies, with the gap widening for HBM4E.
evidence.label: third-party estimate

evidence.claim: Micron will have TSMC make both standard and custom HBM4E logic dies, targeting 2027; custom base dies expected to carry higher gross margins
evidence.label: company guidance

evidence.claim: HBM is ~8% / 9% / 13% of total DRAM bit supply and ~18% / 22% / 30% of DRAM wafer input at end-2025 / 2026 / 2027. Blended HBM ASP forecast +121% YoY in 2027 on HBM4/4E mix and shortage.
evidence.label: third-party estimate

evidence.claim: HBM4 base-die sourcing: Samsung uses its own 4 nm logic process, SK hynix uses TSMC, Micron makes HBM4 base dies in-house
evidence.label: reported fact

evidence.claim: Micron: HBM TAM rising from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028), ~40% CAGR. Recalled from the Dec-2025 FQ1-26 earnings call; NOT re-verified in this session.
evidence.label: company guidance

The size is almost all own estimate, and per-die price is the weakest input (no price is disclosed; only Herald's '3-4x core die' ratio). name: HVLP4/HVLP5 (hyper-very-low-profile) electrodeposited copper foil for M8U/M9 ultra-low-loss laminates
definition: IN: HVLP grade 4 and 5 ED copper foil (typically 12-35 um; profile Rz roughly <=1 um for HVLP4, lower for HVLP5) sold to CCL makers for ultra-low-loss laminates (M8U/M9). End uses: AI accelerator boards, compute and switch trays, NVLink midplanes and orthogonal backplanes, and 1.6T/3.2T switch boards. OUT: HVLP1-3 (noted as the slower sub-segment), RTF, standard HTE foil, lithium-battery foil, and carrier ultra-thin foil (MicroThin) for IC substrates.
value_chain_path: AI data-centre hardware -> server/switch PCB -> ultra-low-loss CCL (M8U/M9) -> electrodeposited copper foil -> HVLP4/HVLP5 grade
size_2026_usd: $0.17-0.31B for HVLP4/5 only (own estimate); all HVLP grades for AI servers ~$0.5-0.7B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: About 75-85% volume: HVLP4+ tonnage rises ~5-8x, from ~6-8.5 kt to ~35-55 kt. About 15-25% price/mix: HVLP5 carries a premium, while HVLP4 processing fees hold through the 2027-28 shortage and then likely fall 20-30%. Copper is passed through and is not growth. Pricing power is real in 2026-28 (Japanese hikes of 5-10%; Morgan Stanley gap of 31% in 2027), but 2029-30 growth must be volume-led.
math: TOP-DOWN 2026: AI-server HVLP demand ~24 kt (Chinese brokerage estimate); HVLP4+ share ~25-35% -> 6-8.5 kt. Price build: copper ~$10-12/kg (own, LME-linked, unverified) plus HVLP4 processing fee ~$18-25/kg. The fee is own estimate, set by Goldman's 'about 10x HTE fee' and by SMM's HVLP1 fee of CNY55-63k/t (~$7.7-8.8/kg). Total $28-37/kg; 6-8.5 kt x $28-37/kg = $0.17-0.31B. BOTTOM-UP 2026 SUPPLY: Mitsui VSP capacity ~840 t/mo by Sep-2026 (~10 kt/yr), assuming 35-50% is HVLP4+ (unverified) -> 3.5-5 kt. Co-Tech HVLP3+4 100-150 t/mo, about half HVLP4 -> 0.6-0.9 kt. Defu ~70 t/mo HVLP4 -> ~0.8 kt. Furukawa, Circuit Foil and others -> 0.8-1.5 kt. Total ~5.7-8.2 kt, consistent with demand. 2030: AI HVLP demand 50 kt in 2027 (brokerage), then +15-25%/yr -> 85-120 kt; HVLP4+ share 45-60% -> 38-72 kt demand. Capacity cap: Mitsui 1,400 t/mo by FY2030 (16.8 kt/yr, not all HVLP4+), Co-Tech >=600 t/mo by 4Q27 (7.2 kt), China 10-25 kt, others 5-10 kt -> ~39-59 kt. So shipments of ~35-55 kt at $25-32/kg = $1.0-1.8B. CAGR: (1.0/0.31)^0.25-1 = 34%; (1.8/0.17)^0.25-1 = 80%; central (1.4/0.24)^0.25-1 = 55%.
catalyst_timing: 2H26: M9 CCL begins volume (EMC); Rubin trays on M8U. 2027: M9 midplanes and orthogonal backplanes for Rubin Ultra/Kyber-class racks, wider 1.6T switch deployment; Co-Tech plant 3 starts 1Q27 and reaches ~600 t/mo HVLP3+4 by 4Q27; HVLP4 gap peaks (31%). 2028: Mitsui reaches ~1,200 t/mo VSP; gap narrows to ~20%; 3.2T/224G-SerDes boards pull HVLP5. FY2030: Mitsui at 1,400 t/mo. 2031+: Mitsui's new Malaysia plant.
key_suppliers: Mitsui Mining & Smelting / Mitsui Kinzoku (5706.T; 'VSP' foil; Taiwan + Malaysia): est. 50-60% of 2026 HVLP4 supply. Co-Tech Development (8358.TWO): est. 10-15%. Furukawa Electric (5801.T): est. 5-10%. Circuit Foil Luxembourg (Solus Advanced Materials, 336370.KS): est. ~5%. Fukuda Metal Foil & Powder (5821.T): small. China: Defu Technology (301511.SZ), Tongguan Copper Foil (301217.SZ) and others, est. 10-20% combined and rising. Brokerage commentary: Mitsui + Co-Tech control 80-90% of effective high-end supply. Shares are own estimates.
supply_tightness: Tight through 2028. Morgan Stanley: HVLP4 shortfall 31% in 2027 and 20% in 2028; long certification cycles, low yields, and upstream equipment limit additions. Digitimes-cited sources: ~1,500 t gap in 2026 widening to ~2,500 t in 2027. Chinese entrants run HVLP4 yields of ~60%. Japanese suppliers raised prices 5-10%. Nvidia reportedly secures foil directly rather than through CCL makers. Mitsui's additions are deliberately paced (840 -> 1,200 -> 1,400 t/mo, new plant only from 2031). Qualification through CCL, PCB and Nvidia/ODM takes about 9-18 months.
substitution_risk: Medium. (1) CPO and cabled/flyover designs shorten PCB copper traces in scale-out networking, while NVLink midplanes and orthogonal backplanes move scale-up traffic onto PCBs (net positive to ~2029). (2) Better RTF/HVLP3 with new bonding treatments could cover some M8 designs. (3) Lower grades are commoditising: SMM now publishes HVLP1 quotes. HVLP4/5 itself has no direct substitute at 224G SerDes.
cyclicality_risk: High after 2028. Overcapacity in Chinese battery foil is being retooled toward HVLP. CCL makers are double-ordering during the 2026-27 shortage. Processing fees likely fall 20-30% once the gap closes, which would cut the price part of growth.
faster_sub_niche: Split: HVLP4/5 grows much faster than HVLP1-3, where Chinese capacity is commoditising (SMM's HVLP1 quote is the signal), so HVLP4/5 is analysed here. Within it, HVLP5 grows fastest from near zero: Co-Tech sampling end-2026, Mitsui reportedly in mass production. It is still too small in 2026 to size separately.

name: Quartz (Q-glass, fused-silica) electronic glass cloth for M9-class CCL
definition: IN: woven high-purity fused-silica fibre cloth (SiO2 >=99.9%; Dk ~3.7, Df ~0.0005-0.001, CTE <1 ppm/C) used in M9 and later ultra-low-loss laminates. End uses: AI-rack midplanes and orthogonal backplanes, 1.6T/3.2T switch boards, and later possibly low-CTE substrate cores. OUT: aerospace/radome quartz fabrics; NE/NER/Low-Dk2/NEZ (Low-Dk3) glass cloth; T-glass.
value_chain_path: AI racks and switches -> high-speed PCB -> M9 ultra-low-loss CCL -> reinforcement glass cloth -> quartz (Q-glass) cloth
also_serves_megatrends: LEO satellites and radomes (legacy quartz-fabric market)
size_2026_usd: $0.1-0.3B (own estimate; third-party figures conflict by more than 30x). Above the $50M emerging line but early-stage
volume_vs_price: Volume is more than all of the growth: metres shipped rise roughly 5-15x. ASP per metre likely falls 30-50%, from today's scarcity price of CNY250-450/m to roughly CNY100-180/m, as Chinese capacity (Feilihua, Sinoma, Grace Fabric, International Composites) qualifies. Today's price reflects shortage and is not durable.
math: BOTTOM-UP 2026: Feilihua expects H1-26 quartz e-cloth sales of ~CNY150M (company), implying ~CNY0.35-0.6B for the year (~$50-85M; own extrapolation). If Feilihua is 25-45% of global qualified supply (own; Shin-Etsu and Asahi Kasei lead in Japan) -> ~$110-340M. At CNY250-300/m that is ~3-8M m shipped, versus a claimed 16.85M m of 2026 demand (Huatai). That implies the demand figure is a wish list or that supply is the binding constraint. Stated 2026 range: $0.1-0.3B. 2030: 25-60M m (own) x CNY100-180/m = CNY2.5-10.8B ≈ $0.35-1.5B. This assumes M9 with Q-glass becomes standard for Nvidia midplanes/orthogonal backplanes from 2027 and for 1.6T/3.2T switch cores. CAGR: central (0.8/0.18)^0.25-1 ≈ 45%; the range is wide because the end market may choose NEZ instead.
catalyst_timing: 2H26: M9 CCL volume begins (EMC says it was first to qualify); Rubin midplane on M9. 2027: Kyber/NVL576-class orthogonal backplanes and 1.6T switches; Nittobo NEZ Low-Dk3 launches as a competitor; Chinese quartz-yarn capacity (Feilihua's CNY300M raise) comes online. 2028-29: price compression; possible use in substrate cores.
key_suppliers: Shin-Etsu Chemical (4063.T; SQX quartz cloth). Asahi Kasei (3407.T; reported targeting mass production in 2026). Hubei Feilihua Quartz Glass (300395.SZ; quartz yarn and cloth, still in customer certification). Sinoma Science & Technology / Taishan Fiberglass (002080.SZ). Grace Fabric Technology / Honghe (603256.SS). International Composites (301526.SZ). Fulltech Fiber Glass (1815.TW; M9 quartz-cloth qualification per Digitimes). Shares unverified; own estimate is that Japanese suppliers hold most 2026 volume qualified in the Nvidia chain, with Feilihua ~20-40% of global.
supply_tightness: Tight in 2026-27. Industry inventory is reportedly near zero. A new furnace/kiln takes at least ~2 years. Drawing quartz fibre and weaving fine-denier cloth have low yields. Prices have risen in several rounds since Oct-2025 (+10% again in Mar-2026). Several Chinese listed firms have announced capacity, so tightness is likely transient.
substitution_risk: High. Nittobo's NEZ (Low-Dk3) glass arrives in 2027 and is easier to drill and cheaper. Quartz's hardness drives up PCB drilling cost. M8U-class NE-glass laminates may cover many 1.6T designs. CPO and cabled backplanes reduce PCB reach. If Nvidia standardises on NEZ for midplanes, the niche stays below $0.5B.
cyclicality_risk: Very high. China A-share speculation is driving capacity announcements, and demand is concentrated in a handful of Nvidia rack designs. Price per metre is likely to halve by 2028-29.
faster_sub_niche: Q-glass for M9 midplanes, orthogonal backplanes and 1.6T/3.2T switch cores is the fast part and is analysed here. Q-glass for substrate cores and low-CTE uses starts after 2028. Low-Dk2 cloth is larger today but grows more slowly.

name: CoWoS-L-class 2.5D integration (RDL interposer + local silicon bridges)
definition: IN: 2.5D chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging services using an RDL/organic interposer with embedded local silicon interconnect (LSI) bridges and deep-trench capacitors: CoW assembly, molding and on-substrate attach. Providers: TSMC CoWoS-L and OSAT equivalents (ASE/SPIL FOCoS-Bridge, Amkor), with Intel EMIB-T as a competing format. Measured as packaging/interposer service revenue, excluding the logic dies, HBM and substrate. OUT: CoWoS-S (monolithic silicon interposer), CoWoS-R without bridges, InFO, SoIC, panel-level CoPoS/FOPLP.
value_chain_path: AI accelerators -> advanced packaging -> 2.5D heterogeneous integration -> interposer technology -> CoWoS-L (RDL + LSI bridge) large-reticle interposers
size_2026_usd: $8-12B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: About 80-85% wafer volume: industry CoWoS-class capacity roughly 2.5-3x from 2026 to 2030, plus a rising CoWoS-L share. About 15-20% revenue per wafer: interposers grow from 5.5x to 9.5x reticle with more LSI bridges and capacitors, plus TSMC price discipline. Not a shortage-price story after 2027, since TrendForce expects 2.5D tightness to ease in 2027.
math: 2026: TSMC CoWoS capacity goes from roughly 75-80k wpm (end-2025, unverified) to 95-140k wpm by end-2026 (JPMorgan 95k; Economic Daily News 120-140k), giving ~1.0-1.3M 12-inch wafers in 2026. CoWoS-L share 60-70% (own) -> 0.6-0.9M wafers; OSATs add 0.1-0.2M CoWoS-L-class wafers. Revenue per wafer $9-14k (own, unverified; packaging + interposer + bridges) -> ~$6.3-15B; stated as $8-12B. 2030: TSMC ~260k wpm by end-2028 (EDN) and an own-estimate 280-350k by 2030, plus OSAT 60-100k, gives ~4.0-5.0M wafers/yr at ~85% utilisation. CoWoS-L share ~80-90%, less 10-25% of volume migrating to CoPoS panels -> 2.8-4.0M wafers x $9-12k = $25-48B; stated as $25-42B. CAGR: (25/12)^0.25-1 = 20%; (42/8)^0.25-1 = 51%; central (33/10)^0.25-1 = 35%.
catalyst_timing: 2026-27: TSMC AP7 (Chiayi) and AP8 (Tainan) ramp. KGI forecasts ~170k wpm by end-2027 (raised from 155k). 2027: Rubin Ultra-class packages (4 reticle-size dies, 16 HBM sites) raise interposer area per package, so fewer packages per wafer and more wafers per GPU. 2028: EDN reports ~2x the end-2026 capacity (~260k wpm). 2028-29: CoPoS panel-level begins substituting at the largest body sizes.
key_suppliers: TSMC (2330.TW / TSM): est. 85-90% of CoWoS-class output in 2026. ASE Technology incl. SPIL (3711.TW / ASX): est. 5-8% (CoW overflow and oS back-end; FOCoS-Bridge). Amkor (AMKR): est. 2-4% (Arizona, with TSMC). Intel Foundry (INTC): EMIB-T alternative, est. 0-3%. Bottleneck sub-suppliers: Disco (6146.T), Advantest (6857.T), TCB/reflow suppliers (BESI, ASMPT, K&S, Hanmi), Ajinomoto ABF, Resonac/Namics underfill. Shares are own estimates.
supply_tightness: Tight in 2026: TSMC plus OSATs approach ~200k wpm industry-wide (EDN). Capacity forecasts keep getting revised up (KGI raised end-2027 to 170k). A new advanced-packaging fab takes ~18-24 months. TSMC allocates capacity across Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD and others. TrendForce expects the shortage to moderate by 2027 as orders spill over to OSATs and TSMC adds >60% capacity.
substitution_risk: Medium after 2028. Panel-level CoPoS (TSMC) and FOPLP take the largest bodies. Intel EMIB-T and Samsung I-Cube/SoP compete for ASICs. Silicon bridges embedded in the substrate could move value to substrate makers. Within the niche, CoWoS-L cannibalises CoWoS-S.
cyclicality_risk: High. The ~2x-by-2028 plan is sized against AI capex that may plateau. Customer concentration is high (Nvidia >50% of CoWoS). Duplicate booking of CoWoS slots by ASIC programmes was seen in 2024-25. OSAT capacity added for overflow is the first to go idle in a slowdown.
faster_sub_niche: Split: CoWoS-L grows; CoWoS-S declines and CoWoS-R stays a niche. CoWoS-L is analysed here. Within it, packages of 5.5x reticle or more with 12 or more HBM sites (Rubin Ultra, Feynman, largest ASICs; 2027+) grow fastest. LSI bridge dies are made inside TSMC and cannot be sized separately.

name: Low-CTE glass cloth (T-glass class) for AI package-substrate cores and prepregs
definition: IN: low-CTE (~2.8-3 ppm/C), high-modulus glass yarn and woven cloth (Nittobo T-glass and equivalents from AGY, Nan Ya, Taiwan Glass, Grace Fabric, Taishan) used in the core and prepreg of ABF and BT package substrates. Main uses: AI GPUs/ASICs (largest), plus AI smartphone application processors and memory packages. OUT: low-Dk cloth for CCL (NE/NER/Low-Dk2/NEZ), quartz cloth, E-glass, glass-core substrates.
value_chain_path: AI accelerators -> packaging -> FC-BGA ABF substrate -> core laminate / prepreg reinforcement -> low-CTE T-glass yarn & cloth
size_2026_usd: $0.22-0.33B (own estimate, derived from Nittobo's segment guidance)
volume_vs_price: 2025-26 growth was price-heavy: several T-glass price increases pushed Nittobo's Electronic Materials operating margin to ~39% in FY3/26. For 2026-30, about 85-95% volume (Nittobo capacity 3x by FY3/29, plus Taiwanese and Chinese entrants) and 5-15% price/mix (Nittobo plans no further hikes as of Aug-2026; next-gen T-glass in 2028 may carry a premium). That makes the forward growth relatively durable.
math: 2026: Nittobo Electronic Materials guidance for FY3/27 is JPY77.8B (raised from JPY77.0B; OP JPY28B), up from JPY49.3B in FY3/26 (+58%). At JPY145-155/$ that is ~$0.50-0.54B. Assume T-glass is 40-55% of the segment (own; the rest is NE/NER low-Dk and other cloth) -> $0.21-0.29B. With Nittobo at ~90% T-glass share (TrendForce), the global low-CTE cloth market is ~$0.23-0.33B. 2030: Nittobo capacity 3x the FY3/26 level by FY3/29 (Nikkei via TrendForce). Own assumption: industry volume 2.5-3.5x 2026 by 2030 including qualified Taiwanese/Chinese yarn, ASP flat to +10% -> 2.5-3.85x -> $0.55-1.27B; stated as $0.6-1.1B. CAGR: (0.6/0.33)^0.25-1 = 16%; (1.1/0.22)^0.25-1 = 50%; central (0.85/0.27)^0.25-1 ≈ 33%. DEMAND CROSS-CHECK: Goldman sees the ABF substrate supply gap at 14% (2H26), 34% (2027) and 51% (2028), which is consistent with T-glass demand outgrowing tripled supply.
catalyst_timing: 2026: allocation-constrained, with most capacity booked by Nvidia, Microsoft, Google and Amazon. Mid/late-2027: new Nittobo Fukushima capacity comes online. By Mar-2028: Nittobo Taiwan capacity doubled versus 2025. 2028: next-gen T-glass (customers may include Nvidia and Apple); peak ABF shortage. FY3/29: Nittobo at 3x. 2029-30: glass-core substitution begins at the largest AI packages.
key_suppliers: Nitto Boseki / Nittobo (3110.T): ~90% of T-glass and 60-70% of NER-glass (TrendForce). AGY (private, US; S-2 glass, small electronics share). Nan Ya Plastics (1303.TW; developing low-CTE cloth). Taiwan Glass (1802.TW). Grace Fabric (603256.SS). Taishan Fiberglass / Sinoma (002080.SZ). Asahi Kasei (3407.T; weaving). Shares for non-Nittobo suppliers are unverified, about 10% combined.
supply_tightness: Severe. TrendForce: no new Nittobo capacity before mid-2027 (Nikkei says late 2027). Hyperscalers and Nvidia have booked most premium cloth, and Apple is negotiating allocations. Nittobo's president says even tripling capacity 'will not be enough'. Investment is JPY80B across Japan and Taiwan. Alternative yarns need 12-24 months of qualification at substrate makers and chip OEMs. Counterpoint and Goldman both tie ABF substrate lead-time stretch to T-glass.
substitution_risk: Low through 2028. Medium in 2029-30, when glass-core substrates remove the woven-glass core for the largest AI packages and lower-modulus alternative low-CTE yarns qualify.
cyclicality_risk: Moderate. Nittobo's tripling plus new entrants could create a surplus in 2029-30 if AI substrate demand plateaus. Substrate makers double-ordered during the 2026-27 shortage. Nittobo is disciplined on price, which reduces bust risk.
faster_sub_niche: Split: T-glass for large-body AI GPU/ASIC ABF cores grows faster than T-glass for smartphone/memory BT substrates; the AI part drives the estimate. Next-gen T-glass (2028) is the fastest sub-piece but too early to size. Low-Dk NE/NER cloth (same supplier) is a separate niche that belongs to the CCL chain.
