name: Large-body, high-layer-count ABF FC-BGA substrates for AI accelerators and custom ASICs (>=100 mm, >=20 layers)
definition: IN: FC-BGA build-up substrates with ABF (or equivalent) dielectric, body roughly >=70-100 mm per side and >=16-20 layers, carrying 2.5D AI GPU, custom-ASIC and >=51.2T switch packages, plus high-end server CPUs made on the same lines. OUT: PC/notebook/consumer ABF (<55 mm, <=12 layers), BT and coreless memory substrates, glass-core substrates, interposers.
value_chain_path: AI accelerators -> advanced packaging -> package substrate -> FC-BGA ABF build-up substrate -> large-body (>=100 mm, >=20 L) AI/HPC class
size_2026_usd: $5-7B (own estimate; ~50-55% of an estimated $10-12B ABF substrate market, unverified)
volume_vs_price: About 55-65% volume: substrate area x layer count. AI package count roughly doubles, and area/layers per package rise 60-100% as interposers grow toward 9.5x reticle. About 35-45% price: long-term-agreement prices +10-15% per quarter and spot +20% per quarter expected 3Q26-2027, plus pass-through of a possible >=30% ABF film increase. The price share is shortage-driven and at real risk of reversal in 2029-30.
math: 2026 BOTTOM-UP: Ibiden Electronics FY3/26 sales JPY243B (reported). FY3/27 Q1 electronics sales +37.7%, so FY3/27 electronics ~JPY320-360B (~$2.1-2.4B, own). AI/server ~75% -> ~$1.6-1.8B. Ibiden share of the AI class 25-35% (own) -> market $4.6-7.2B; stated as $5-7B. UNIT CHECK: ~15-20M AI accelerator/ASIC/switch packages (own) x $250-400 per substrate (own) = $3.8-8B. 2030: 30-40M packages x $400-650 per substrate (area/layer growth +60-100%, minus 10-20% price normalisation from the 2028 peak) = $12-26B; stated as $13-22B. CAGR: (13/7)^0.25-1 ≈ 17%; (22/5)^0.25-1 ≈ 45%; central (17/6)^0.25-1 ≈ 30%.
catalyst_timing: 3Q26-2027: LTA and spot price increases. Supply gap 10-14% in 2H26, 20-34% in 2027 and up to ~51% in 2028 (Goldman). FY2027+: Ibiden's JPY280B Ono expansion reaches mass production; Unimicron KF2 and the second Yangmei plant arrive in 2027. 2027-28: Rubin Ultra and Feynman bring larger bodies. 2029+: glass-core risk and capacity catch-up.
key_suppliers: Ibiden (4062.T): est. 25-35% of the AI-accelerator class (Nvidia lead). Unimicron (3037.TW): est. 20-25%; AI ~60% of revenue. Nan Ya PCB (8046.TW): est. 8-12%. Samsung Electro-Mechanics (009150.KS): est. 8-12%. Kinsus (3189.TW): est. 5-8%. AT&S (ATS.VI): est. 3-6%. Shinko Electric (private, JIC-owned): est. 3-6%. supply_tightness: Goldman: ABF supply gap 14% (2H26), 34% (2027), 51% (2028). ABF vacuum laminator lead times reportedly extend to 2031. Substrate makers' contract liabilities are rising again as customers prepay for capacity. Nvidia and Broadcom are negotiating capacity reservations (Counterpoint). The T-glass shortage is lengthening substrate lead times. Ajinomoto is reportedly considering a >=30% film increase.
substitution_risk: Medium from 2029. Glass-core substrates for the largest AI packages; more routing moving into CoWoS-L RDL or panel-level interposers could cap layer-count growth; EMIB-style bridges embedded in substrates shift value but keep it within substrate makers.
cyclicality_risk: High. ABF went through a 2021-22 boom and a 2023-24 bust. Ibiden alone plans JPY500B of electronics capex over FY26-28, and Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB, Kinsus, SEMCO, AT&S and Chinese entrants all add capacity in 2027-29. Double ordering and capacity-reservation behaviour are visible now. The price part of growth (35-45%) is the most exposed.
faster_sub_niche: Split: substrates of >=100 mm and >=20 layers for Nvidia/AMD GPUs and hyperscaler ASICs grow faster than the CPU/switch ABF class and much faster than PC ABF (roughly flat). Equipment sub-niche: ABF vacuum laminators (lead time reportedly to 2031) are an acute bottleneck but are small and unsized (unverified).

name: Die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding equipment
definition: IN: sequential and collective die-to-wafer hybrid bonders (bumpless Cu-Cu + SiCN/SiO2 dielectric bonds, sub-10 um pitch, ~50-200 nm placement accuracy), plus upgrades and service. Uses: TSMC SoIC-style logic-on-logic and SRAM-on-logic, EIC-on-PIC bonding for CPO, and from ~2028 HBM4E-16H/HBM5-20H core-die stacking. OUT: wafer-to-wafer bonders (EVG, TEL; image sensors, 3D NAND, backside power), TCB/fluxless TCB, and upstream CMP/plasma/metrology tools.
value_chain_path: AI accelerators -> advanced packaging -> 3D integration (SoIC / 3D HBM / CPO) -> bonding equipment -> D2W hybrid bonders
size_2026_usd: $0.3-0.5B (own estimate; BESI hybrid-bonding revenue est. EUR0.2-0.3B plus ASMPT, captive SEMES and others)
size_2030_usd: $0.6-1.4B (own estimate, bracketed by the UBS-implied bear case and BESI's EUR1.65B HB + advanced-TCB 2030 TAM)
volume_vs_price: About 80% units: the installed base grows from >150 tools to several hundred, with HBM lines needing tens of tools each. About 20% ASP: sub-50 nm, higher-throughput tools sell at higher prices, but ASMPT, Hanmi and SEMES cap pricing. Not shortage pricing; BESI's 65.7% gross margin reflects technology lead.
math: 2026: BESI's Q1-Q3 revenue guidance midpoint is EUR715.8M YTD; adding Q4 of ~EUR0.27-0.32B gives FY ~EUR0.98-1.04B (own). Hybrid-bonding share 20-30% (own; not disclosed) -> EUR0.2-0.3B, about 60-100 systems at EUR2.5-4M (own ASP, unverified). Other vendors add 30-60% -> $0.3-0.5B. 2030: BESI's TAM for HB + advanced TCB is EUR1.65B; if HB is 55-70% (BESI says it becomes the largest assembly segment) -> EUR0.9-1.15B (~$1.0-1.3B). Bear case: UBS sees BESI HB revenue of EUR424M; at ~65% share that is a ~$0.7B market. Unit sanity check: Samsung's reported ~50-tool D2W line alone ≈ $150-200M. CAGR: (1.4/0.3)^0.25-1 ≈ 47%; central (1.0/0.4)^0.25-1 ≈ 26%; a delayed HBM case gives ~10%.
catalyst_timing: 2026-27: TSMC SoIC capacity growth for AI GPUs/ASICs, CPO EIC-PIC bonding, and new hyperscaler customers (BESI won one in Q2-26). 2027: BESI's HVM-ready sub-50 nm tools. 2028: earliest HBM use (16-high HBM4E) if yields allow. 2029-30: HBM5 20-high (SK hynix). BESI frames adoption around AI products in 2027-2030.
key_suppliers: BE Semiconductor Industries (BESI.AS): est. 60-70% of D2W HB, also sold as the Applied Materials (AMAT) Kinex integrated line; AMAT holds a ~9% stake [STALE: 2025]. ASMPT (0522.HK): est. 10-15%. SEMES (Samsung captive): est. 5-15%. Shibaura Mechatronics (6590.T), Hanmi Semiconductor (042700.KS) and Hanwha Semitech: early stage. W2W suppliers excluded: EV Group (private), TEL (8035.T). Shares are own estimates.
supply_tightness: Moderate. Few tools meet HVM-grade accuracy and throughput; BESI has 21 HB customers (up from 15 at end-2025) and a 65.7% gross margin. Qualification cycles are 12-24 months per customer process. Capacity is not a hard constraint (BESI can scale assembly), so pricing power comes from technology rather than scarcity.
substitution_risk: High for HBM, low for logic. For HBM, fluxless/advanced TCB keeps being extended: JEDEC height relaxations (exact value unverified) and the HBM4E-12H mainstream delay HB. SK hynix requires 90-98% yield and a 3-5 year lifetime before adopting HB. For logic SoIC there is no real alternative below ~9 um pitch, but W2W can substitute where die sizes match.
cyclicality_risk: High. Equipment orders are lumpy and front-loaded (one Samsung line ≈ 50 tools). Customer concentration is high (TSMC, Samsung, SK hynix, Micron). Delays in HBM adoption have already hit expectations (UBS EUR424M vs ~EUR936M priced in).
faster_sub_niche: Split: HBM D2W hybrid bonding grows fastest from near zero but inflects only in 2028-30 (16H HBM4E / 20H HBM5), so it is flagged too early. Logic SoIC + CPO D2W drives 2026-28 and is the main body of this estimate.

name: Molybdenum ALD/CVD metallization replacing tungsten (ALD-Mo tools + Mo oxychloride/chloride precursors)
definition: IN: 300mm ALD/CVD Mo fill and liner tools, plus the Mo precursors they consume (MoO2Cl2, MoOCl4, MoCl5, any organometallic Mo). Uses: 3D NAND word lines, logic middle-of-line contacts and vias at GAA nodes, DRAM contacts. OUT: Mo sputter targets (display/PVD), W tools and WF6, Ru/Co metallization, non-semiconductor Mo.
value_chain_path: Leading-edge front-end fab -> deposition / metallization -> contact and word-line metal fill -> W-to-Mo transition -> ALD/CVD Mo tools + MoO2Cl2/MoOCl4/MoCl5 precursors
also_serves_megatrends: AI data-center storage (enterprise QLC SSD -> 300-400+ layer NAND)
AI accelerators/CPUs on GAA nodes (logic MOL contacts/vias)
size_2026_usd: $0.5-1.0B combined (own estimate). Tools $0.45-0.8B, anchored on Lam's $2B+ multi-year Mo ALD target (company guidance). Precursors $50-200M (own estimate, unverified).
volume_vs_price: About 80-90% volume: the share of wafers converting from W to Mo, times the word-line count per wafer, which rises every NAND generation (218L -> 3xxL -> 4xxL). Price is a modest headwind after ~2028: the precursor premium over WF6 erodes as Korean and Chinese second sources qualify. Tool ASP is flat to up. Growth is not shortage-priced.
math: All inputs are own estimates, not verified this session. (1) NAND precursors: global NAND capacity ~1.5-1.7M wpm. Mo-filled share is ~10-20% in 2026 (0.15-0.3M wpm) and rises to ~45-65% by 2030 (0.7-1.0M wpm) as >=200L nodes convert. Assumed precursor cost $20-50 per Mo wafer, scaling with word-line count. 2026: 0.15-0.3M x 12 x $20-40 = $36-144M. 2030: 0.7-1.0M x 12 x $20-50 = $170-600M. (2) Logic and DRAM contacts/vias: 0.3-0.6M wpm (2026) rising to 1.0-2.0M wpm (2030), at $3-10/wafer: $10-70M -> $40-240M. Precursors total $50-200M (2026) -> $0.2-0.8B (2030), CAGR ~30-45%. (3) Tools: Lam's '$2B+ Mo ALD over 3-5 years' implies ~$0.4-0.7B/yr for Lam alone. Adding AMAT, TEL and China domestic at 10-30% gives $0.45-0.8B (2026) and $0.5-1.1B (2030); the NAND conversion wave peaks 2026-28, then logic and DRAM take over. Combined: $0.5-1.0B (2026) -> $0.8-1.9B (2030).
catalyst_timing: 2025-26: Halo ramps at multiple NAND makers as >=200L capacity converts (Lam, 2025). 2026-27: memory-led capex upcycle (ASML Q1-26 bookings ~EUR13B, mostly memory, for 2027 shipments); 300-400+ layer nodes (Samsung V10, SK hynix 321L+, Kioxia/SanDisk BiCS10; node names from prior knowledge, unverified). 2026-28: Mo in logic MOL at GAA nodes (Lam foundry win, June-quarter 2025). 2027-29: DRAM contacts. After 2028: Ru competes for the tightest logic vias.
key_suppliers: Tools: Lam Research (LRCX), est. 70-90% of HVM ALD-Mo (own estimate; Lam says it is the only ALD-Mo supplier in foundry-logic production). Also Applied Materials (AMAT), Tokyo Electron (8035.T), and China domestic Naura (002371.SZ) and Piotech (688072.SS) for YMTC/CXMT. Precursors: Entegris (ENTG), Merck KGaA/EMD Electronics (MRK.DE), Air Liquide (AI.PA), SK Trichem (SK Inc. JV), Soulbrain (357780.KQ), Hansol Chemical (014680.KS), DNF (092070.KQ), Adeka (4401.T), UP Chemical/Yoke (002409.SZ). Precursor shares unverified. Geography: US, EU, Korea, Japan; China localizing.
supply_tightness: Tools: effectively one HVM ALD-Mo supplier in 2025-26 by Lam's own claim. Qualification takes 12-24 months per layer and node, and conversions are tied to new NAND nodes. Precursors: solid oxychloride sources need special ampoule/vapor delivery and ppb-level metal and oxygen control, so there are 2-4 qualified suppliers per fab. Capacity adds are cheap and fast, though, so precursor supply is not a multi-year bottleneck. Mo feedstock is plentiful (China is the largest miner, roughly 40%; unverified). Pricing power is moderate and comes from qualification, not shortage.
substitution_risk: Inside 2030, low in NAND, where Mo is the consensus W successor. In logic, Ru (later subtractive Ru) takes the tightest vias/lines from about A14/A10. W persists in relaxed layers. CVD/PVD-Mo from AMAT/TEL shifts share between suppliers, not niche size.
cyclicality_risk: High exposure to NAND capex: a 2023-style collapse is possible after the 2026-28 AI-storage upcycle. Tool demand is front-loaded and could be double-ordered. China rules already cut Lam revenue by ~$700M (per a secondary summary). Chinese NAND makers (YMTC) localize both tools and precursors. Precursor ASP deflates as second sources qualify.
faster_sub_niche: Mo precursors grow faster: a consumable driven by the installed base, likely <$200M in 2026 and $0.2-0.8B by 2030, ~30-45% CAGR. ALD-Mo tools grow ~5-20% because the conversion wave is front-loaded into 2025-28. Precursors alone probably lack a path to $1B by 2030, so the combined segment is the unit to rank.

evidence.claim: Lam's 2025 Investor Day materials set a $2B+ cumulative shipment target for ALD molybdenum (ALTUS Halo) over 3-5 years. They describe Halo as ramping at multiple NAND customers in CY2025 as fleets convert to >=200 layers, and ramping in foundry/logic with GAA.

name: EUV metal-oxide photoresists (tin-oxo MOR: spin-on and dry-deposited)
definition: IN: metal-oxide (mainly tin-oxo cluster) negative-tone EUV photoresists for Low-NA and High-NA EUV layers. Covers spin-on MOR materials and dry-resist precursors and process (vapor-deposited, dry-developed). OUT: chemically amplified EUV resists (CAR), ArF/KrF resists, underlayers, developers, coater/developer tracks. Dry-resist chamber revenue is noted but excluded from sizing.
value_chain_path: Leading-edge front-end fab -> lithography -> EUV patterning materials -> EUV photoresist -> metal-oxide (tin-oxo) resist: spin-on MOR + dry-deposited resist
also_serves_megatrends: High-NA EUV adoption (needs ~20-30nm thin resists; MOR absorbs EUV several times more strongly than CAR)
size_2026_usd: $20-100M MOR materials (own estimate; emerging, plausibly <$50M; unverified)
size_2030_usd: $0.2-0.7B MOR materials (own estimate); dry-resist equipment revenue extra, unverified
volume_vs_price: About 70% volume: share gain against CAR, plus EUV exposures growing ~15-20%/yr. About 30% price/mix: MOR and High-NA-grade resists carry a per-litre premium over CAR. Dry resist moves part of the value from materials to precursors and Lam chambers.
math: Own estimates; resist $/exposure is an unverified assumption. EUV Low-NA fleet ~350-400 tools by end-2026, from ASML cumulative shipments (2025 count unverified) plus ~65 Low-NA in 2026 per the ASML CEO. At ~0.5-0.9M wafer passes per tool per year, that is ~175-300M EUV exposures in 2026. At $2-4 resist per exposure, the EUV resist TAM is ~$0.4-1.2B. MOR share of 3-8% (select DRAM layers plus logic pilots) gives $20-100M. 2030: ~600-700 Low-NA plus 40-70 High-NA tools give ~350-550M exposures; at $3-5 per exposure the TAM is $1.0-2.7B. MOR share of 15-30% gives $0.2-0.7B. CAGR (0.2/0.1)^0.25 ~19% at the low end; central (0.4/0.05)^0.25 ~60%.
catalyst_timing: 2025-27: DRAM 1c/1d EUV layer insertion. SK hynix has co-developed MOR with Inpria since 2022; Lam dry resist was reportedly selected by a DRAM maker in 2025 (unverified). 2027-28: Intel 14A High-NA risk production and HVM, where thin resist is needed. 2028-29: TSMC A14 and DRAM High-NA insertion. Adoption pace is gated by fab tin-contamination protocols.
key_suppliers: JSR/Inpria: JSR has been private under JIC since 2024; Inpria est. majority of spin-on MOR volume (own estimate). Lam Research (LRCX; dry resist). Tokyo Ohka Kogyo (4186.T). Shin-Etsu Chemical (4063.T; EUV CAR leader, MOR status unverified). Fujifilm (4901.T). Sumitomo Chemical (4005.T). Dongjin Semichem (005290.KQ). Entegris (ENTG; MOR collaboration with Inpria, undated report). Irresistible Materials (private, UK; non-tin alternative). Geography: US (Inpria, Oregon), Japan, Korea.
supply_tightness: Only about 1-2 qualified sources per format. Qualification takes 2-3 years per layer and includes tin cross-contamination controls (dedicated tracks, bevel/backside clean). The binding constraint is qualification, not capacity. JSR invested in HVM scale-up after the acquisition. Pricing power is high while there are effectively single sources.
substitution_risk: High-absorption CARs. Low-NA EUV double patterning instead of High-NA (TSMC's path) reduces urgency. Dry resist and spin-on MOR cannibalize each other. Non-tin metal resists. EUV layer counts could also plateau if High-NA slips.
cyclicality_risk: A consumable tied to EUV exposures, so overbuild risk is low. Main risks: DRAM capex cycles and slower High-NA insertion. China capacity is irrelevant (no EUV in China).
faster_sub_niche: Unclear. Spin-on MOR (JSR/Inpria) is likely first in DRAM. Dry resist (Lam) moves revenue into equipment and precursors, which could exceed the materials value per layer. Both start from near zero; track per-maker announcements.

name: 300mm wafer-to-wafer (W2W) permanent bonding + post-bond thinning module for backside power and bonded memory
definition: IN: 300mm W2W permanent bonders. Covers fusion/dielectric bonding for BSPDN carrier attach and Cu-dielectric hybrid W2W bonding for CMOS-bonded-array (CBA) NAND and cell-on-periphery (CoP) DRAM. Also includes plasma activation and alignment, plus the linked post-bond edge trim, back-grind, CMP / Si etch-back thinning and bond-void/overlay metrology. OUT: die-to-wafer hybrid bonding (BESI/AMAT for HBM/SoIC), temporary bond/debond, TCB, legacy stacked-CIS capacity.
value_chain_path: Leading-edge front-end fab -> backside power delivery / wafer-level 3D integration -> wafer-to-wafer permanent bonding -> fusion/hybrid W2W bonders + post-bond edge-trim/grind/CMP thinning
also_serves_megatrends: AI logic (BSPDN on Intel 18A/14A, TSMC A16/A14-SPR, Samsung SF2Z)
size_2026_usd: $0.4-1.0B module equipment (own estimate, unverified); bonders alone ~$0.15-0.4B
cagr_2026_2030: 10-25% for equipment (central ~19%); 25-40% for bonded wafer starts (installed base)
volume_vs_price: About 85% volume: bonded wafer starts excluding CIS rise from ~0.3-0.45M wpm (2026) to ~0.9-1.55M wpm (2030). ASP rises modestly with tighter hybrid-bond overlay and in-situ metrology. Equipment revenue follows capacity additions, not installed base, so it is lumpier than wafer starts.
math: Own estimates; tool ASPs, throughput and capex intensity are unverified. Bonded starts excluding CIS, 2026: BSPDN 30-60k wpm (Intel 18A ramp, first TSMC A16) plus CBA NAND 250-400k wpm (Kioxia/SanDisk, YMTC, early Samsung/SK hynix) = 0.28-0.46M wpm. 2030: BSPDN 150-300k, CBA NAND 0.7-1.1M, DRAM CoP 50-150k = 0.9-1.55M wpm. Additions: ~0.08-0.15M wpm/yr (2026) and ~0.15-0.28M wpm/yr (2027-30). Module capex per 10k wpm is ~$40-80M: 1-2 bonders at $8-15M, 2-3 CMP tools, 2-3 edge-trim/grind tools, and void/overlay metrology. 2026: 8-15 x $40-80M = $0.3-1.2B; 2030: 15-28 x $40-80M = $0.6-2.2B. Cross-check: a bonder at ~20 wph x 720 h x 75% does ~11k bonds per month, so ~90-140 bonders are needed for 1.0-1.55M wpm.
catalyst_timing: Intel 18A PowerVia HVM ramp at Fab 52 for Panther Lake (2025-26). TSMC A16 Super Power Rail HVM 2H26, volume 2027. Samsung SF2Z 2027. TSMC A14-SPR 2029. Samsung V10 (~400+ layer) NAND hybrid bonding 2026-27 (YMTC patent licence reported Feb 2025). Kioxia/SanDisk CBA since BiCS8. DRAM 4F2/CoP 2028-30.
key_suppliers: W2W bonders: EV Group (private, Austria; est. 50-70% of 300mm W2W, own estimate), Tokyo Electron (8035.T), SUSS MicroTec (SMHN.DE), Piotech (688072.SS) for Chinese NAND. Thinning and edge trim: DISCO (6146.T; dominant in grinders, est. >70%, own estimate), Tokyo Seimitsu/Accretech (7729.T). CMP: Applied Materials (AMAT), Ebara (6361.T), Hwatsing (688120.SS). Metrology and overlay correction: KLA (KLAC), ASML. Wafer pull: Shin-Etsu (4063.T), SUMCO (3436.T), GlobalWafers (6488.TWO), Siltronic (WAF.DE), SK Siltron (private).
supply_tightness: Concentrated: EVG and TEL dominate HVM W2W bonding. Qualification takes 12-24 months. Hybrid W2W needs sub-100nm alignment (spec unverified). Tool lead times are ~9-15 months (unverified). This is not a hard bottleneck because capacity adds are modest capex, but DISCO has notable pricing power in grind/edge-trim.
substitution_risk: BSPDN-less designs: TSMC's A14 base node has no SPR, and mobile SKUs skip BSPDN. CMOS-under-array NAND (no bonding) may persist at some makers (Micron's path unverified). Die-to-wafer bonding could replace W2W in some DRAM/logic stacks. Monolithic CFET comes later.
cyclicality_risk: NAND capex boom-bust and double-ordering during the 2026-27 memory upcycle. Chinese domestic bonders capture YMTC/CXMT demand. Intel foundry execution risk on 18A/14A volumes. Equipment revenue follows capacity additions, not wafer starts.
faster_sub_niche: Bonding-driven 300mm prime-wafer consumption grows faster: each BSPDN wafer adds a permanent carrier, and each CBA/CoP wafer adds a separate CMOS wafer. That is ~0.3-0.45M wpm rising to 0.9-1.55M wpm, a 25-40% unit CAGR, worth ~$0.3-0.7B (2026) -> $1.0-2.6B (2030) at $90-140 per wafer (own estimate). But it is a slice of the commodity 300mm market (~$12-14B, priced on total supply/demand, currently in surplus), so the equipment module remains the ranked unit. BSPDN-spec carrier wafers alone are emerging (<$80M in 2026).

name: High-NA (0.55NA) EUV lithography scanners

value_chain_path: Leading-edge front-end fab -> lithography -> EUV scanners -> 0.55NA anamorphic EUV (EXE:5200B/5400) -> (sub-supply: Zeiss anamorphic optics, Trumpf drive laser)
also_serves_megatrends: AI logic at Intel 14A and TSMC A10-class nodes

size_2030_usd: EUR3.8-9.0B (~$4.4-10B) (own estimate: 10-20 units x EUR380-450M; 20/yr is ASML's stated capacity)
volume_vs_price: About 80% units (single digits rising to 10-20/yr) and ~20% ASP (EXE:5400 productivity upgrade, ~+3-5%/yr). Monopoly list pricing, not shortage pricing.
math: Units x ASP. 2026: 4-9 x EUR350-400M = EUR1.4-3.6B. 2030: capped at ASML's 20/yr capacity. Demand build: Intel 14A 3-8/yr (only if an external customer is secured); DRAM (SK hynix, Samsung, Micron) 4-8/yr; TSMC 0-6/yr (A16/A14 publicly do not need High-NA; the A10-class decision is ~2027-28); R&D (imec, Rapidus) 0-2. name: FEOC-compliant (non-PFE) LFP stationary-storage cells made in North America for US grid BESS
definition: IN: ESS-grade LFP/LMFP prismatic or pouch cells (>=280Ah) made in US, Canadian or Mexican plants by companies that are not 'prohibited foreign entities' (PFE) under OBBBA (LGES, Samsung SDI, SK On, Tesla, Ford, GM-LGES). Covers cells from dedicated ESS lines and from converted EV lines, sold into US utility-scale and C&I BESS. Measured at cell value. OUT: cells made in China or by PFE-controlled/licensed makers; EV cells; Korean NCA/NMC ESS cells (they compete inside the same pool but are excluded from the sizing); integration and EPC value (a DC block adds roughly 1.6-2x cell value).
value_chain_path: Power generation, grid & electrification -> Grid-scale energy storage (BESS) -> DC block / battery container -> Li-ion ESS cells -> large-format LFP ESS cells -> FEOC-compliant North American LFP ESS cells
also_serves_megatrends: AI data centers (firming, behind-the-meter storage, load smoothing)
EV-line repurposing during the EV slowdown
size_2026_usd: $0.8-1.6B (own estimate, cell level: ~12-20 GWh x $65-80/kWh)
volume_vs_price: More than all of the growth comes from volume. Unit volume grows about 40-55% a year as the non-PFE share of US ESS cells rises from ~20-30% to ~65-85%. ASP falls about 4-7% a year as EV-line conversions add capacity and the 45X cell credit ($35/kWh) is competed away. Demand is created by policy (MACR thresholds plus Section 301), not by shortage pricing, so the growth lasts only as long as the policy does.
math: TOP-DOWN. US BESS deployments: ~50-70 GWh in 2026 (third-party ranges from WoodMac/SEIA/BNEF, unverified this session), rising to ~70-100 GWh by 2030. Non-PFE share: 20-30% in 2026, 65-85% by 2030. That share is forced by the OBBBA material-assistance cost ratio (MACR) for storage, 55% in 2026 rising 5 pp a year to 75%, and by the 25% Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV Li-ion from 1 Jan 2026, which stacks on other duties. 2026 = 12-20 GWh x $65-80/kWh = $0.8-1.6B. 2030 = 55-85 GWh x $52-65/kWh = $2.9-5.5B. BOTTOM-UP CAPACITY (own estimate). LGES Holland, MI ~16.5 GWh (2025). LGES Arizona ESS line ~16 GWh (2026, unverified). Additional LGES US line conversions (unverified). Tesla Nevada LFP ~7-10 GWh (unverified). Samsung SDI and SK On line conversions, 2026-27 (sizes unverified). Ford Kentucky ~20 GWh (2027). Together that is ~80-120 GWh of nameplate by 2028, which can exceed non-PFE demand and caps ASP.
catalyst_timing: 1 Jan 2026: Section 301 tariff of 25% on Chinese non-EV Li-ion takes effect. Projects starting construction after 31 Dec 2025 face MACR (55% in 2026, then +5 pp a year). 2026: PFE limits on 45X start. 2026: Treasury FEOC/MACR guidance decides whether Chinese-licensed (CATL-tech) lines qualify. Aug 2027-Jul 2030: LGES ~$4.3B LFP ESS contract (reported as Tesla). 2027: Ford Energy shipments begin. 2028-2030: MACR reaches 70-75%.
key_suppliers: Estimated shares of 2026 North American non-PFE ESS cells (own estimates): LG Energy Solution (373220.KS) 45-60%; Tesla in-house Nevada LFP (TSLA) 10-20%; Samsung SDI (006400.KS) 5-15%; SK On (SK Innovation 096770.KS) 5-10%; AESC (private, Envision-controlled, PFE status uncertain) 0-15%. From 2027: Ford (F) and GM/LGES Ultium. Plants are in MI, AZ, NV, GA, IN, KY and TN.
supply_tightness: Cell capacity is NOT the binding constraint, because idle EV lines convert in ~6-12 months. The binding constraints are: (1) Non-Chinese LFP cathode, graphite anode, LiPF6/electrolyte and separator, since MACR counts component cost. (2) Qualifying new cells in integrators' DC blocks under UL9540A and NFPA 855 (~6-12 months). (3) Bankability: warranty and degradation data. US-made cells carry a premium of ~$15-35/kWh over Chinese cells (own estimate), which 45X largely offsets.
substitution_risk: Medium. Chinese makers may route supply through non-PFE structures in SE Asia, the Middle East or Morocco, though OBBBA's 'effective control' tests likely block this. Korean NCA/NMC prismatic ESS cells (e.g., Samsung SDI) compete within the non-PFE pool. Sodium-ion is a risk only after 2028.
cyclicality_risk: High exposure to policy: Treasury guidance, possible legislative change after 2028, and how strictly licensing is treated. Overbuild from EV-line conversions could start a price war among Korean makers. Announced capacity is double-counted. US BESS demand is also sensitive to interconnection delays and tax-credit transferability.
faster_sub_niche: Non-Chinese LFP cathode active material and graphite anode for US ESS cells. These are needed to clear the rising MACR. US revenue is near zero in 2026 and should inflect in 2027-2028 (LG Chem, L&F, POSCO Future M, Syrah Vidalia). Flagged EMERGING (<$50M in 2026) and not analyzed further.

name: Large stationary solid-oxide fuel cell (SOFC) systems for data-center and C&I on-site prime power
definition: IN: SOFC systems of >=100 kW per module, fuelled by natural gas, biogas or H2, deployed as on-site prime or bridge power for data centers, utilities' distributed capacity and C&I sites. Revenue = product + installation + service. Covers Bloom Energy Servers, Doosan/Ceres SOFC, MHI SOFC hybrids and FuelCell Energy SOFC. OUT: residential micro-CHP SOFC (Ene-Farm); PAFC/MCFC/PEM stationary; SOEC electrolyzers.
value_chain_path: Power generation, grid & electrification -> Distributed / behind-the-meter generation -> Fuel cells -> Solid-oxide fuel cells -> Large stationary SOFC systems for data-center prime power
also_serves_megatrends: AI data centers (speed-to-power, bypassing interconnection queues)
size_2026_usd: $2.8-3.6B (own estimate; Bloom ~85-90%)
volume_vs_price: About 90-100% of growth is volume (MW shipped). Price per kW is roughly flat to -3% a year: Bloom passes on cost-downs, but data-center buyers pay a premium for speed to power. Growth lasts as long as grid interconnection delays (often 4-7 years in US ISOs) and gas-turbine sell-outs to ~2029-2030 persist.
math: TOP-DOWN. Bloom capacity ~1 GW/yr in 2025, rising to 2 GW/yr by end-2026 (company guidance). 2026: shipments ~0.9-1.2 GW x $2.5-3.0k/kW product + install (own estimate) = $2.3-3.6B, plus service ~$0.2-0.3B. 2030: 2.5-4 GW/yr (requires a further capacity step, unverified) x $2.3-2.8k/kW = $5.8-11B, plus service $0.5-0.8B, plus non-Bloom SOFC $0.3-1B = $7-12B. REVENUE CHECK. Bloom revenue $1.47B in 2024 (reported). Q3-2025 $519M, +57% y/y (reported). FY2025 ~$1.9-2.1B (unverified). FY2026 guidance/consensus ~$2.6-3.4B (unverified). That implies ~40-60% growth in 2026, decelerating to 25-35% a year afterwards.
catalyst_timing: Bloom reaches 2 GW/yr of capacity by end-2026. Brookfield's program of up to $5B (announced Oct 2025) deploys over 2026-2028. AEP up to 1 GW of data-center fuel cells (2025-2027). Oracle OCI sites. The 2027-2029 behind-the-meter wave arrives while heavy-duty GT slots are sold out.
key_suppliers: Estimated shares (own estimates): Bloom Energy (BE, NYSE) ~85-90%; Doosan Fuel Cell (336260.KS; Ceres-licensed SOFC, mass production from ~2025-26) 2-5%; Mitsubishi Heavy (7011.T; SOFC-GT hybrid) ~1%; FuelCell Energy (FCEL) <2%. Ceres Power (CWR.L) earns licensor royalties. Smaller European players: Elcogen, SolydEra, Convion. Upstream: Chaozhou Three-Circle (CCTC, 300408.SZ) supplies SOFC electrolyte substrates/cells (share unverified).
supply_tightness: There is effectively one supplier at scale, but it is not supply-bottlenecked: Bloom can add ~1 GW of stack capacity in roughly 12-18 months (own estimate). Upstream exposures are scandia/yttria-stabilized zirconia (scandium supply is only tens of tonnes a year), nickel and interconnect alloys. Pricing power comes from deployment speed (90-120 days claimed), not scarcity.
substitution_risk: Medium-high. Recips and aeroderivatives cost ~$1.2-2.0k/kW (own estimate) and become easier to procure from 2027. Heavy-duty CCGTs return as slots free up after 2029, alongside grid interconnection. SMRs are a 2030s competitor. SOFC's electric efficiency (~54-60% LHV) beats recips but not CCGT.
cyclicality_risk: High. Customers are concentrated (hyperscalers, Brookfield, AEP). Projects depend on financing. Bridge-power orders are the first cut if AI capex pauses. Natural-gas price exposure. Execution risk specific to Bloom.
faster_sub_niche: Split: SOFC for AI data-center prime/bridge power grows faster than SOFC for C&I/utility. Est. 40-60% CAGR from ~$1.5-2B in 2026 (own estimate), but more cyclical. Analyzed the whole niche because Bloom does not disclose the split.

name: Grid-forming (GFM) power conversion systems and controls for utility-scale BESS
definition: IN: bidirectional central/string PCS and MV power skids for utility BESS. Their firmware runs the inverter as a voltage source (virtual synchronous machine / droop) and they are certified to grid-forming specs (AEMO voluntary spec / access standards, NESO GBGF, ERCOT NOGRR 272 advanced grid support, China 构网型 standards). Includes incremental overload hardware (1.2-3x transient current) and EMT model / TSO study work. OUT: grid-following PCS; PV and wind inverters; STATCOM/SVC; synchronous condensers.
value_chain_path: Power generation, grid & electrification -> Grid-scale BESS -> Power conversion system (PCS) -> Utility-scale BESS PCS -> Grid-forming PCS + control firmware
also_serves_megatrends: Renewables integration / loss of system inertia from coal retirements
AI data centers (weak-grid and islanded microgrids)
size_2026_usd: $0.3-0.8B (own estimate, full GFM PCS value). The incremental GFM premium alone is only ~$0.05-0.2B.
volume_vs_price: Almost entirely volume and share shift: GFM rises from ~5-12% of new utility BESS PCS in 2026 to ~35-55% in 2030 (own estimate). The GFM price premium (+10-30% on PCS) likely erodes toward zero by 2029-30 as GFM becomes standard, and the underlying PCS price deflates (China ~RMB0.10-0.15/W). Growth is volume-driven, so durable, but the niche risks being absorbed into 'PCS'.
math: 2026. Global BESS installs ~350-450 GWh at ~2.7 h average duration, so ~130-170 GW of PCS. Blended PCS price ~$25-40/kW (China ~$15-20/kW; Western markets ~$45-80/kW), so a PCS market of ~$4-6B. GFM at a 5-12% share with a 15-30% premium gives $0.3-0.8B. 2030. ~250-350 GW of PCS x $22-32/kW = $6-10B; GFM at a 35-55% share gives $2.5-5.5B. All are own estimates built on BNEF/CNESA/InfoLink-type installation ranges that were not re-verified this session.
catalyst_timing: ERCOT NOGRR 272 advanced-grid-support requirements for new ESRs, phased 2025-2027 (exact effective dates unverified). Australia's ARENA-funded ~2 GW grid-forming fleet commissions 2025-2027. GB stability markets and the GBGF spec. German TSOs' market-based inertia procurement from ~2026 (unverified). China's 2025-2027 new-type storage action plan (180 GW by 2027) promotes grid-forming storage in desert/Gobi bases and weak grids (Xinjiang, Tibet). NERC IBR registration and standards in 2026.
key_suppliers: Sungrow (300274.SZ; #1 global PCS, est. 20-25% of PCS); Huawei (private); SMA Solar (S92.DE); Tesla (TSLA, in-house Megapack); Power Electronics (private, Spain); Hitachi Energy (6501.T); EPC Power (private, US); Dynapower (Sensata, ST); Ingeteam (private); Gamesa Electric (Siemens Energy group); Kehua (002335.SZ); Sinexcel (300693.SZ); NARI/NR Electric (600406.SS); Hopewind (603063.SS). GFM-specific shares are unverified.
supply_tightness: Hardware (IGBT/SiC modules, magnetics) is not tight. The barriers are software and compliance: field-proven GFM above 100 MW, validated PSCAD/EMT models, TSO studies (6-18 months) and interoperability with plant controllers. Roughly 8-12 vendors are credible outside China (own estimate). Pricing power is moderate and shrinking.
substitution_risk: Medium. Synchronous condensers (Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, ABB, Andritz) and E-STATCOMs can supply system strength. Regulators may accept grid-following PCS plus condensers. Wind and PV GFM inverters come later.
cyclicality_risk: Medium-high. Chinese PCS price war. BESS demand swings with tariffs and ITC rules. Definitional risk: once GFM is default, the niche disappears into PCS.
faster_sub_niche: GFM PCS for non-China markets (Australia, ERCOT, GB, Middle East, Chile) carries 2-4x the $/kW of Chinese domestic PCS. Est. 50-70% revenue CAGR there versus ~30-45% in China (own estimate).

name: SF6-free high-voltage switchgear (52-145 kV now, 245-420 kV later): vacuum/clean-air and C4-FN-mixture GIS and dead-tank breakers
definition: IN: GIS bays, dead-tank and live-tank circuit breakers, GIL and HV disconnectors at >=52 kV that interrupt with vacuum and insulate with synthetic/clean air (Siemens Energy 'Blue', Japanese dry-air designs) or use fluoronitrile/fluoroketone mixtures (GE Vernova g3, Hitachi Energy EconiQ). OUT: MV (<52 kV) RMUs and switchgear (their EU ban took effect in 2026, a one-step change); SF6 retrofill and recycling services; conventional SF6 gear.
value_chain_path: Power generation, grid & electrification -> Transmission substations -> HV switchgear & circuit breakers -> Gas-insulated switchgear / dead-tank breakers -> SF6-free HV switchgear (vacuum/clean-air and C4-FN)
also_serves_megatrends: Grid expansion / offshore wind and data-center substations
size_2026_usd: $0.7-1.6B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: About 80-90% share shift: the SF6-free share of HV gear in EU/UK/California/Japan/Korea/Australia rises from ~6-10% to ~30-45%. About 10-20% is price, since SF6-free bays carry an est. 10-30% premium. Regulation drives it, not shortage, so it is durable, but 2026-27 is damped by pre-ban SF6 orders and steps up from 2028.
math: Addressable HV switchgear (>=72.5 kV GIS + breakers) outside China ~$11-15B in 2026 (own estimate from OEM segment scale; China's domestic market ~$6-9B is excluded). SF6-free share ~6-10% gives $0.7-1.5B. By 2030 the drivers are the EU 52-145 kV ban from 1 Jan 2028 (with tender-based derogations), CARB's phase-out, UK alignment and voluntary utility commitments. A ~30-45% share of a ~$13-17B pool gives $3.9-7B; after a derogation haircut, $3.5-6B. SUPPLIER CHECK (own estimates, unverified): Siemens Energy Blue ~€0.3-0.6B; Hitachi Energy EconiQ HV ~$0.2-0.4B; GE Vernova g3 ~$0.1-0.3B; Japanese dry-air makers (Mitsubishi Electric, Meidensha, Toshiba) ~$0.1-0.3B. Total $0.7-1.6B.
catalyst_timing: EU Regulation 2024/573 bans new SF6 switchgear in steps: <=24 kV from 2026, 52-145 kV from 1 Jan 2028, 24-52 kV from 2030, >145 kV from 1 Jan 2032 (derogations if tenders yield no SF6-free offer). CARB's SF6 GIE phase-out runs by voltage class over 2025-2033. ECHA's universal PFAS restriction is being decided in 2026-27 and could restrict C4-FN. TSO framework tenders (TenneT, Amprion, 50Hertz, National Grid) run 2026-2028.
key_suppliers: Estimated shares of SF6-free HV (own estimates): Siemens Energy (ENR.DE; vacuum + clean air 'Blue', leader at 72.5-145 kV) 35-45%; Hitachi Energy (6501.T; EconiQ incl. 420 kV) 20-30%; GE Vernova (GEV; g3) 10-20%; Mitsubishi Electric (6503.T), Meidensha (6508.T) and Toshiba (private since 2023), all dry-air, 10-15% combined. Also: Hyosung Heavy Industries (298040.KS), LS Electric (010120.KS), HD Hyundai Electric (267260.KS). China: Pinggao (600312.SS) and China XD (601179.SS) are piloting eco-gas GIS.
supply_tightness: High barriers. Capacity for HV vacuum interrupters is concentrated (Siemens Berlin, Meidensha, Toshiba, Mitsubishi Electric). Type-testing at high-power labs (KEMA, CESI, IPH) takes 12-24 months. C4-FN supply was disrupted by 3M's PFAS-manufacturing exit (end-2025), so g3/EconiQ makers need alternative gas producers. Utilities want 2-5 years of service experience before broad adoption.
substitution_risk: Medium. Derogations, where no SF6-free offer exists or costs are prohibitive, could delay adoption. SF6 stays legal above 145 kV until 2032. C4-FN itself faces PFAS risk, which would shift share within the niche toward vacuum/clean-air.
cyclicality_risk: Low-moderate. Demand follows multi-year utility frameworks. Pre-ban SF6 pull-forward in 2026-27 creates a dip then a step-up in 2028.
faster_sub_niche: Split: HV vacuum interrupters for 72.5-145 kV single-break breakers are <$100M in 2026 and could reach ~$0.3-0.6B by 2030 (own estimate; Siemens Energy dominant). Flagged EMERGING. MV SF6-free (<52 kV) is larger (~$2-4B, own estimate) but its EU step-change already happened in 2026, so it grows only ~8-12%. The 52-145 kV HV segment was kept as the faster one.

evidence.claim: EU F-gas Regulation (EU) 2024/573, Annex IV, bans placing new SF6 switchgear on the market by voltage class: <=24 kV from 2026, 52-145 kV from 1 Jan 2028, 24-52 kV from 2030, >145 kV from 1 Jan 2032, with limited derogations.
evidence.label: reported fact
evidence.source: EUR-Lex, Official Journal of the EU

evidence.label: reported fact
evidence.source: California Air Resources Board rulemaking. Class dates not re-verified.

evidence.claim: 3M committed to exit all PFAS manufacturing by end-2025. This covers Novec 4710 (C4-FN), the fluoronitrile used in g3/EconiQ-type gas mixtures.
evidence.label: reported fact

evidence.label: reported fact

name: 765 kV-class EHV autotransformers and shunt reactors for new US 765 kV backbones (ERCOT, MISO, PJM, SPP)
definition: IN: for US projects, single-phase 765/345 kV autotransformers (typically 500-750 MVA per phase, built in banks of 3 plus a spare), 765 kV shunt reactors (~100-300 MVAr) and, where noted, 800 kV breakers/GIS. OUT: <=500 kV LPTs; India and China UHV/EHV markets (served by domestic makers, not a technology transition there); HVDC converter transformers.
value_chain_path: Power generation, grid & electrification -> Transmission -> AC substations -> Large power transformers & reactors -> 765 kV EHV autotransformers and shunt reactors for US backbones
also_serves_megatrends: AI data-center load growth (ERCOT large loads)
size_2026_usd: $0.15-0.35B (own estimate: replacements/expansions on the existing AEP/APCo 765 kV system plus the first new-program deliveries)
volume_vs_price: About 75% volume (dozens of new 765 kV stations across ERCOT, MISO Tranche 2.1, PJM and SPP) and about 25% price. EHV transformer prices have risen a lot since 2020; industry commentary suggests roughly +60-80% (unverified). Further price escalation is limited after ~2028 as new US capacity comes online.
math: PROGRAMS. US 765 kV programs approved or near approval: ERCOT 765 kV STEP (~$30-33B planner estimate, including Permian import paths approved Apr 2025); MISO Tranche 2.1 ($21.8B, of which 765 kV backbone est. 40-60%); PJM 2024 RTEP window (~$5.9B, incl. Valley Link 765 kV); SPP 2024 ITP (~$7.7B, incl. first 765 kV lines). That is ~$45-60B of 765 kV-related capex, in service 2029-2034. EQUIPMENT SHARE. Substations ~25-35% of capex; major equipment ~45-55% of substation cost; so equipment ~12-18% of capex = $5.5-11B over 2027-2034, or ~$1.0-2.0B/yr by 2030 (deliveries start ~2028). UNIT CHECK. ~150-250 single-phase 765 kV autotransformers and ~60-120 reactors x ~$8-15M (auto) / ~$4-8M (reactor) = $1.5-4.5B for transformers and reactors alone. All own estimates.
catalyst_timing: Apr 2025: PUCT approves the Permian 765 kV import paths. 2025-26: decisions on ERCOT's eastern 765 kV portions (unverified). 2025-2027: utility CCN filings. 2025-2027: major equipment orders placed to reserve 2028-2031 production slots. 2029-2032: energization. 2032-2034: MISO Tranche 2.1 in service.
key_suppliers: Estimated shares (own estimates): Hitachi Energy (6501.T; historic US 765 kV leader; South Boston, VA LPT expansion) 30-40%; HD Hyundai Electric (267260.KS; Montgomery, AL) 15-25%; Hyosung Heavy Industries (298040.KS; Memphis, TN, expansion to 765 kV reported) 10-20%; Siemens Energy (ENR.DE; EU plants, planned Charlotte, NC LPT plant ~2027) 10-20%. Others: GE Vernova/Prolec GE (GEV; 765 kV capability unverified); Mitsubishi Electric (6503.T); Toshiba (private); SGB-SMIT; Indian exporters (Hitachi Energy India, CG Power).
supply_tightness: Very tight. Few plants worldwide can build and test 765 kV units: they need >1,000 kV impulse test bays, large vapour-phase drying ovens and special heavy-haul logistics. Lead times were ~3-5 years in 2025. 800 kV RIP bushings and EHV OLTCs/reactor components are also constrained. Utility design reviews and qualification take 12-24 months. Chinese supply is effectively excluded (tariffs, security).
substitution_risk: Low-medium. 345 kV double circuits or HVDC are alternatives (ERCOT chose 765 kV over 345 kV in 2025). GETs and reconductoring may defer some lines.
cyclicality_risk: Medium-high on timing: CCN delays, cost overruns, and political pushback on ratepayer cost. The small 2026 base makes the CAGR very sensitive to slippage. Lumpy after 2032.
faster_sub_niche: 765 kV shunt reactors and 800 kV RIP bushings. They have fewer qualified suppliers, and reactor count per mile rises on ERCOT's long 765 kV corridors. Similar or higher CAGR from a smaller base (unverified).

name: Single-crystal / directionally-solidified hot-section airfoil castings (blades and vanes) for heavy-duty gas turbines, new units plus hot-gas-path (HGP) spares
definition: IN: investment-cast nickel-superalloy turbine blades (buckets) and vanes (nozzles), SX/DS for stages 1-2 and DS/equiaxed for later stages, for heavy-duty (>100 MW) and large industrial gas turbines. Covers new-unit sets and replacement HGP spares, including core/shell, casting, and the caster's own machining and coating. Valued at external price or OEM transfer price. OUT: aero-engine airfoils, compressor blades, airfoil repair services, combustors/transition pieces.
value_chain_path: Power generation, grid & electrification -> Gas-fired generation -> Heavy-duty gas turbines -> Hot-gas-path components -> SX/DS turbine blade & vane castings
also_serves_megatrends: Coal-to-gas switching in Asia and the Middle East
Aerospace (shared casting capacity and alloys compete for furnaces)
size_2026_usd: $2.7-4.8B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: About 55-65% volume: new-unit GW +12-15% a year and spares +6-10% a year as the installed base runs at higher capacity factors. About 35-45% price: long-term agreements are being re-priced, with casting prices rising high-single to low-double digits a year while the shortage lasts (own estimate). The price share is the less durable part and fades once Chinese second sources and new furnaces qualify (~2028+).
math: NEW UNITS. Global heavy-duty GT deliveries ~45-60 GW in 2026: GE Vernova ~16-20 GW ramping to 20 GW/yr by H2-26; Siemens Energy ~12-16; MHI ~12-16; others 5-8. By 2030 ~70-86 GW: GE ~24, Siemens 18-22, MHI 20-25, others 8-15 (unverified). Hot-section airfoil content ~$20-30M/GW (own estimate: ~300-450 turbine airfoils per H-class unit at ~$25-40k average; stage-1 SX blades higher). New-unit castings: 2026 ~$0.9-1.8B; 2030 ~$1.5-2.8B. SPARES. ~1.5-2.5x new-unit value: 2026 ~$1.8-3.0B; 2030 ~$2.8-4.5B. TOTAL: $2.7-4.8B (2026) and $4.5-7.5B (2030). SUPPLIER SUM, 2026 IGT airfoil revenue (own estimates): PCC Airfoils $1.0-1.5B; Howmet $0.8-1.1B; Doncasters $0.3-0.5B; CPP $0.2-0.4B; Chromalloy castings $0.2-0.4B; MHI in-house $0.3-0.6B; Doosan in-house and Chinese casters $0.1-0.4B. Total ~$2.9-4.9B, consistent with the top-down figure.
catalyst_timing: H2-2026: GE Vernova reaches 20 GW/yr of heavy-duty capacity. ~2028: further step toward ~24 GW/yr reported (unverified). 2026-2028: Siemens Energy and MHI capacity steps. Hyperscaler- and utility-driven CCGT FIDs in 2026-2028 lead to CODs in 2028-2031. A spares wave follows as the 2028+ H/J fleet reaches its first HGP intervals (~24-32k equivalent operating hours).
key_suppliers: Estimated shares (own estimates): PCC / PCC Airfoils (Berkshire Hathaway, BRK) 30-40%; Howmet Aerospace (HWM) 20-30%; Doncasters (private, UK) 8-12%; Consolidated Precision Products (private, US) 5-10%; Chromalloy (private, US) 5-8%; MHI in-house (7011.T) 8-12%. Others: Doosan Enerbility (034020.KS) in-house; Chinese entrants Yingliu (603308.SS) and Wanze (000534.SZ) qualifying with Western OEMs (unverified).
supply_tightness: Tight. Large SX IGT blades need large-bore Bridgman/LMC furnaces, ceramic cores (few suppliers, often in-house) and rhenium-bearing alloys (rhenium supply ~tens of tonnes a year). Large SX parts have low casting yields (~50-70%, own estimate). OEM part qualification takes 12-24 months, and new furnace lines take ~18-30 months. OEM commentary through 2025 named castings and forgings as the gas-turbine bottleneck. Strong pricing power through ~2028.
substitution_risk: Low through 2030. Ceramic matrix composites appear in some IGT shrouds/nozzles, but CMC rotating blades in heavy-duty IGT are not expected before 2030. Additive manufacturing is limited to burners, some vanes and repair. Airfoil repair and life extension partly substitute for new spares.
cyclicality_risk: Medium-high. Gas turbine super-cycles have bust before (orders collapsed after 2002). Slot reservations can mean double ordering. AI load forecasts may be revised. Chinese casters entering Western supply chains after 2027 add capacity and price pressure.
faster_sub_niche: Split: new-unit SX stage-1/2 castings for H/J-class (7HA.03, 9HA, SGT5-9000HL, M501JAC) grow ~15-22%. That beats spares (~8-12%), because H/J units take a larger share of orders and carry more SX content per stage. Kept as the faster sub-niche.

name: VSC-HVDC (MMC) converter valves and stations, +/-320-525 kV, 1-2 GW
definition: IN: modular multilevel VSC converter valves (submodules with press-pack/StakPak IGBTs and DC capacitors), valve cooling, control and protection, and the converter-station scope sold within HVDC EPC contracts, onshore and offshore. OUT: LCC thyristor UHVDC (mostly China/India), HVDC cables, offshore platform steel/topside fabrication, DC breakers.
value_chain_path: Power generation, grid & electrification -> Transmission -> HVDC -> Converter stations -> VSC-MMC converter valves and stations
size_2026_usd: $7-11B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: About 70% volume (GW of converter capacity delivered roughly doubles as 2023-25 awards move into execution) and about 30% price (prices per GW rose sharply in 2022-25, and OEMs now require capacity-reservation fees and risk sharing). Mostly durable because backlogs are contracted, though offshore wind slippage is a risk.
math: Converter-station value ~$0.6-1.0B per GW for a 2 GW 525 kV onshore + offshore pair, excluding cable and platform steel (own estimate). Deliveries ~10-14 GW-equivalent in 2026 give ~$7-11B; ~20-26 GW in 2030 gives ~$14-22B. SUPPLIER SUM, 2026 HVDC revenue (own estimates, unverified): Hitachi Energy ~$3-4B; Siemens Energy ~€2.5-3.5B; GE Vernova ~$1-1.5B; Chinese VSC makers ~$1.5-2.5B; others ~$0.3-0.6B. VSC is ~70-80% of the non-China total.
catalyst_timing: Execution of TenneT 2 GW program systems (2026-2031, with some sites re-phased). UK Eastern Green Links and Scottish links (2027-2030). German corridor and offshore systems (Amprion, 50Hertz). US VSC lines (2027-2030). India's VSC pilots. China's offshore wind VSC.
key_suppliers: Estimated shares of non-China VSC (own estimates): Hitachi Energy (6501.T) 35-45%; Siemens Energy (ENR.DE) 30-40%; GE Vernova (GEV) 15-25%. China: NR Electric (state-owned, unlisted), NARI (600406.SS), XJ Electric (000400.SZ), China XD (601179.SS), TBEA (600089.SS). India: BHEL with Hitachi Energy. IGBT supply: Hitachi Energy semiconductors (in-house), Infineon (IFX.DE), Toshiba (private), CRRC Times Electric (688187.SS / 3898.HK).
supply_tightness: Tight. Only three Western OEMs execute 525 kV VSC. Factory and engineering capacity (valve halls, test, engineers) is reserved into ~2029-2030. Press-pack IGBTs, DC capacitors and converter transformers are long-lead items. Customers sign multi-year capacity-reservation frameworks.
substitution_risk: Low. HVAC is used only for short offshore distances. LCC is for point-to-point bulk lines. Multi-terminal DC grids (2030+) are an extension, not a substitute.
cyclicality_risk: Medium. Offshore wind auction failures (e.g., Germany's zero-bid 2025 round) and TSO capex re-phasing can delay revenue. Contracts with fixed prices signed in 2021-23 still carry margin risk.
faster_sub_niche: Press-pack/StakPak IGBT modules for MMC valves: ~$0.4-0.9B in 2026 (own estimate, unverified), similar CAGR but tighter supply (Hitachi Energy Lenzburg, Infineon, Toshiba, CRRC Times Electric). Offshore 2 GW systems were the fastest in 2023-25 but now face slippage. Onshore VSC interconnectors and US/India VSC may lead growth in 2027-30.

name: AP1000 nuclear-island long-lead equipment for Western new build (ultra-large forgings, RPV/SG fabrication, canned-motor RCPs, ASME III pumps/valves)
definition: IN: long-lead items (LLI) of the Westinghouse AP1000 nuclear island procured for units outside China/Russia (US, Poland, Bulgaria, later Canada etc.): ultra-large forgings (RPV shells/heads, SG tubesheets/channel heads, nozzles), RPV + closure head, 2 steam generators, pressurizer, 4 canned-motor reactor coolant pumps, CRDMs/integrated head package, passive-safety tanks/heat exchangers, ASME Section III safety-class pumps and valves (incl. squib valves); measured as supplier equipment revenue plus Westinghouse procurement margin on these items. OUT: turbine island, civil/EPC labour, structural modules, fuel, digital I&C, China's domestic CAP1000 supply chain, APR1400/EPR equipment (adjacent, same supplier set).
value_chain_path: Nuclear -> new build -> Gen III+ large LWR (AP1000) -> nuclear island -> long-lead items ordered pre-FID (DOE LLI program) -> ultra-large forgings / RPV-SG fabrication / canned-motor RCPs
also_serves_megatrends: US industrial policy + Japan/Korea FDI pledges ($80B Commerce program)

math: Top-down BOM per AP1000 unit (own estimate): RPV+head $120-200M; 2 SGs $150-250M; pressurizer $25-40M; 4 canned-motor RCPs $100-180M; CRDM/IHP $40-70M; ASME III pumps+valves $120-200M (Flowserve alone cites a ~$100M organic / ~$115M with Trillium addressable 'prize' per reactor); passive tanks/HX $40-80M => ~$0.6-1.0B nuclear-island LLI per unit. Orders (base): 10 US (DOE program) + 3 Poland + 2 Bulgaria = 15 units x $0.6-1.0B = $9-15B intake placed 2026-2028. CW says contract revenue follows a ~5-year bell curve -> ~20-25% of intake recognized per year at peak -> 2030 revenue ~$2.0-3.3B. Bear: 4-6 units ordered by 2028 -> $0.5-1.2B. Canned-motor RCPs: Curtiss-Wright (NYSE: CW, EMD) - effectively sole qualified AP1000 RCP supplier (~100%, own assessment). RPV/SG/pressurizer: Doosan Enerbility (KRX: 034020; supplied Vogtle 3/4 heavy components; est. 50-70% of Western AP1000 heavy components historically, unverified), ENSA (Spain, SEPI), Mitsubishi Heavy (TSE: 7011, possible), BWXT (NYSE: BWXT; planning US deep-water large-component plant, acquired PCG with AP1000 component history). Ultra-large forgings: Japan Steel Works (TSE: 5631), Doosan (captive), Framatome Creusot (mostly EPR), Japan Casting & Forging, Sheffield Forgemasters (UK MoD), Larsen & Toubro (NSE: LT); Chinese CFHI/Shanghai Electric excluded politically for US/EU. supply_tightness: Few qualified ultra-large forging presses outside China (~5-7 shops); RPV/SG lead times ~3-5 years; RCPs delivered over a ~5-year bell curve; ASME III N-stamp + 10 CFR 50 App. B qualification takes years. Becomes binding if >6-8 units' LLI are ordered within ~18 months while naval programs (2 Virginia + 1 Columbia per year, Ford-class on 4-year cadence) compete for the same capacity. Suppliers are passing through cost (CW 'adjusting prices') and getting customers/government to co-fund capacity (CW $80M Chesapeake expansion with Navy industrial-base money; BWXT $21M DOE award).

Larger risks: program cancellation, or utilities choosing gas if turbine slots open. Within AP1000 the canned-motor RCP is design-locked (low substitution); forgings could migrate among Japanese/Korean/Indian shops.
cyclicality_risk: High. History of order cliffs (1970s cancellations; 2008-2012 'renaissance' with ~30 US COL applications and only 4 units started). Double counting: Westinghouse's 91-unit pipeline, DOE's 10, Commerce's 10 and 'another 10' utility opportunities overlap. Supplier capacity additions (BWXT US plant, CW Chesapeake, Doosan) could overbuild if FIDs slip past 2028.
faster_sub_niche: Split pre-FID LLI tranche (DOE program) vs post-FID balance. Fastest: canned-motor RCPs (CW, sole source) and ultra-large RPV/SG forgings, which sit first on the critical path and are being ordered before FID. name: HALEU (5-20% U-235) enrichment and deconversion
definition: IN: production of HALEU UF6 from enrichment cascades and its deconversion to oxide or metal for advanced-reactor fuel fabrication, incl. DOE-funded HALEU production contracts and commercial offtakes. OUT: LEU <5% and LEU+ 5-10% (separate candidate), TRISO and metallic fuel fabrication (too early), downblended HEU/EBR-II material and surplus plutonium (treated as substitutes).
value_chain_path: Nuclear -> fuel-cycle front end -> enrichment -> high-assay LEU (HALEU) -> HALEU UF6 cascades + UF6-to-oxide/metal deconversion
also_serves_megatrends: Energy security (Russia/TENEX was the only commercial HALEU seller)
size_2026_usd: $0.05-0.12B, almost all DOE contract revenue (own estimate; Centrus Technical Solutions revenue $32.1M Q1 + $22.7M Q2 2026, mostly HALEU operations); commercial HALEU sales ~$0 - EMERGING

math: Physics (own calc): 19.75% HALEU from natural feed at 0.25% tails needs ~42 kgU feed and ~41 SWU per kgU. At ~$200/SWU and ~$290/kgU feed+conversion, material+SWU cost ~ $20-21k/kgU before FOAK premium -> price assumption $25-40k/kgU (own estimate). 2030 Western HALEU output 5-15 tU (Centrus base build-out includes 12 t HALEU capacity, first new capacity 2029; others later) x $25-40k = $0.13-0.6B, plus DOE milestone revenue (Centrus $900M award, potentially >$1B, paid ratably on milestones -> ~$0.1-0.25B/yr) and deconversion fees -> $0.25-0.8B. CAGR (0.5/0.08)^(1/4)-1 ~ 58% at midpoints. A $1B market is a 2031-2033 event unless DoD/Janus pulls demand forward.
catalyst_timing: Jan 2026 DOE $900M HALEU enrichment award to Centrus (being finalized); first Centrus Oak Ridge centrifuge 2026; Piketon first new capacity 2029; X-energy definitive HALEU offtake (Aug 2026); Oklo LOI for up to 5 Aurora powerhouses from 2029; Aurora INL start-up 2028; Oklo A3F fuel fab start-up 2027; DOE HALEU deconversion award pending; Russian LEU waivers end 1 Jan 2028; Janus microreactor award expected 2026.
key_suppliers: Centrus Energy (NYSE American: LEU) - only operating US HALEU cascade (16 centrifuges; ~2 t HALEU UF6 produced cumulatively), ~100% of operating Western output in 2026 (own assessment); Urenco (private; UK/NL governments + RWE/E.ON) - Capenhurst HALEU later in decade; Orano (French state) - US plans; Global Laser Enrichment (Silex ASX: SLX 51% / Cameco 49%) - post-2030; General Matter (private, unverified scale); BWXT (NYSE: BWXT) - HEU downblending and NNSA centrifuge program. Deconversion: no commercial plant; Centrus-Oklo JV under study.
supply_tightness: Extreme: operating Western HALEU capacity on the order of ~1 t/yr; centrifuge manufacturing being re-established (Centrus $560M Oak Ridge program, ~42-month first-cascade timeline); NRC Category II security; deconversion to metal/oxide not available at scale. substitution_risk: High medium-term: DOE surplus plutonium (~20 t tranche) as HALEU-equivalent at ~10-13% Pu (Oklo); recovered EBR-II and downblended HEU; reactor designs that use LEU (NuScale, BWRX-300, AP300) or LEU+; Gen-IV programs slipping.
cyclicality_risk: Overbuild risk if 4-5 entrants (Centrus, Urenco, Orano, GLE, General Matter) all add HALEU capacity while advanced-reactor fleets slip into the 2030s; demand concentrated in a handful of developers (X-energy, TerraPower, Oklo, Kairos).
faster_sub_niche: Deconversion (UF6 -> metal/oxide) is the scarcer step (no commercial plant) and may earn higher margins, but its revenue pool is much smaller than HALEU SWU; neither is commercial before 2028-2029.

name: High-purity hafnium (by-product of nuclear-grade zirconium Zr/Hf separation)
definition: IN: reactor-grade/high-purity hafnium (sponge, crystal bar, oxide, HfCl4 feed) produced when Hf is separated from Zr to make nuclear-grade zirconium, sold into Ni-base and Nb-Hf (C103) superalloys, naval/PWR control rods and semiconductor precursors; parent nuclear-grade Zr sponge/ingot noted as slower sub-segment. OUT: zircon sand, industrial Zr chemicals, captive cladding-tube fabrication (Westinghouse/Framatome/GNF), formulated ALD precursor margins (Merck, Entegris etc.).
value_chain_path: Nuclear -> fuel fabrication -> cladding -> nuclear-grade zirconium (Zr/Hf separation) -> high-purity hafnium by-product
also_serves_megatrends: Next-gen jet engines (Ni superalloys; ATI content >2x legacy engines)
size_2026_usd: $0.25-0.5B for hafnium (own estimate; volumes/prices unverified); Western nuclear-grade Zr + Hf combined ~$1.0-1.5B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: ~55-70% price, ~30-45% volume. Hf supply is inelastic (tied to nuclear Zr output, +3-6%/yr) while engine, missile and semiconductor demand grows faster and China restricts exports -> price-led and therefore less durable if Chinese exports normalise.
math: Hf:Zr ~1:50 in zircon, so Hf output is mechanically tied to nuclear-grade Zr production; global Hf ~70-100 t/yr (USGS-style estimate [STALE], unverified). Price: ~$1,000/kg (2020-21) to ~$5,000-7,000/kg in 2023 per trade press [STALE: 2023-24, unverified]; ATI says 2026 guidance uses near-current prices. 2026: 80 t x $3-6k/kg = $0.24-0.48B. 2030: 90-110 t x $3.5-7k/kg = $0.32-0.77B. Supplier cross-check: ATI 'zirconium and related products' just under 10% of ~$4.6B 2025 revenue = ~$0.40-0.45B (covers Zr, Hf, Nb), for one of three Western producers.
catalyst_timing: Ongoing Chinese export limits (per ATI, 2026); next-gen engines rising from ~35% to >50% of installed fleet by 2030; missile ramps (ATI missile revenue ~4x in Q2 2026); ATI naval nuclear contract through 2030 at ~2x prior value; new-build Zr demand from ~2028.
key_suppliers: Framatome (EDF; CEZUS, France) - largest Hf producer (est. 40-50% of world, unverified); ATI (NYSE: ATI; Albany, OR) - 'one of three qualified Western producers' (est. 15-25%); Westinghouse Western Zirconium (Ogden, UT) (est. 10-20%); TVEL/Chepetsky (Russia), CNNC Jinghuan / State Nuclear Baoti (China), NFC (India) - largely inaccessible to Western aerospace/defense. Shares own estimates.
supply_tightness: Three qualified Western producers; new Zr/Hf separation capacity plus aerospace/nuclear qualification takes years; ATI reported Hf/Zr and exotic-alloy lead times extending up to 2x within a quarter (Feb 2026) and is re-pricing via LTAs.
substitution_risk: Medium: Zr- or La-doped dielectrics in semis; Hf content can be trimmed in some superalloys; B4C/Ag-In-Cd alternatives for control rods.
cyclicality_risk: Price spikes followed by Chinese supply normalisation (2023 pattern); a nuclear-grade Zr capacity step-up would raise by-product Hf supply and cap prices.
faster_sub_niche: Split hafnium (8-18%, price-led, multi-megatrend) vs nuclear-grade Zr sponge/ingot (~4-7%, volume-led, nuclear only); hafnium is the faster sub-niche.

evidence.claim: ATI is one of three qualified Western producers of high-purity hafnium and zirconium for aerospace and nuclear; China is limiting exports to these markets; improved Hf/Zr pricing helped lift AA&S segment margin to a record 23.7% (+930 bp y/y).
evidence.label: reported fact

evidence.claim: ATI's new naval nuclear contract is ~USD 1B over 5 years, ~2x the prior contract, with ~2/3 of the increase from price/mix and ~1/3 from volume.

evidence.claim: ATI acknowledged 'big moves on the hafnium market'; zirconium and related products are just under 10% of revenue (2025 revenue USD 4.6B); 2026 guidance uses near-current prices; lead times for hafnium, zirconium and other exotic alloys extended up to 2x vs a quarter earlier.
evidence.label: reported fact

evidence.claim: Industry forecasts cited by ATI: next-generation engines rise from ~35% to >50% of the installed fleet by 2030, with ATI content per engine >2x legacy; ATI missile revenue up ~4x in Q2 2026 (C103 and Ti-6-4 for PAC-3/THAAD).
evidence.label: third-party estimate

evidence.claim: Counter-signal: BWXT reports zirconium tubes and large forgings have been obtainable so far for its nuclear programs.
evidence.label: company guidance

notes: Strong evidence of tightness and pricing power (ATI), weak evidence on market size (USGS/Argus/Fastmarkets not retrievable). A genuine multi-megatrend bottleneck, but growth is mostly price, so likely mid-pack economy-wide.

name: Low-cost kinetic counter-UAS interceptors (<~$150k per shot)
definition: IN: expendable hit-to-kill or proximity-fuzed interceptors built to defeat Group 1-3 UAS and one-way-attack drones at <~$150k per shot. That covers (i) interceptor drones (quadcopter, fixed-wing or jet, ~$2k-80k), (ii) Coyote Block 2-class jet interceptors (~$100-125k), and (iii) 70 mm laser-guided rockets bought for C-UAS (APKWS, Thales FZ275 LGR). OUT: SAMs (Stinger, IRIS-T, CAMM, PAC-3), gun systems and programmable ammo, directed energy, EW/jamming, sensors and C2.
value_chain_path: Defense & rearmament -> integrated air & missile defense -> counter-UAS -> kinetic effectors -> low-cost interceptors (<$150k) -> interceptor drones / Coyote-class / guided-rocket C-UAS
also_serves_megatrends: homeland & critical-infrastructure security (airports, energy sites, EU 'drone wall' after Sept-2025 incursions)
size_2026_usd: $1.5-3.0B (own estimate): Coyote ~$0.4-0.7B + APKWS-class C-UAS share ~$0.3-0.6B + interceptor drones ~$0.5-1.5B (mostly Ukrainian domestic; Western <$0.2B)
volume_vs_price: More than 90% volume. ASPs fall (interceptor drones from ~$5k toward ~$2k; Coyote cost-down; APKWS price cuts), so revenue grows more slowly than units. Durable volume growth, not shortage pricing.
math: 2030 top-down (own estimate): interceptor drones 1-2M units/yr (Ukraine 0.5-1M; NATO, Gulf and Asia 0.3-1M) x $2-5k = $2-6B. Coyote-class 4,000-8,000/yr x $90-120k = $0.4-1.0B. Guided rockets used as C-UAS 30-50k/yr x $20-28k = $0.6-1.4B. Total ~$3-8.4B, central ~$5-7B. 2026 base: Coyote ~$0.4-0.7B/yr (the Army's ~$5.04B multi-year Coyote award spread over ~8 years is ~$0.6B/yr); APKWS ~25-30k units x ~$25-30k = $0.6-0.9B, of which ~40-60% is C-UAS; interceptor drones ~100-300k units x $3-5k = $0.3-1.5B. Sum ~$1.5-3.0B. Midpoint growth $2.2B -> $6.5B = ~31% CAGR.
catalyst_timing: Sept 2025: Russian drone incursions into Poland, then the EU Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030 (16 Oct 2025) with a European Drone Defence Initiative (initial capability end-2026, full end-2027). 2025-26: Ukraine targets ~1,000 interceptor drones per day. FY2026-27 US budgets and JIATF-401 consolidating C-UAS buys (Aug 2025). Gulf and Red Sea demand. Domestic C-UAS authorities for 2026 World Cup and 2028 Olympics.
key_suppliers: RTX/Raytheon (NYSE: RTX): Coyote, ~100% of US low-cost jet interceptors. BAE Systems (LSE: BA.): APKWS, ~80-90% of Western 70 mm LGR. Thales (EPA: HO): FZ275 LGR, ~10-15%. Anduril (private): Anvil, Roadrunner (the latter above $150k, so excluded). Ukrainian makers (Wild Hornets 'Sting', others; fragmented). European startups: Frankenburg (EE), Nordic Air Defence (SE), Tytan (DE), Alpine Eagle (DE), Origin Robotics (LV), MARSS (UK), Cambridge Aerospace (UK). US: Perennial Autonomy, AeroVironment (Nasdaq: AVAV) via BlueHalo. Interceptor-drone shares are unverified and highly fragmented.
supply_tightness: Mixed. Coyote and APKWS: few qualified suppliers, constrained by seeker, small engine and rocket-motor sub-tiers. Interceptor drones: low airframe barriers, but bottlenecks in non-Chinese thermal cameras, NDAA-compliant motors/magnets, and terminal-guidance autonomy. Low pricing power at airframe level; moderate at Coyote/APKWS.
substitution_risk: HEL/HPM (near-zero cost per shot) after ~2028. Gun systems with programmable airburst (Rheinmetall Skyranger). EW. Cheaper interceptor drones cannibalise Coyote/APKWS ASPs.
cyclicality_risk: HIGH. A Ukraine ceasefire would remove the largest volume pool. Low entry barriers invite dozens of EU/US startups, leading to price deflation and possible double-ordering across national pilot programs.
faster_sub_niche: Western (NATO, Gulf, Asia-Pacific) interceptor drones: ~$0.1-0.3B (2026) -> $1.5-4B (2030), CAGR ~60-100%+ (own estimate, low confidence). Its 2026 base is near the emerging threshold. Guided-rocket C-UAS grows more slowly (~15-25%).

name: Small expendable turbine engines (~50-1,500 lbf turbojets and small turbofans) for cruise missiles, affordable-mass munitions, decoys and jet OWA/target drones
definition: IN: engines for Tomahawk (Williams F107), JASSM/LRASM (F107 / Teledyne J402), Harpoon, NSM, SCALP/Storm Shadow (Safran TRI 40/60), Taurus, MALD, and low-cost cruise missiles (ERAM, USAF FAMM, Anduril Barracuda, MBDA One Way Effector, Lockheed CMMT). Also jet one-way-attack and target drones, and jet C-UAS interceptors. OUT: CCA-class engines >2,000 lbf (FJ44/F130 class), APUs, ramjets/scramjets, piston engines (Shahed-class).
value_chain_path: Defense & rearmament -> munitions -> long-range strike / 'affordable mass' -> air-breathing propulsion -> small expendable turbojets/turbofans (<=1,500 lbf) -> low-cost turbojet sub-segment
also_serves_megatrends: autonomous combat aircraft (shared engine supply base with CCAs)
size_2026_usd: $0.8-1.4B (own estimate)
volume_vs_price: ~80% volume (Tomahawk/JASSM rate increases plus thousands of low-cost cruise missiles). ~20% mix and price: new 800-1,500 lbf engines carry higher ASPs than sub-300 lbf drone engines, and near-term shortage pricing exists, partly offset by cost-per-lbf reduction.
math: 2026 (own estimate): Tomahawk 100-250 x $0.25-0.4M = $0.03-0.1B. JASSM/LRASM 700-1,100 x $0.2-0.35M = $0.14-0.39B. Other Western cruise/anti-ship (NSM, Harpoon, SCALP, Taurus, Exocet, Korea/Japan/Turkey) 1,000-2,000 x $0.1-0.3M = $0.1-0.6B. Decoys/targets 500-1,000 x $0.05-0.2M = $0.03-0.2B. Low-cost cruise/jet OWA 2,000-8,000 x $20-80k = $0.04-0.64B. Total ~$0.35-1.9B, central $0.8-1.4B. 2030: Tomahawk 800-1,000 x ~$0.3M = $0.24-0.3B. JASSM/LRASM 1,100-1,500 x $0.3M = $0.33-0.45B. Other Western 2,000-3,000 x $0.15-0.3M = $0.3-0.9B. Affordable mass 15,000-40,000 x $30-80k = $0.45-3.2B. Decoys/targets/C-UAS $0.2-0.5B. Total $1.5-5.4B, central $2-4B. Engine ASPs are own estimates, not disclosed by suppliers.
catalyst_timing: Aug 2025: DSCA notified up to 3,350 ERAM for Ukraine (~$825M). June 2025: MBDA unveiled the One Way Effector with a stated goal of ~1,000/month. 2026: USAF FAMM down-selects and RTX framework to take Tomahawk above 1,000/yr (recalled, unverified). Lockheed JASSM/LRASM capacity toward ~1,100+/yr. 2026-27: Kratos/GE GEK800 into production, GEK1500 after. FY2027 budgets.
key_suppliers: Williams International (private, US; F107/FJ33; est. 40-55% of Western value). Safran Power Units/Microturbo (EPA: SAF; ~10-20%). Teledyne CAE (NYSE: TDY; J402; ~5-10%). Kratos (Nasdaq: KTOS) with GE Aerospace (NYSE: GE) on GEK800/GEK1500 (<5% in 2026, rising). PBS Aerospace (CZ, private; TJ100/TJ150, strong in sub-300 lbf; US subsidiary). Hanwha Aerospace (KRX: 012450). Kale Arge / TEI (TR). Motor Sich / Ivchenko-Progress (UA). Pratt & Whitney (RTX) small expendable engines. Beehive Industries (US startup, additive-manufactured). Chinese makers supply Iran/Russia (excluded). All shares are own estimates.
supply_tightness: Tight. Few US-qualified suppliers; Williams is effectively single-site for F107. Engine-airframe qualification takes 2-4 years. Hot-section castings, bearings and fuel controls compete with a record commercial-aerospace backlog. Kratos has said engines pace affordable-mass programs (recalled). New entrants (Kratos/GE, Beehive, PBS US) start low-rate production only from 2026-27. Pricing power moderate-high through ~2028.
substitution_risk: Piston-prop OWA drones (Shahed-class) for slow, cheap missions. Rocket-boosted short-range designs. Automotive-turbocharger-derived engines could deflate ASPs. Ramjets for high-speed niches.
cyclicality_risk: Moderate. Program cancellations or consolidation (FAMM/ERAM follow-ons), Ukraine ceasefire, and startup overcapacity after 2028. Double-ordering risk is low because engines are long-lead, single-qualified parts.
faster_sub_niche: 300-1,500 lbf low-cost turbojets for affordable-mass cruise missiles (ERAM, FAMM, OWE, Barracuda class): ~$0.1-0.4B (2026) -> $0.6-2.5B (2030), CAGR ~40-60% (own estimate). The legacy Tomahawk/JASSM engine slice grows ~15-25%.

THAAD 100 -> 350 x $1-2M = $0.1-0.2B -> $0.35-0.7B. SM-family/ESSM 400 -> 900 x $0.4-1.0M = $0.16-0.4B -> $0.36-0.9B. AMRAAM/AIM-9X 1,500 -> 3,000 x $50-120k = $0.08-0.18B -> $0.15-0.36B. Javelin/Stinger/JAGM/Hellfire 10-20k x $5-20k = $0.05-0.4B. PrSM 200 -> 1,000 x $0.3-0.5M. US total ~$0.9-2.2B (2026) -> $2.0-4.5B (2030). Supplier cross-check: L3Harris Aerojet Rocketdyne segment ~$2.5-2.8B (2025, incl. liquid engines, strategic and hypersonic; unverified). Add Europe/Asia ~$1.2-2B -> $2.5-4B.
catalyst_timing: Jan 2026: Department of War $1B investment in L3Harris Missile Solutions, with an IPO targeted for H2 2026 (recalled). Jan-Feb 2026: PAC-3/THAAD/RTX frameworks. July 2025: OBBBA munitions funding. 2026-28: qualification of second sources (X-Bow on GMLRS, Ursa Major on Navy Mk 104, Anduril). Europe: SAFE loans, Nammo/Roxel/Bayern-Chemie expansions, and Avio's US SRM plant (announced 2025).
key_suppliers: US duopoly: L3Harris Aerojet Rocketdyne (NYSE: LHX; Missile Solutions IPO pending; est. 40-50% US tactical) and Northrop Grumman (NYSE: NOC; est. 35-45%). Europe: Nammo (NO/FI state + Patria), Roxel (MBDA/Safran JV), Bayern-Chemie (MBDA), Avio (BIT: AVIO), Diehl. Asia/other: Hanwha Aerospace (KRX: 012450), IHI Aerospace (TSE: 7013), Roketsan (TR, state), Rafael/Tomer (IL). Shares are own estimates.
supply_tightness: Very tight 2023-2027. SRMs paced Javelin, GMLRS and SM output. Qualification 2-4 years; new casting/mixing bays 2-3 years with explosive-safety siting. cyclicality_risk: Moderate. Overbuild risk after ~2029 as 4-6 new entrants qualify alongside incumbent expansions. Low double-ordering risk (government-qualified, program-specific motors).

name: Ammonium perchlorate (AP) oxidizer - Western merchant supply
definition: IN: military- and space-grade AP (ground and unground) for composite solid propellants, made outside China/Russia. OUT: Chinese/Russian AP; perchlorates for pyrotechnics/airbags; HTPB and other propellant ingredients.
value_chain_path: Defense & rearmament -> munitions -> missiles -> solid rocket motors -> composite propellant -> AP oxidizer
size_2026_usd: $0.3-0.5B Western (own estimate). AMPAC alone ~$0.2-0.35B (unverified; disclosed in NewMarket's specialty-materials segment).
volume_vs_price: ~60% volume / ~40% price. Sole-source position plus government-funded capacity lets the producer pass through capex. Price share is higher than in C4, so less durable.
math: Top-down (own estimate): US tactical SRM propellant ~4-8 kt/yr (2026) x AP fraction 0.65-0.70 = 2.6-5.6 kt. Space/strategic: SLS ~1.26 kt propellant per launch (~0.88 kt AP); Vulcan GEM 63XL ~48 t propellant each x 40-80 boosters/yr = 2-4 kt propellant (~1.4-2.8 kt AP); strategic is small. US AP demand ~6-12 kt (13-26 Mlb) x $15-30/kg (unverified) = $0.1-0.36B, consistent with the AMPAC estimate. 2030: tactical propellant 2-2.5x, space flat-to-up, so AP volume ~1.6-2x plus price.
catalyst_timing: SRM capacity ramps 2026-2029 (L3Harris, NOC, new entrants); Sentinel SRM production late decade; launch cadence of SLS/Vulcan; possible DoD funding for a second AP source (unverified).
key_suppliers: American Pacific Corp (AMPAC), Cedar City UT, owned by NewMarket Corp (NYSE: NEU) since Jan 2025 ($700M deal): sole North American AP producer, ~85-95% of US supply. Japan Carlit (TSE: 4275): Japan. India: ISRO captive AP plant. Europe: merchant AP capacity at scale unverified. China: multiple producers (excluded).
supply_tightness: Extreme single-point-of-failure. One qualified US plant since the 1988 PEPCON explosion. A new plant needs ~4-6 years for permitting, construction and propellant requalification. Every US SRM prime depends on AMPAC. Pricing power high.
substitution_risk: Low before 2030. AN- or ADN-based 'green' oxidizers and AP-free propellants are lab or low-TRL for tactical use.
cyclicality_risk: Tied to SRM demand. DoD can pressure margins or fund a competitor; a second source would cap price.
faster_sub_niche: None identifiable. Fine/ultrafine AP for high-burn-rate tactical motors may grow faster but is not disclosed.
