name: Data-center LPDDR5X/LPDDR6, fastest sub-niche: SOCAMM2 modules for AI CPUs and LPDDR-based inference accelerators
definition: In scope: low-power DRAM (LPDDR5X now, LPDDR6 from ~2027) shipped into data-center compute: (i) SOCAMM/SOCAMM2 detachable modules (JEDEC) on Nvidia Vera and other Arm CPUs; (ii) soldered LPDDR5X on Grace; (iii) LPDDR on inference accelerator cards (Qualcomm AI200/AI250, Intel Crescent Island). Revenue = DRAM + module value. Out of scope: HBM, DDR5 RDIMM/MRDIMM, CXL DDR5 expanders, and all phone/PC LPDDR (incl. LPCAMM2).
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> compute trays -> CPU/accelerator memory subsystem -> LPDDR-class DRAM (vs HBM / DDR5) -> SOCAMM2 modules (LPDDR5X dies + module PCB/connector)
also_serves_megatrends: AI PC/edge (same LPDDR dies and packaging lines)
size_2026_usd: Data-center LPDDR total $4-12B (own estimate). SOCAMM2 sub-niche $1-4B (own estimate), up from ~zero in 2025.
size_2030_usd: Data-center LPDDR total $12-45B; SOCAMM2 $8-30B (own estimates, low confidence)
volume_vs_price: Bits drive growth. LPDDR per Nvidia rack goes from ~17-18 TB (GB200/GB300 NVL72) to ~54 TB on Vera Rubin NVL144 (75 TB 'fast memory' minus ~21 TB HBM4), and higher again on Rubin Ultra. The 2026 base is inflated by shortage pricing (DRAM contract prices jumped in 4Q25-1H26), so ASP per GB likely falls 30-50% by 2030. Net: bit CAGR ~50-80% vs ASP about -10 to -15%/yr, so revenue CAGR is well below bit CAGR. Treat the 2026 price as non-durable.
math: 2026 bits: GB300 at 45-60k racks x ~18 TB = 0.8-1.1 EB; Vera Rubin at 5-15k racks x ~54 TB = 0.27-0.81 EB; Grace/Vera standalone and others ~0.1-0.2 EB. Total ~1.2-2.1 EB (1.2-2.1bn GB) x $3.5-6/GB = $4-12B. Rack counts unverified. SOCAMM2 = Vera-based ~0.3-0.9 EB x $3.5-6/GB = ~$1-5B. 2030: 6-15 EB of data-center LPDDR (Rubin Ultra/Feynman racks at 54-200+ TB each, LPDDR inference cards at 768 GB each) x $2-3/GB = $12-45B. SOCAMM2 is ~60-70% of that. Supplier-revenue cross-check: Samsung, SK hynix and Micron do not disclose it (unverified).
catalyst_timing: Vera Rubin volume ramp 2H26-2027; Rubin Ultra (Kyber rack) 2H27; JEDEC SOCAMM2 standardization 2025-26 enables multi-vendor sourcing; Qualcomm AI200 ships in 2026 and AI250 in 2027 (768 GB LPDDR per card; Humain 200 MW from 2026); Intel Crescent Island (160 GB LPDDR5X) sampling 2H26; LPDDR6 adoption 2027-28.
key_suppliers: Samsung Electronics (005930.KS), SK hynix (000660.KS), Micron (MU; first to announce SOCAMM in Mar 2025, sampled 192 GB SOCAMM2 in Oct 2025). Own-estimate shares of data-center LPDDR: roughly one-third each, +/-10pp (unverified). CXMT is effectively excluded from Nvidia supply by the export-control environment. Module connectors/PCBs: suppliers unverified.
supply_tightness: Very tight in 2026. Only three qualified suppliers, and LPDDR5X competes with HBM and DDR5 for the same 1b/1c-nm wafer capacity. New DRAM cleanroom space (SK hynix M15X/Yongin, Samsung P4/P5, Micron Idaho from ~2027) mostly lands in 2027-28. Nvidia qualification of high-capacity SOCAMM2 stacks is a gate. Pricing power currently sits with suppliers.
substitution_risk: DDR5 MRDIMM/CXL on x86 hosts; HBF (high-bandwidth flash, SanDisk/SK hynix, samples ~2026-27) for inference KV-cache; Nvidia cutting per-CPU capacity; GDDR7 on prefill accelerators (Rubin CPX).
cyclicality_risk: High. Memory supercycle with likely double-ordering in 2026, and DRAM oversupply risk in 2028-29 as new fabs land. Revenue CAGR is very sensitive to price.
faster_sub_niche: SOCAMM2 (detachable, Vera era) grows far faster than soldered Grace LPDDR5X, which declines after 2027 as Grace racks roll off. Inside SOCAMM2, the module adds little value beyond the DRAM, so drilling further does not change the story.

name: Cryogen-free dilution refrigerators (mK cryostats) for superconducting and spin-qubit quantum computers
definition: In scope: pulse-tube pre-cooled 3He/4He dilution refrigerator systems reaching <20 mK, including large-format 'quantum data-center' platforms, integrated cryogenic wiring and attenuation kits, upgrades and service. Out of scope: standalone 4K cryocoolers, 4K cryostats for photonic qubits, room-temperature control electronics, qubit chips, and He-3 sold as a commodity (treated as a bottleneck input).
value_chain_path: Quantum computing -> hardware stack -> cryogenic infrastructure -> mK dilution refrigerators -> (inputs: pulse-tube cryocoolers, He-3/He-4 mixture, cryogenic flex wiring, HEMT/TWPA amplifiers)
also_serves_megatrends: Particle physics, dark-matter and astronomy detectors (TES/KID arrays)
size_2026_usd: $350-650M (own estimate): ~400-700 systems x ~$0.6-1.0M blended, plus upgrades and service
volume_vs_price: Roughly half volume, half price. Units grow ~10-18%/yr. Blended ASP rises ~5-10%/yr from the mix shift to large multi-module platforms with more cooling power at 100 mK and denser wiring. He-3 cost pass-through adds further price.
math: Top-down (own estimate): ~200-300 academic/national-lab mK groups plus ~50-100 industrial QC programs. Each industrial roadmap (IBM, Google, AWS, Rigetti, IQM, Alice&Bob, Fujitsu/RIKEN, Chinese programs) adds several to dozens of large cryostats over 2026-30. 2026: ~400-700 systems at $0.4-1.5M (lab-class) and $2-6M (large platforms, unverified) = $350-650M. 2030: 700-1,100 systems, ~25% large-format = $0.8-1.6B. Supplier sum (unverified): Bluefors (incl. Cryomech, acquired 2023) is believed to be the majority supplier with revenue in the low hundreds of EUR millions. Oxford Instruments NanoScience (sold to Quantum Design for ~GBP 60M in 2025) is tens of GBP millions. Maybell, ICEoxford, Leiden, Zero Point, FormFactor, ULVAC and Chinese domestic makers are each likely <$50M. Sum ~$350-600M.
catalyst_timing: IBM roadmap: Loon/Kookaburra/Cockatoo steps 2025-28, then Starling (200 logical qubits) in 2029 at Poughkeepsie. DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative: Stage B from late 2025, Stage C ~2027. National programs: Japan, EU Quantum Act (2026), UK NQCC, India NQM, Korea. US quantum export controls (Sept 2024) are forcing a Chinese domestic dilution-fridge build-out. He-3 supply contracts (Interlune-Bluefors) start in 2028.
key_suppliers: Bluefors (private, Finland; est. 50-70% share ex-China, unverified; owns pulse-tube maker Cryomech). Quantum Design / ex-Oxford Instruments NanoScience (private, US/UK). Maybell Quantum (private, US). ICEoxford (UK). Leiden Cryogenics (NL). Zero Point Cryogenics (Canada). FormFactor (FORM). ULVAC (6728.T). China domestic: QuantumCTek-affiliated and CETC institutes (unverified). Pulse tubes: Cryomech/Bluefors and Sumitomo Heavy Industries (6302.T).
supply_tightness: Tight on inputs. He-3 comes mainly from tritium decay (US DOE isotope program, Russia) and CANDU tritium. Prices are reportedly in the thousands of $ per litre (unverified). Pulse-tube supply is concentrated in two firms. Lead times are ~6-12 months (unverified). Few firms can build >1 W @ 100 mK class platforms, and export controls split the market.
substitution_risk: Modality risk. Trapped-ion, neutral-atom and photonic platforms need no mK dilution fridge (photonics needs only ~4 K). If they reach early fault tolerance first, DR growth roughly halves. Cryo-CMOS and multiplexing cut wiring per qubit but do not remove the need for a fridge.
cyclicality_risk: Medium-high. Quantum equity-funding exuberance (2025 raises) can reverse, academic budgets are volatile (US NSF/DOE), and anchor customers such as IBM and Google could in-source designs.
faster_sub_niche: Large-format quantum-data-center cryoplatforms (Bluefors KIDE-class, multi-module) and high-density cryogenic flex wiring probably grow 35-50%, but each is <$150M in 2026 (unverified). He-3 itself is the true bottleneck but too small and too early to be its own niche (see too_early).

name: PFAS-removal adsorptive media for drinking water (GAC + PFAS-selective single-use ion-exchange resin), incl. change-out/reactivation service
definition: In scope: granular activated carbon (virgin and reactivated) and PFAS-selective anion-exchange resins consumed in PFAS treatment at public water systems (US, EU, Canada, Australia, Japan), plus media change-out, reactivation and spent-media disposal service. Out of scope: RO/NF membrane system capex, industrial wastewater, DoD/airport groundwater remediation contracting, analytical testing, and PFAS destruction technology (listed as too early).
value_chain_path: Water infrastructure -> drinking-water treatment -> emerging-contaminant removal -> PFAS treatment trains -> adsorptive media (GAC / PFAS-selective IX) + change-out, reactivation and disposal service
also_serves_megatrends: PFAS litigation settlements funding utility capex (3M, DuPont/Chemours/Corteva)
size_2026_usd: $0.7-1.5B global (own estimate; US ~55-65%)
volume_vs_price: Mostly volume. Installed US PFAS treatment rises from ~25-35% of required systems in 2026 to ~60-80% by 2030, and EU DWD limits apply from Jan 2026. Price adds ~3-5%/yr from tight coal-based GAC capacity, protected by US antidumping duties on Chinese activated carbon. Once installed, media is replaced every ~6-24 months, so revenue becomes an annuity, which makes the growth durable.
math: EPA's 2024 rule analysis: ~6-10% of ~66,000 public water systems (~4,000-6,700) need action, at an annualized cost of ~$1.5B/yr. An AWWA-commissioned estimate put it above $3.8B/yr. Own estimate: media plus change-out is ~30-45% of lifecycle cost. At full build-out (~2031), US annual media/service spend is ~$1.2-2.0B. With ~25-35% installed in 2026, that is ~$0.4-0.8B. Add the EU (DWD 0.1 ug/L sum-of-20 PFAS from 12 Jan 2026) at ~$0.2-0.5B and rest of world at ~$0.1-0.2B, giving $0.7-1.5B in 2026. 2030: US $1.1-2.0B + EU $0.5-1.0B + RoW $0.2-0.4B = $1.8-3.4B. Supplier cross-check: Veolia targets ~EUR 1bn of PFAS revenue by 2030 (all services); Calgon Carbon (Kuraray) is the largest US PFAS GAC and reactivation supplier; Arq built its Red River GAC plant for the PFAS market.
catalyst_timing: EU DWD PFAS parametric values apply from 12 Jan 2026, with member-state monitoring and treatment 2026-28. In the US, EPA said in May 2025 it would keep the 4 ppt MCLs for PFOA/PFOS but extend compliance from 2029 to 2031 and rescind the PFHxS/PFNA/HFPO-DA/hazard-index limits. The final rule and DC Circuit litigation status are unverified as of Oct 2026. US initial monitoring is due 2027. 3M settlement payments run 2024-2036. Bipartisan Infrastructure Law emerging-contaminant SRF funds (~$9B) are disbursing through FY2026.
key_suppliers: GAC: Calgon Carbon (Kuraray 3405.T; US leader, est. 30-40% of US municipal PFAS GAC, unverified), Jacobi (Osaka Gas 9532.T), Norit (private), Arq (ARQ), Haycarb (Colombo: HAYC), Donau Carbon (private). IX resin: Purolite (Ecolab ECL), DuPont (DD, AmberLite), LANXESS (LXS.DE, Lewatit), Mitsubishi Chemical (4188.T), ResinTech (private). Service/systems: Xylem/Evoqua (XYL), Veolia (VIE.PA), AqueoUS Vets (private), Clean Harbors (CLH, disposal/incineration).
supply_tightness: Medium. US coal-based (bituminous) GAC capacity is concentrated and protected by antidumping duties. Reactivation furnaces need RCRA/air permits with ~2-4 yr lead times. PFAS-selective resins come from ~5 makers. NSF/ANSI 61 certification plus 6-12 month utility pilot tests slow switching between suppliers.
substitution_risk: RO/NF (high capex, concentrate disposal), novel sorbents (cyclodextrin and fluorinated sorbents; scale unverified), and source switching or blending. US regulatory rollback is a bigger risk than technical substitution.
cyclicality_risk: Low on demand (regulated consumable). Timing risk comes from US deadline shifts (2029->2031) and litigation. GAC prices cycle with coal and coconut-shell supply.
faster_sub_niche: PFAS-selective single-use IX resin (smaller footprint, long bed life for PFOA/PFOS) and spent-media reactivation/disposal service likely grow 25-35%, vs 15-25% for GAC (own estimate). Destruction technology is too early (see too_early).

name: DSP-based active electrical cables (AECs), 400G/800G/1.6T: finished cable assemblies (total AEC market at first sale)
definition: IN: finished copper twinax cables with a PAM4 retimer/DSP in one or both connector ends (straight, Y/X-breakout, and mux 'switch' AECs). Form factors QSFP112/QSFP-DD/OSFP at 50/100/200G per lane, ~2-7 m reach, sold to hyperscalers/ODMs for NIC-to-ToR, ToR-to-leaf and in-rack/rack-to-rack scale-up links. Value is counted once at first sale of the finished cable: Credo-branded AECs at Credo's selling price; assembler-branded AECs built on merchant DSPs/modules at the assembler's price. OUT: passive DAC, linear-redriver ACC (NVIDIA LinkX ACC, Semtech CopperEdge-based cables), AOC/LPO/LRO optics, Active LED Cables, passive NVLink-type cartridges, board-level retimers. Sub-measure: non-silicon assembly value-add (raw twinax, connector shells, paddle-card PCB, assembly/test, assembler margin).
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> rack & cluster interconnect -> short-reach (<7 m) electrical links -> DSP-retimed copper (AEC) vs passive DAC/ACC vs optics -> finished AEC cable assemblies (400G/800G/1.6T)

name: Merchant scale-up fabric switch silicon for XPU domains (PCIe6/7 AI-fabric, UALink and ESUN/SUE Ethernet scale-up switches)
definition: IN: merchant switch ICs used to build accelerator scale-up domains with load/store or low-latency Ethernet semantics: Astera Scorpio X (and Scorpio P where deployed as AI fabric), Broadcom Tomahawk Ultra and Tomahawk 5/6 deployed for scale-up, Marvell UALink/ESUN switches (XConn-derived), and Upscale AI and other UALink start-ups. OUT: NVIDIA NVLink Switch (captive), Google ICI/OCS (captive), scale-out leaf/spine Ethernet/InfiniBand switches, general-purpose server/storage PCIe switches, retimers.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> accelerator racks -> scale-up fabric (XPU-to-XPU) -> switch silicon -> merchant (non-NVLink) PCIe/UALink/ESUN scale-up switches
also_serves_megatrends: AI data centers: custom ASIC/XPU programs (AWS, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, others)
merchant GPU racks adopting open scale-up (AMD UALink-class racks)
size_2026_usd: $0.6-1.8B (own estimate; central ~$1.0B). Astera Scorpio $0.3-0.5B (own estimate: ~20% of $308.4M Q1-26 revenue = ~$62M/quarter, guided to become Astera's largest line by end-2026). Broadcom scale-up Ethernet (Tomahawk Ultra/TH5/TH6 in XPU scale-up) $0.3-1.2B (own estimate, very uncertain; Broadcom does not split scale-up from its ~$2.8B/quarter AI networking). Marvell/Upscale/others <$0.1B.
volume_vs_price: Roughly 65-75% volume / 25-35% ASP-mix. Volume: custom XPU shipments (~3.5-5M in 2026 to 8-14M in 2030, own estimate), plus larger scale-up domains (8-16 -> 64-144 -> 512+ XPUs) that need multi-tier switching, so switches per XPU rise. Price: higher radix (Scorpio X up to 320 lanes; Tomahawk 6 at 102.4T), 200G->400G lanes and in-network compute raise ASP per switch while $/lane falls. Not shortage-driven, so the growth is durable if the open standards consolidate.
math: 2026: 3.5-5M custom XPUs (own estimate) x merchant scale-up switch content $150-350 per XPU (own estimate) = $0.5-1.75B, consistent with the supplier build-up above. 2030: 8-14M XPUs, plus merchant-switch GPU racks, x $400-800 per XPU x 70-90% merchant capture = $2.2-10B; central ~$6B. Astera cites total connectivity silicon >$1,000 per XPU, with switches the largest part; Google stays captive and NVLink Fusion uses NVIDIA's switch. Sanity check: Astera's TAM claim of ~$25B in five years (>10x) across its whole portfolio.
catalyst_timing: 2026: Scorpio X ramps with custom-ASIC hyperscalers (AWS is the likely anchor; Astera holds a purchase-linked warrant agreement with AWS of up to $6.5B); Broadcom Tomahawk Ultra/TH6 in Ethernet scale-up. 2027: first UALink 1.0 (200G) switch deployments (Astera, Marvell, Upscale AI), ESUN (OCP) designs, Broadcom Tomahawk 7 (200T). 2028+: 400G SerDes and optically attached (NPO/CPO) scale-up switches. These change the physical layer but still need switch silicon.
key_suppliers: Astera Labs (ALAB, Nasdaq; Scorpio P/X; Taiwan-centric supply chain); Broadcom (AVGO, Nasdaq; Tomahawk Ultra/6/7, 200G/400G SerDes); Marvell (MRVL, Nasdaq; UALink/ESUN switches via XConn, Teralynx); Upscale AI (private; UALink/ESUN); Cisco (CSCO; Silicon One, scale-up role unverified); Microchip (MCHP; Switchtec, minor). Captive, excluded: NVIDIA (NVDA) NVLink Switch. Foundry: TSMC N5/N3.
supply_tightness: Tight. Only 2-4 merchant suppliers combine 200G-class SerDes with large-radix switch IP; design cycles run 2-3 years and qualification 12-24 months. Large-die switches compete for N3/N5 wafers, large ABF substrates and advanced packaging. Pricing power is strong: Astera reports that the Scorpio mix shift is raising its overall ASPs.
substitution_risk: (1) NVLink Fusion: XPU vendors that adopt NVIDIA's NVLink switch shrink the merchant TAM. (2) In-house switch ASICs (Google is already captive; AWS Annapurna could internalize). (3) Switchless topologies (torus/mesh, direct XPU-to-XPU). (4) Standards fragmentation (UALink vs ESUN/SUE vs PCIe vs NVLink Fusion) splits volume and R&D. Optics is not a substitute for switch silicon; it only changes the SerDes/attach.
cyclicality_risk: Lumpy and platform-tied: each XPU generation is a separate win or loss. Very concentrated customer base (Astera: Asia ship-to ~89% of Q1-26 revenue, China 29%). Custom-ASIC program delays or capex digestion hit hard, with double-ordering risk around generation transitions. Export controls cap the China upside, and Chinese domestic substitutes will serve Chinese clusters.
faster_sub_niche: UALink/ESUN-standard switches: near-zero revenue in 2026 (emerging; first deployments 2027) -> $1-3B by 2030 (own estimate). PCIe-based Scorpio X carries 2026-27 volume.

name: Row/hall-scale liquid-to-liquid CDUs of 1 MW and up for AI DLC halls
definition: IN: stand-alone liquid-to-liquid coolant distribution units of 1 MW or more (in-row, end-of-row or gallery/hall-scale skids). They separate facility water from the technology cooling loop (TCS) and contain plate HX, pumps, filtration and controls. Includes OEM and hyperscaler-spec units built by partners (e.g., Google Project Deschutes-class). OUT: in-rack CDUs (<~250 kW), liquid-to-air sidecars and in-row L2A heat exchangers, rear-door HX, chillers, dry coolers, TCS piping and fluid services, cold plates/manifolds (candidate A), quick disconnects (already covered), 800 VDC power sidecars (already covered).
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> thermal management -> direct-to-chip liquid cooling -> coolant distribution units -> liquid-to-liquid CDUs >=1 MW (row/hall-scale)
also_serves_megatrends: Heat reuse / district heating (EU Energy Efficiency Directive; 45C+ return water)
Data-center water and energy efficiency regulation (chiller-less designs)
size_2026_usd: $0.4-1.5B for MW-class L2L CDUs (own estimate; central ~$0.8B). All CDU types ~$1.0-3.0B (own estimate). Not verified against Dell'Oro/Omdia this session.
volume_vs_price: Volume makes up more than 100% of the growth. Liquid-cooled AI IT MW grows ~25-40%/yr, and the MW-class share of CDU capacity rises from ~40-55% to ~75-88% (~+10-15%/yr) as 200-600 kW racks outgrow liquid-to-air units. $/kW falls ~5-10%/yr from unit up-sizing (1 MW -> 2.5 MW -> 5-10 MW skids), competition from >20 entrants, and hyperscaler/OCP spec standardisation. Volume-driven, so durable. No shortage-pricing component is assumed.
math: Top-down, own estimates. 2026: liquid-cooled AI IT commissioned 6-12 GW x ~0.9 liquid heat fraction x ~1.2 N+1 redundancy = ~6.5-13 GW of CDU capacity. MW-class share 40-55% = 2.6-7 GW, x $110-170/kW = $0.3-1.2B, widened to $0.4-1.5B for service/controls content and uncertainty. 2030: liquid-cooled AI IT commissioned 18-35 GW/yr (consistent with ~$3-4T cumulative AI infrastructure at ~$50B/GW; deliberately below the most aggressive hyperscaler plans) x 1.08 = 19-38 GW, x 75-88% MW-class = 14-33 GW, x $80-120/kW = $1.1-4.0B, widened to $1.5-5.0B. CAGR decomposition (central): GW x1.32/yr x share x1.155/yr x price 0.93/yr = ~1.41 (41%); low case 1.19 x 1.09 x 0.90 = 17%; high case 1.41 x 1.19 x 0.96 = 61%. Per-rack check: a 2.3 MW CDU serves ~8-10 Vera Rubin NVL72 racks (~190-230 kW) but only ~3 Kyber NVL576 racks (~600 kW), so CDU MW per accelerator roughly doubles 2026->2030 while per-accelerator cold-plate value does not. Bottom-up cross-check (unverified): Vertiv backlog of ~$15B at end-2025 is mostly thermal + power; Boyd Thermal guides ~$1.7B 2026 sales across cold plates and CDUs; Schneider paid $850M for 75% of Motivair. A total-CDU market of $1-3B is consistent with these, but no vendor discloses MW-class CDU revenue.
catalyst_timing: Vera Rubin NVL72 (~45C supply water, fully liquid-cooled) ramps 2H26-1H27. Liquid-ready greenfield campuses commission 2026-2028 (Stargate sites, Meta, xAI, Microsoft Fairwater-class; specific site counts unverified). Rubin Ultra / Kyber ~600 kW racks arrive 2H27-2028 and need >=2.5 MW units and hall-scale skids. Expect the L2A-to-L2L crossover in retrofit halls during 2027-28. Vertiv's Q3-2026 call (late Oct 2026) is the next datapoint for liquid-cooling orders and backlog. I could not check the Q2-2026 call this session.
key_suppliers: Vertiv (VRT, NYSE; CoolChip CDU family to ~2.3 MW; est. 20-30% share, unverified). Schneider Electric / Motivair (SU, Euronext Paris; est. 10-20%). nVent (NVT, NYSE; est. 5-10%). CoolIT Systems (KKR, private, Canada; est. 5-10%). Boyd Thermal (being acquired by Eaton, ETN, NYSE). Delta Electronics (2308.TW). Lite-On (2301.TW). Kaori Heat Treatment (8996.TW; CDUs and brazed-plate HX). Supermicro (SMCI, captive DLC-2, in-row to ~1.8 MW). HVAC entrants: Johnson Controls (JCI), Carrier (CARR), Trane (TT), Modine/Airedale (MOD), Daikin (6367.T), LG Electronics (066570.KS), Stulz and Rittal (private). China: Envicool (002837.SZ), Shenling (301018.SZ). Hyperscaler designs (Google Deschutes) are built by contract partners. All shares are own estimates, unverified.
supply_tightness: Moderate and easing. Qualified vendors number more than 20, so there is no single-source bottleneck. Lead times for MW-class units were reportedly ~16-40 weeks during the 2025-26 ramp (unverified). Sub-component constraints: brazed/gasketed plate HX capacity (Alfa Laval, SWEP/Dover, Danfoss, Kaori), large variable-speed pumps, controls and sensors. Pricing power sits mainly with the integrated vendors (Vertiv, Schneider), who bundle CDU + TCS + commissioning + service. Expect $/kW erosion from 2027 as JCI, Carrier, Trane, LG, Daikin and Chinese vendors scale.
substitution_risk: Medium. (1) Hyperscaler OCP CDU specs (Google Deschutes) commoditise hardware and move value to contract manufacturers. (2) Hall-scale 5-10 MW skids or plant-level heat exchangers could shift value to HVAC majors at a lower $/kW. (3) In-rack CDUs could hold share if rack-scale integrators (Supermicro, ODMs) bundle cooling. (4) Two-phase or immersion are small risks before 2030. 'CDU-less' direct facility water into the rack is unlikely given water-quality separation practice.
cyclicality_risk: High. The niche is tied to AI capex: a 2027-28 digestion pause would hit orders directly. Vertiv-style backlogs may include double-ordering by colos and neoclouds hedging site timing. More than 20 new entrants plus Chinese capacity (Envicool, Shenling) risk overbuild and price wars by 2028. Delays in power availability push site commissioning, and CDU shipments slip with them.
faster_sub_niche: Units of 2 MW and up (incl. 5-10 MW hall-scale skids) serving >=200 kW racks (Vera Rubin, Kyber): own estimate 45-65% CAGR from roughly $0.2-0.6B in 2026, because 1-1.5 MW units are displaced from 2027. One level deeper, brazed/gasketed plate heat exchangers for CDUs grow with CDU MW without the integration $/kW deflation. Data to size it were not available this session.

name: Microchannel lid cold plate (MLCP): integrated package lid + microchannel cold plate for 3.5 kW+ accelerators
definition: IN: a single copper (or Cu-composite) part that replaces both the package lid/IHS and the separate cold plate, with microchannels (roughly 50-150 um) formed in the lid and coolant flowing directly over the die area. It is attached at the package level at TSMC or the OSAT. Includes NRE, samples and production units. OUT: conventional skived cold plates mounted on a lidded package (candidate A), bare lids without fluid channels (lid-maker revenue), in-silicon etched microfluidics (too early), two-phase evaporators.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> thermal management -> direct-to-chip liquid cooling -> tray/package-level heat acquisition -> microchannel lid cold plate (MLCP) merging lid and cold plate
also_serves_megatrends: Advanced packaging (CoWoS-L, 4-reticle packages, HBM4E stacks) - thermal limit on package power
Custom AI ASICs (TPU, Trainium, MTIA) at 2+ kW after 2028
size_2026_usd: $5-40M (own estimate; EMERGING, sampling and NRE only; no production revenue verified)
size_2030_usd: $0.3-4B (own estimate; central ~$1.5-2B if NVIDIA adopts it on Rubin Ultra/Feynman; bear case $0.3-0.8B if it is limited to top SKUs or slips)
cagr_2026_2030: 2026-30 >150% (base effect, not meaningful); 2027-30 60-120% (own estimate, conditional on adoption)
volume_vs_price: Growth comes from adoption volume starting at zero. The ASP premium over a conventional cold plate (own estimate 2-4x; supply-chain claim 3-5x, unverified) is mix and content gain, not shortage pricing. After 2029, expect 10-15%/yr price-downs as bonding yields mature and more vendors qualify. The net content gain to the thermal chain is smaller than the headline multiple because the separate lid (~$20-60) and one TIM layer go away.
math: Own estimates. Conventional GPU cold-plate ASP: ~$120-250 at 1.4 kW (B300), ~$150-300 at 1.8-2.3 kW (Rubin), ~$200-400 for an advanced microfin plate at ~3.6 kW (Rubin Ultra). MLCP ASP: $300-900 (2-4x conventional). 2026: sampling/NRE across 2-4 vendors = $5-40M. 2027: early Rubin Ultra builds if adopted, 0.1-0.5M units x $400-900 = $0.05-0.4B. 2030: Rubin Ultra + Feynman + some custom-ASIC packages of 3-10M/yr x adoption 40-100% x $300-800 = $0.4-8B; trimmed for the probability that adoption slips, giving a $0.3-4B range with ~$1.5-2B central. Bear: confined to the top NVIDIA SKU from 2028, ~1-1.5M units x $300-500 = $0.3-0.8B.
catalyst_timing: Taiwanese supply-chain reports in 2H25 put NVIDIA MLCP evaluation first on Rubin, then on Rubin Ultra (2H27) / Feynman (2028). The generation has already shifted once in reports (unverified). Watch for: qualification and design-in decisions in 1H27; pilot-line capex at Jentech/AVC/Auras; TSMC/OSAT lid-attach process readiness. In this model the production ramp is 2028-2029.
key_suppliers: Jentech Precision (3653.TW; incumbent lid/stiffener supplier for NVIDIA CoWoS packages; natural MLCP owner). Asia Vital Components (AVC, 3017.TW; largest NVIDIA cold-plate/loop supplier). Auras Technology (3324.TW). Delta Electronics (2308.TW) and Cooler Master (private) are possible entrants. Package-level attach happens at TSMC (2330.TW) or ASE/SPIL (3711.TW). Shares cannot be estimated yet (pre-production). All supplier roles are from 2H25 Taiwanese media reports and were not re-verified.
supply_tightness: Potentially very tight. Only 2-4 vendors have shown MLCP capability. The part must pass package-level reliability tests (warpage and coplanarity over 100mm+ bodies, lid-attach and leak reliability, coolant chemistry against bonded joints). Qualification takes ~12-24 months and involves TSMC/OSAT as well as NVIDIA. Diffusion-bonding/brazing and precision-skiving capacity has to be built ahead of demand. Early pricing power is likely to be high.
substitution_risk: High. (1) NVIDIA may stay with a lidded package plus an advanced microfin cold plate and better TIM (liquid metal/indium) for Rubin Ultra, delaying MLCP to Feynman or later. (2) In-silicon microfluidics (Microsoft/Corintis; TSMC integrated microcooler work) could leapfrog MLCP after ~2029. (3) Jet-impingement single-phase plates (Flex/JetCool) or two-phase DTC could cover 3-4 kW without merging the lid. (4) Value may be split between lid makers and thermal-module makers, so no single supplier captures the full ASP.
cyclicality_risk: Single-customer and single-platform risk: revenue is binary on an NVIDIA generation decision. Pilot capacity built for a slipped generation risks stranded capex. Taiwanese equity markets priced the MLCP theme well ahead of revenue in late 2025 (reported).
faster_sub_niche: none - MLCP is already the narrowest layer. Next-level variants (custom-ASIC MLCP, two-sided/backside MLCP) do not change the growth story before 2030.

math: Own estimates. Liquid-cooled accelerators 2026: 7-12M (NVIDIA rack-scale GB300/VR 3.6-5.0M; NVIDIA liquid-cooled HGX 0.3-0.8M; Google TPU 2-3.5M; AWS/AMD/Meta/Microsoft/China 1.5-3.5M). Content per NVIDIA GPU, from a GB300 NVL72 rack BOM excluding QDs and CDU: 72 GPU plates x $150-250 + 36 CPU plates x $60-120 + 18 NVSwitch plates x $100-200 + NIC/VRM plates + 18 compute-tray loops x $300-600 + 9 switch-tray loops x $200-400 + rack manifold pair $3-6k = ~$25-45k/rack, or ~$350-625/GPU. ASIC trays ~$120-300/chip. 2026 = 4.0-5.8M x $350-625 + 3.2-7M x $120-300 = $1.8-5.7B, narrowed to $2.0-4.0B by supplier cross-check (Boyd Thermal ~$1.7B 2026E across plates and CDUs; AVC, Cooler Master and Auras liquid-cooling splits undisclosed). 2030: 18-30M liquid-cooled accelerators x $200-400 ex-MLCP = $3.6-12B, trimmed to $4-10B. TDP link: GPU plate value rises sub-linearly with TDP (1.4 kW -> 3.6 kW raises plate value only ~1.5-2x), which is why this layer grows near unit volume while CDUs grow with MW.

name: Fully driverless robotaxi ride-hail service revenue - US/West (fare + platform take)
definition: IN: gross fares, including any aggregator take (Uber/Lyft), for rides given with no human safety operator on board, in the US, Europe, Japan and Australia. Waymo (direct app plus Uber in Austin/Atlanta), Tesla rides without a monitor, Zoox paid rides, May Mobility/Avride/Nuro-Lucid-Uber driverless rides. OUT: rides with a safety driver or monitor, free or pilot rides, consumer FSD subscriptions, AV trucking/delivery, vehicle sales.
value_chain_path: Autonomy -> L4 autonomous vehicles -> passenger robotaxi -> mobility service layer -> fully driverless ride-hail fares + platform take -> US/West geography
also_serves_megatrends: Embodied/physical AI (end-to-end driving models, AI compute)
Fleet electrification (all robotaxis are BEVs; depot charging)
Airport/freeway mobility and rental-car industry repositioning
size_2026_usd: $0.45-0.9B (own estimate; about 85-95% Waymo). Tesla, Zoox and others together under $0.05B (own estimate). Unverified in-session.
size_2030_usd: $3-13B (own estimate; central about $6-7B): Waymo $2.5-7B, Tesla $0.2-4B (widest uncertainty), Zoox $0.1-0.6B, Nvidia-Hyperion/Uber ecosystem incl. Nuro-Lucid $0.2-1.5B, Europe/Japan $0.05-0.3B
volume_vs_price: Volume does all the work. Paid rides grow about 80-130%/yr: fleet growth (Waymo about 2.5k vehicles at the start of 2026 toward 20-50k by 2030; own estimate) times stable-to-rising utilization (20-28 rides per vehicle per day). Price/ASP is a headwind of about -5% to -12%/yr. Waymo currently charges a premium over UberX (third-party reports in 2025). That premium should shrink as fleets densify, as Tesla undercuts on price, and as cheaper 6th-gen/Hyundai/Ojai vehicles lower cost per mile. This is durable, volume-driven growth, not shortage pricing.
math: 2026 top-down: Waymo average weekly paid rides 0.55-0.75M. This assumes about 0.40-0.45M at the start of 2026 (reported in press, unverified) and an exit of 0.7-1.0M (the reported 1M/week goal, unverified). That gives 29-39M rides x $15-22 blended fare = $0.43-0.86B. Others add $0.01-0.05B, for a total of $0.45-0.9B. Cross-check: about 2.5-6k Waymo vehicles x 20-28 rides per vehicle per day is consistent with 0.4-1.0M rides/week. 2030: Waymo 20-50k vehicles x 20-25 rides/day x 365 x $12-17 = $1.75-7.8B, narrowed to $2.5-7B. Adding Tesla, Zoox, Hyperion-ecosystem fleets and EU/Japan gives $3-13B. CAGR: 0.65 -> 6.5 = 10x, i.e. about 78%/yr. Bear case 0.9 -> 3 = 35%. Bull case 0.45 -> 13 = 132%.
catalyst_timing: 2026: Waymo launches/expansions (Miami, Washington DC, Dallas with Avis, Nashville with Lyft, Denver and others, freeway and airport service, London prep), Zoox paid service in Las Vegas, the Tesla Austin/Bay Area monitor-removal steps, and the Nuro-Lucid-Uber Bay Area launch (late 2026). 2027: Nvidia-Uber Hyperion fleets start (up to 100k vehicles over time), Cybercab volume, Waymo Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Ojai at scale. 2028-2030: the multi-city scale-out with densification is the main revenue inflection. The weekly-ride exit-rate milestones in 2026 are the key tell (unverified).
key_suppliers: Waymo (Alphabet, GOOGL/NASDAQ): about 85-95% of 2026 revenue (own estimate). Tesla (TSLA/NASDAQ): about 1-5%. Zoox (Amazon, AMZN/NASDAQ): under 2%. Uber (UBER/NYSE) and Lyft (LYFT/NASDAQ) as aggregators taking a share of gross fares. May Mobility (private), Avride (Nebius, NBIS/NASDAQ), Nuro (private) with Lucid (LCID/NASDAQ) and Uber, Mobileye (MBLY/NASDAQ) with VW/MOIA, Wayve (private) with Uber in London. All shares are own estimates and unverified.
supply_tightness: Tight on vehicles and permits, not on demand. Waymo's Jaguar I-Pace supply is finite (2,000+ more vehicles assembled with Magna in Mesa through 2026, per 2025 company guidance). Zeekr-built Ojai faces tariffs, and Hyundai volume only arrives later. City-by-city CPUC/DMV/state approvals and depot real estate with high-power charging gate growth. There are few qualified driverless operators (effectively Waymo at scale, with Tesla and Zoox following), so pricing power exists today but should erode as Tesla and the Hyperion fleets enter.
substitution_risk: Robotaxis are the substitute for human ride-hail. The main risks are (a) consumer-owned unsupervised L4 (e.g. Tesla FSD unsupervised on owners' cars) diverting trips from ride-hail after about 2028, (b) a Tesla price war compressing fares faster than modelled, and (c) transit and micromobility at the short-trip end.
cyclicality_risk: Very capital-intensive and funding-dependent (vehicles at $40-150k+ each, depots). Waymo relies on Alphabet and external raises; GM shut Cruise down in Dec 2024 after its Oct 2023 incident. There is overbuild risk if utilization lags city launches. Incident/regulatory shock risk is high: one serious at-fault injury can trigger permit suspensions, NHTSA recalls or investigations (e.g. Waymo's 2025 school-bus probe and recall, unverified details), or state-level pauses. This is not a classic double-ordering cycle, but revenue is lumpy around city launches and permit events.
faster_sub_niche: Not a separate niche: Waymo airport and freeway trips (longer, higher-fare) raise revenue per vehicle. The fastest-growing piece in % terms is non-Waymo driverless rides (Tesla and the Hyperion/Uber fleets), but from a near-zero base and with high uncertainty. Waymo remains the dollar driver through 2030.

name: Merchant L4 robotaxi sensor + compute kit (lidar sets, L4 compute, cameras/radar, roof-pod/cleaning integration) sold to operators that do not make their own
definition: IN: autonomy hardware that robotaxi/L4 operators buy from third parties: robotaxi-grade lidar sets (long-range main plus near-field blind-spot units), L4 compute (Orin-X/Thor domain controllers, Hyperion 10), automotive cameras, 4D radar, roof-pod housings and sensor-cleaning modules. Buyers: Pony, WeRide, Baidu (lidar), Zoox, Nuro, May, Avride, Motional, Mobileye/VW, Uber-Hyperion fleets. OUT: captive hardware (Waymo in-house lidar and pod, Tesla vision-only and AI4/AI5), consumer ADAS lidar/compute, the base vehicle.
value_chain_path: Autonomy -> L4 autonomous vehicles -> passenger robotaxi -> vehicle hardware layer -> autonomy sensor/compute kit -> merchant-sourced lidar + L4 compute + sensors (sub-niche: L4 compute)
also_serves_megatrends: L2+/L3 consumer ADAS (same lidar/compute supply base and fabs)
size_2026_usd: $0.1-0.35B (own estimate): L4 compute $25-110M, robotaxi lidar $25-100M, other sensors/pods/cleaning/integration about $50-140M. Unverified.
cagr_2026_2030: 35-80% (central about 55-65%; full band 14-134%; own estimate). L4 compute sub-niche 60-100%; robotaxi lidar 25-60%.
volume_vs_price: Volume up, price down hard. Merchant-equipped robotaxi builds go from about 6-13k (2026) to about 65-215k (2030), i.e. +80-100%/yr. Kit value per vehicle falls about 12-20%/yr: lidar ASP deflation (Hesai 2024 blended ASP about RMB 4.1k per unit, about $570) and Pony Gen-7 cutting kit BOM by 70%. Compute is the exception: content per vehicle holds or rises (4x Orin-X -> 2x Thor -> next-gen for end-to-end/VLA models), giving rising content per unit. Revenue growth is therefore volume minus deflation, and as a flow (new builds) it is lumpier than service revenue (a stock).
math: 2026: China merchant-equipped builds 5-10k (Pony, Apollo RT6 lidar content, WeRide, others) x merchant content $7-17k (lidar $2-5k, compute $2-5k, cameras/radar $1-2k, pod/cleaning/harness/redundant power $2-5k) = $35-170M. Total $0.45-3.4B, taken as $0.6-3B. Central: 0.2 -> 1.5 = about 65%/yr.
catalyst_timing: 2026: Pony Gen-7 and WeRide Thor-based fleets ramp, Nuro-Lucid-Uber production vehicles. 2027: Nvidia-Uber Hyperion 10 fleets start (up to 100k vehicles over time), the main merchant-compute catalyst. 2027-2028: Mobileye/VW ID.Buzz AD and Stellantis/Lucid Hyperion L4 builds. Merchant compute volume comes later than the lidar ramp, which is already flowing in China.
key_suppliers: L4 compute: NVIDIA (NVDA/NASDAQ) about 70-90% of merchant L4 compute (own estimate); Horizon Robotics (9660.HK), Qualcomm (QCOM/NASDAQ), Black Sesame (2533.HK); domain-controller assembly by Quanta (2382.TW), Desay SV (002920.SZ) and others. Lidar: Hesai (HSAI/NASDAQ, 2525.HK) about 50-70% of merchant robotaxi lidar; RoboSense (2498.HK) about 20-35% (WeRide and others); Seyond, Ouster (OUST/NASDAQ), Valeo (FR.PA). Sensor cleaning: Valeo, Kautex (Textron, TXT), dlhBowles (private). Shares are own estimates and unverified.
supply_tightness: Loose. Lidar capacity is in the millions of units per year (Hesai and RoboSense sized for ADAS) against robotaxi demand in the tens of thousands, so there is no pricing power; suppliers price robotaxi lidar as a reference win. Compute: Thor supply is adequate after 2025 delays. Qualification takes 12-24 months per operator, but the supplier set is concentrated (Nvidia, Hesai, RoboSense) without being a bottleneck.
substitution_risk: High. (1) Vertical integration: Waymo makes its own lidar, pod and compute integration; Tesla uses vision only with in-house AI4/AI5; XPeng plans robotaxis on its own Turing chips (announced 2025, unverified details); Baidu may internalize compute. (2) Lidar count per vehicle falls with camera + 4D-radar fusion and Hyperion's single-lidar reference. (3) Chinese lidar is barred or restricted in US fleets: Hesai is on the DoD 1260H list, and US connected-vehicle rules restrict Chinese hardware/software. This splits the market, and Western robotaxi lidar goes to Ouster/Aeva/Valeo/in-house.
cyclicality_risk: High. Kit revenue is a derivative of fleet ADDITIONS, so any operator funding pause, incident or permit freeze cuts orders immediately (Cruise in 2023-24 is the precedent). Chinese overcapacity in lidar means continued ASP deflation. Double-ordering risk is low because volumes are small and operator-specific.
faster_sub_niche: L4 compute (Thor-class domain controllers, Hyperion 10): 2026 $25-110M -> 2030 $0.25-1.2B (60-100% CAGR; own estimate). Content per vehicle rises with each generation for end-to-end/VLA driving models, and the Nvidia-Uber 100k plan creates a merchant channel. Robotaxi-grade lidar is the SLOWER sub-niche (25-60%), deflationary and below $1B even in 2030. Overall, SERVICE grows faster than HARDWARE (about 75-95% vs about 55-65% central) and is more durable.

name: HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) nearline HDDs, 3.5-inch, >=30 TB
definition: Drive-level revenue from 3.5-inch nearline/enterprise HDDs that record with laser-heated HAMR heads on FePt media. Products: Seagate Mozaic 3+/4+/5+ (Exos M ~30-44 TB+), Western Digital HAMR (volume from ~2027), Toshiba HAMR (~2027-28). IN: HAMR CMR and SMR SKUs sold to hyperscalers, AI clouds, storage OEMs and channel. OUT: PMR/ePMR/UltraSMR/MAMR nearline drives (incl. WD 11-platter ePMR and Toshiba 12-disk MAMR), client and surveillance drives, and component revenue.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> data storage -> nearline capacity tier (HDD, ~85-90% of DC exabytes) -> recording-technology transition (PMR/ePMR/MAMR -> HAMR) -> HAMR nearline drives
also_serves_megatrends: AI training data lakes and inference corpora (RAG, generated video)
Data-retention regulation and sovereign cloud build-outs
size_2026_usd: $2.5-5.5B (own estimate). About 100% Seagate; WDC and Toshiba HAMR revenue is ~0 in 2026 apart from qualification units.
volume_vs_price: Almost all volume and share shift. HAMR exabytes grow ~55-75%/yr: industry nearline EB grows +15-22%/yr, and HAMR's share of industry nearline EB rises from ~12-27% in 2026 to ~55-85% in 2030. $/TB falls ~3-8%/yr after the tight 2025-26 pricing period. Units grow slower than EB (~35-50%/yr) because average capacity per HAMR drive rises from ~34-38 TB to ~50-70 TB. Industry HDD unit capacity is roughly flat (makers add EB through areal density, not new lines), so this niche mainly cannibalizes PMR/ePMR revenue. Total nearline HDD revenue grows only ~5-15%/yr (own estimate).
math:
2026 top-down: Seagate CY2026 revenue ~$11.5-13.5B (own estimate, extrapolated from FY26-Q1 $2.63B reported, the Dec-qtr guide of $2.70B +/- $0.10B, and 2026 pricing). Mass capacity ~80% gives $9.2-10.8B. HAMR at 30-50% of mass-capacity revenue gives $2.8-5.4B.

EB cross-check: Seagate CY2026 mass-capacity EB ~650-800 EB x HAMR share 35-55% = ~230-440 EB. At $12-14/TB (own derivation: FY26-Q1 mass-capacity revenue / EB ~ $13/TB), that is $2.8-6.2B. Adopted range: $2.5-5.5B.

2030: industry nearline EB ~1.7-1.9 ZB in 2026 (own estimate; Seagate ~180 EB/qtr and WDC ~200 EB/qtr in the Sept-2025 quarter, recalled, plus Toshiba). Growing at 15-22%/yr gives 3.0-4.0 ZB. Multiply by a HAMR share of 55-85% (Seagate ~90-95%, WDC 40-85%, Toshiba 20-50%) and $9-12/TB: $15-41B.
catalyst_timing:
- Mozaic 4+ (4 TB/disk, ~40-44 TB) volume ramp during CY2026 (company guidance; exact timing unverified).
- Seagate HAMR passes ~50% of its nearline EB around 2026 (company target as recalled; unverified).
- WDC HAMR: hyperscaler qualification 2026, volume ~1H CY2027 (company guidance as of late 2025; check on WDC's late-Oct-2026 call).
- Toshiba HAMR ~2027-28.
- Seagate Mozaic 5+ ~2027-28.
- Industry-wide HAMR passes 50% of nearline EB ~2028 (own estimate).
key_suppliers:
- Seagate Technology (STX, Nasdaq): ~100% of 2026 HAMR revenue. Vertically integrated heads and media; head wafer fabs in Northern Ireland and Minnesota; HGA/drive assembly in SE Asia and China (prior knowledge). 2030 HAMR share 45-60% (own estimate).
- Western Digital (WDC, Nasdaq): HAMR volume from ~2027; 2030 share 30-45% (own estimate).
- Toshiba Electronic Devices & Storage (unlisted; Toshiba was taken private by the JIP consortium in Dec 2023): HAMR with TDK heads and Resonac media; 2030 share 5-12% (own estimate).
supply_tightness: High. Only one qualified HAMR supplier in 2026, and HAMR head and media processes take years to industrialize. Nearline HDD lead times stretched to ~52+ weeks in 2H25 (TrendForce, third-party). Seagate and WDC said late in 2025 that nearline output was allocated under build-to-order / long-term agreements through CY2026 (recalled). Both makers avoid adding unit capacity and keep capex at ~4-7% of revenue. Result: pricing power and gross margins above 40%.
substitution_risk:
Medium-low.
- ePMR/MAMR stretching (WD 36-40 TB ePMR/UltraSMR; Toshiba 12-disk ~40 TB MAMR in 2027) can delay HAMR at WDC and Toshiba, but not much beyond ~4 TB/disk.
- QLC eSSD substitution is limited by a ~5-8x $/TB gap at 2026 contract prices (own estimate).
- Tape takes cold archive.
The main risk is execution (WDC HAMR yield and reliability), not substitution.
cyclicality_risk: High. Nearline exabytes fell sharply in the 2022-23 hyperscaler digestion. With ~52-week lead times, double ordering and CSP inventory build in 2026-27 are plausible, and a 2027-28 digestion could stall the ramp for 2-4 quarters. No risk from Chinese capacity (there is no Chinese HDD maker).
faster_sub_niche: None. Splitting by capacity point (Mozaic 3+ vs 4+/5+) is only mix shift. The HAMR component layers (glass substrates ~33%, laser diodes ~27% central CAGR) grow SLOWER than drive revenue: platters and heads per drive are roughly fixed while EB per platter rises ~12-18%/yr. Between drives and the glass layer, HAMR drives are the faster sub-niche.

name: High-temperature glass substrates for 3.5-inch nearline HDD media (HAMR FePt media and thin high-platter-count stacks)
definition: Merchant revenue from 95 mm (3.5-inch) glass disk substrates (aluminosilicate / glass-ceramic) sold to media makers (Seagate and WDC captive media; Resonac for Toshiba). IN: substrates for HAMR FePt media and for thin (<=~0.5 mm) substrates in 11-12-platter MAMR/ePMR stacks. HAMR needs glass because ordering L1_0 FePt needs ~550-700C deposition/annealing, beyond the ~300C tolerance of NiP-plated aluminum. OUT: 2.5-inch glass for client/mobile HDDs, aluminum/NiP substrates, finished media, and EUV mask blanks (same supplier, different product).
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> data storage -> nearline HDD -> HAMR media (FePt granular) -> disk substrate -> 3.5-inch high-temperature glass substrates
also_serves_megatrends: Higher platter-count drives (12-disk stacks) independent of HAMR
size_2026_usd: $0.35-0.9B (own estimate; Hoya-dominated; low confidence)
volume_vs_price: Volume-led. 3.5-inch glass substrate units grow ~35-45%/yr, from ~85-170M in 2026 to ~300-840M in 2030. Every HAMR platter needs glass, and HAMR's share of nearline platters rises from ~10-15% to ~55-85%. ASP is roughly flat to -5%/yr: the near-monopoly supplier's pricing power and higher-spec mix (thinner, higher-temperature) offset volume discounts. Growth is slower than HAMR drive revenue because substrates scale with platters, while EB per platter rises ~12-18%/yr.
math:
2026: Seagate HAMR ~230-470 EB / ~34-38 TB average = ~7-13M drives. x 10 platters = 70-130M platters. / ~85% media yield = 80-155M substrates, plus 5-15M WDC/Toshiba qualification/pilot = 85-170M. x ASP $3-6 (own estimate, unverified) = $0.26-1.0B.

Cross-check: Hoya's Information Technology segment is roughly JPY300-370B/yr. HDD substrates are plausibly 25-35% of it (~$0.5-0.85B, including a declining 2.5-inch base). Adopted: $0.35-0.9B.

2030: HAMR EB 1.65-3.4 ZB / 5-6.5 TB per platter = 250-680M platters. Add yield loss: 280-780M. Add 12-disk MAMR glass (20-60M): 300-840M. x $2.5-5 = $0.75-4.2B. Adopted: $0.8-3.5B.
catalyst_timing:
- Seagate Mozaic 4+ ramp in 2026.
- WDC HAMR volume ~1H CY2027 (guided as of late 2025).
- Toshiba 12-disk ~40 TB drives on Hoya glass (2027 target), then Toshiba HAMR (~2027-28).
- Hoya capacity additions (timing and amounts unverified).
key_suppliers:
- Hoya Corp (7741.T): estimated >80% of 3.5-inch nearline glass (own estimate). HDD substrate plants in Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Laos per prior knowledge; verify).
- Possible minor or second sources (unverified): Ohara (5218.T, glass-ceramic), Chinese entrants.
- Customers: Seagate (STX) and WDC (captive media); Resonac (4004.T), merchant media for Toshiba.

name: Wide-bandgap (GaN + SiC) power semiconductors sold into AI-datacenter IT power conversion (device layer)
definition: IN: GaN HEMTs and GaN power ICs (40-1,250 V) plus SiC MOSFETs, JFETs, diodes and modules (650 V-3.3 kV), sold for the AI-server power chain from the AC/MV feed down to the 12 V tray bus. Sockets: rack PSUs/power shelves (5.5-12 kW), 800 VDC and +/-400 VDC power racks/sidecars and rectifiers, data-center SSTs, BBU/supercap converters, 800 V hot-swap/protection, and on-tray 800 V->50/12 V and 48/54 V->12 V converters. OUT: silicon MOSFETs/IGBTs; separately sold controllers and gate drivers; GPU/ASIC core VRs and vertical power modules (covered elsewhere); facility UPS, chillers and HVAC drives; equipment-level value (covered by the 800 VDC equipment candidate). Candidates 2 and 3 below are sub-niches of this one, so do not add them together.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> rack & facility power delivery -> AC/DC and DC/DC conversion stages (PSUs, 800 VDC sidecars, SSTs, tray converters) -> power-semiconductor switches -> wide-bandgap GaN/SiC devices for AI-DC power
also_serves_megatrends: EV traction inverters and onboard chargers
Grid solid-state transformers and MW-class EV chargers
Humanoid/robot joint motor drives (48-100 V GaN)
size_2026_usd: $0.15-0.4B (own estimate; central ~$0.25B; low confidence)
volume_vs_price: Device unit volume grows about 45-70% per year. Two drivers: AI IT power shipped grows about 25-40% per year, and WBG content per kW rises about 10-25% per year. Content rises because 800 VDC adds an all-WBG high-voltage tray stage and GaN takes synchronous-rectification and IBC sockets from silicon. Blended ASP falls about 8-15% per year (own estimate), driven by Chinese GaN pricing (Innoscience), the SiC substrate glut, and 200/300 mm cost-downs. Growth is volume- and penetration-led; it is not shortage pricing. That makes it durable but margin-dilutive.
math: TOP-DOWN 2026: AI accelerated IT power shipped is 14-18 GW (own estimate). Basis: roughly $250B of NVIDIA data-center compute at about $25-30k per kW rack-scale (GB300 NVL72 about 135 kW per rack), plus 4-7 GW of TPU, Trainium and MI-class. WBG content is $7-20/kW (own estimate), built from three parts. (1) A 5.5-8 kW PSU uses 4-12 SiC PFC FETs at $3-6 plus 4-8 GaN LLC FETs at $2-4, giving $4-10/kW. (2) IBC and SR GaN adds $0.5-3/kW. (3) BBU and other uses add $1-3/kW. So 14-18 GW x $7-20/kW = $0.10-0.36B. BOTTOM-UP CROSS-CHECK: Infineon guided about EUR1.5B of FY26 AI power revenue (company guidance, recalled), mostly silicon VR power stages. If 25-35% of it is PSU-related and 25-40% of that is WBG, Infineon's WBG AI-DC revenue is about $0.1-0.23B. At an estimated 35-50% share, the total is $0.2-0.5B. Blended 2026 range: $0.15-0.4B. 2030: 35-70 GW per year (own estimate) x $10-22/kW gives $0.35-1.5B. The $10-22/kW for the 800 VDC chain comprises 1.2 kV SiC in the sidecar ($4-8), HV GaN/SiC on the tray ($4-10), LV GaN ($1-4), BBU and protection ($1-3), and SST averaged over the fleet ($0-2), after about 35% cumulative ASP erosion. Adding SST upside gives $0.6-1.6B. The CAGR range pairs low-to-low and high-to-high: $0.25B -> $1.0B is about 41%.
catalyst_timing: 2026: GB300 and Vera Rubin NVL144 stay on 54 V busbars with 8-12 kW PSUs; WBG gains come through PSU penetration. 2026-27: +/-400 VDC (OCP Mt Diablo) racks at Microsoft, Meta and Google. 2H 2027: first volume of the 800 VDC Kyber / Rubin Ultra, which turns on the HV tray sockets. 2028-30: SST pilots move to early volume. Near-term check-points: OCP Global Summit (Oct 2026), Navitas Q3-26 (early Nov 2026), Infineon FY26 results (about mid-Nov 2026, AI-power revenue vs the ~EUR1.5B guide).
key_suppliers: GaN (2026 AI-DC share, own estimates): Infineon incl. GaN Systems (IFX, XETRA) 30-45%; Innoscience (2577.HK) 15-25%; EPC (private) 8-15%; Navitas (NVTS, Nasdaq) 5-10%; Texas Instruments (TXN) 3-8%; others 10-20%: Renesas/Transphorm (6723.T), ST (STM), ROHM (6963.T), Power Integrations (POWI), onsemi (ON). SiC (own estimates): Infineon 25-35%; onsemi 15-25%; ST 10-20%; Wolfspeed (WOLF) 5-12%; ROHM 5-10%; Navitas/GeneSiC 2-5%; Mitsubishi Electric (6503.T) for 3.3 kV modules; China-domestic 10-20%: CR Micro (688396.SH), Sanan (600703.SH), StarPower (603290.SH), BASiC Semiconductor. Customers: Delta (2308.TW), Lite-On (2301.TW), Flex, Megmeet (002851.SZ), Vertiv, Eaton, Great Wall/AcBel.
supply_tightness: This is not a shortage niche. GaN-on-Si wafer capacity is ample, with Innoscience 8-inch at about 13k wafers per month per its prospectus (recalled) and Chinese capacity growing. SiC is in an overbuild bust: Wolfspeed went through Chapter 11 in 2025, and Chinese substrate prices collapsed. The real bottlenecks are elsewhere. (1) Hyperscaler/OEM qualification of HV GaN takes 12-24 months, and only about 4-6 suppliers are qualified for >=5.5 kW AI PSUs. (2) TSMC exits GaN foundry by July 2027, forcing fabless GaN (Navitas, ROHM and others) to requalify at PSMC or GlobalFoundries. (3) Few suppliers are qualified for 2.3-3.3 kV SiC modules. Pricing power is low to negative, except in 3.3 kV modules. Lead times look normal, but this is unverified.
substitution_risk: High at the socket level. In the 54 V architecture, silicon superjunction and trench MOSFETs remain cheaper and good enough for LLC/SR/IBC. At 800 VDC, 1.2 kV SiC competes with stacked 650 V GaN on the tray. Architecture risk: if +/-400 VDC (Mt Diablo) wins over 800 VDC at hyperscalers, the stage looks more like today's 650 V designs, and WBG content rises less. Proprietary module vendors (e.g., Vicor) and switched-capacitor topologies using LV silicon can bypass HV WBG.
cyclicality_risk: (1) SiC already shows severe global overcapacity: Wolfspeed's restructuring, Chinese 150/200 mm substrate oversupply, and device ASPs down sharply in 2024-26 (reported by TrendForce, recalled). (2) GaN faces a Chinese price war led by Innoscience. (3) The AI-capex cycle carries double-ordering risk at PSU makers (Delta, Lite-On) around architecture transitions. (4) Revenue depends heavily on the NVIDIA Kyber timetable.
faster_sub_niche: High-voltage GaN (stacked 650 V and 1,200 V-class) for 800 VDC on-tray isolated DC-DC (800 V->50/12 V), plus sidecar LLC stages. It is under $10M in 2026 (samples and pre-production) and could reach $0.1-0.45B by 2030, a >100% CAGR (own estimate); it is emerging. The 2.3-3.3 kV SiC SST sub-niche grows faster in percentage terms but is too early (see Candidate 3). The slowest sub-niche is 650 V SiC in PSU PFC: a mature socket with heavy ASP erosion, growing about 10-25%.

name: GaN power transistors and GaN power ICs for AI-datacenter power conversion (650 V-class HV + 40-200 V LV)
definition: IN: lateral GaN-on-Si (and GaN-on-sapphire) HEMTs, GaN power ICs with integrated drivers, and bidirectional GaN switches. Sockets: AI rack PSUs and power shelves (PFC, LLC, synchronous rectification), 800 VDC / +/-400 VDC sidecars, on-tray 800 V->50/12 V converters, and 48/54 V->12 V IBCs. OUT: GaN at the GPU core VR (covered under vertical power); non-AI enterprise/telecom PSUs; consumer chargers; GaN RF.
value_chain_path: AI data centers -> rack power delivery -> PSUs / 800 VDC tray DC-DC / 48 V IBC -> power switches -> GaN HEMTs and GaN power ICs
also_serves_megatrends: EV onboard chargers (650 V GaN replacing SiC at 11-22 kW)
Solar microinverters (e.g., Enphase IQ9 commercial GaN microinverter)
Humanoid/cobot joint motor drives (48-100 V GaN inverters)
size_2026_usd: $0.04-0.14B (own estimate; central ~$0.08B; low confidence). Above the $50M emerging threshold at the central estimate, below the $200M floor.
size_2030_usd: $0.25-1.0B (own estimate; central ~$0.45-0.5B). Adding non-AI DC and telecom GaN (~$0.1-0.2B) would bring all data-center GaN close to $1B only in the bull case.
volume_vs_price: Driven by volume and penetration. GaN units per AI kW rise 2-4x between the 54 V PSU era and the 800 VDC tray era. AI kW grows 25-40% per year. 650 V GaN ASPs fall about 10-15% per year (own estimate), led by Innoscience pricing and 200/300 mm cost-downs (Infineon 300 mm, PSMC/GF 200 mm). No shortage premium: if anything, price erosion caps revenue.
math: 2026: 14-18 GW x GaN $2.5-7/kW (own estimate) = $35-126M. The $2.5-7/kW is average AI-fleet content: GaN LLC/PFC in about 40-60% of AI PSUs at $3-8/kW where used, plus GaN in IBC/SR at $0.5-2/kW. Supplier cross-check (own estimates, unverified): Infineon GaN DC $25-60M, Innoscience DC $15-40M, EPC DC $10-25M, Navitas DC $3-12M, TI $3-15M, others $10-25M, for $65-180M across all data-center GaN including non-AI. Consistent. 2030: 35-70 GW x $5-14/kW = $0.18-0.98B. The $5-14/kW blends HV tray GaN at $4-9/kW if GaN wins 50-80% vs SiC, LV GaN at 40-70% share x $3-6/kW, and sidecar/PSU LLC GaN at $1-3/kW, net of about 40% cumulative ASP erosion. Rounded range: $0.25-1.0B.
catalyst_timing: 2026: 8-12 kW PSUs (e.g., 12 kW reference designs from Infineon and Navitas mixing Si/SiC/GaN) ramp with GB300 / Vera Rubin. 2026-27: fabless GaN moves from TSMC (exit by Jul-2027) to PSMC, GlobalFoundries (TSMC-licensed 650 V/80 V) and VIS. 2H27: Kyber 800 VDC brings the first volume HV-GaN tray converters. 2027-29: 1,200 V-class GaN (Power Integrations PowiGaN, Renesas/Transphorm) and bidirectional GaN reach qualification.
key_suppliers: Infineon incl. GaN Systems (IFX, Germany/Austria/Malaysia fabs; est. 30-45% AI-DC share); Innoscience (2577.HK, Suzhou/Zhuhai 8-inch IDM; 15-25%; ST partnership for ex-China capacity); EPC (private, US; LV 48 V leader; 8-15%); Navitas (NVTS, fabless, moving TSMC->PSMC; 5-10%); Texas Instruments (TXN, Dallas + Aizu internal GaN; 3-8%); Renesas/Transphorm (6723.T); STMicroelectronics (STM); ROHM (6963.T, previously TSMC-sourced 650 V); Power Integrations (POWI, 1,250 V PowiGaN); onsemi (ON, vertical GaN in development); AOS (AOSL). All shares are own estimates.
supply_tightness: Moderate and temporary. Overall GaN wafer capacity is not tight (Chinese 8-inch overcapacity; Innoscience about 13k wafers/month recalled). Two real bottlenecks: hyperscaler/PSU-OEM qualification of HV GaN at >=5.5 kW (about 4-6 qualified suppliers; 12-24 months), and the 2026-27 foundry migration after TSMC's exit, which forces fabless requalification. Pricing behavior is aggressively downward; there is no pricing power.
substitution_risk: HIGH. (1) In the 54 V architecture, silicon superjunction (LLC) and silicon trench MOSFETs (SR/IBC) remain cheaper. (2) At 800 V, 1.2 kV SiC on the tray is simpler than series-stacked 650 V GaN. (3) If +/-400 VDC wins, the tray stage uses 650 V devices, where GaN and SiC compete evenly. (4) 800 V->12 V direct conversion could eliminate the 48 V IBC socket, where LV GaN is strongest. (5) Patent litigation (EPC v. Innoscience at the US ITC; Infineon v. Innoscience) could restrict Innoscience in the US market. Outcome details are unverified.
cyclicality_risk: Chinese price war (Innoscience gross margin was only just positive in 2025, recalled). Navitas-type fabless players have weak balance sheets. AI-capex sensitivity. Little double-ordering risk because device lead times are short.
faster_sub_niche: HV GaN (stacked 650 V / 1,200 V-class) for 800 VDC on-tray isolated DC-DC. It goes from under $10M in 2026 to $0.1-0.45B in 2030, a >100% CAGR; it is emerging (own estimate). This is the only GaN socket that 800 VDC creates from zero. LV GaN (40-200 V) for 48/54 V IBC and SR is larger today ($25-70M) but slower at 25-45% CAGR, and it risks losing sockets if direct 800 V->12 V conversion wins.

also_serves_megatrends: Megawatt EV charging (MCS) and e-truck depots

catalyst_timing: 2H27: first volume of Kyber 800 VDC power racks (Delta, Vertiv, Eaton, Lite-On, ABB). 2026-27: +/-400 VDC Mt Diablo sidecars. 2027-28: SST pilots at AI campuses (Eaton via Resilient Power Systems, Hitachi Energy, Heron Power, Delta, SolarEdge and others). 2029-30: SST early volume, if UL/IEEE standards and utility interconnection are resolved.

name: Glass waveguide combiners for display-equipped AI/AR glasses (geometric reflective + diffractive SRG on high-index glass)
definition: IN: the see-through waveguide lens element per eye (in-coupler, pupil expander, out-coupler), valued at the waveguide-component level, merchant or captive-equivalent. Covers (i) geometric reflective/array waveguides (cascaded partial mirrors, Lumus-type) and (ii) diffractive surface-relief-grating waveguides made by nanoimprint or etch on n=1.8-2.0 glass, plus a small SiC share from 2028. OUT: birdbath/freeform combiners (tethered AR viewers), VR pancake lenses, automotive HUD combiners, projector/microdisplay, prescription-lens encapsulation and frame assembly.
value_chain_path: Consumer AI devices -> AI smart glasses -> display-equipped see-through AI/AR glasses -> per-eye optical engine -> waveguide combiner (geometric reflective / diffractive SRG on high-index glass)
also_serves_megatrends: Enterprise and industrial AR (logistics, field service)
Defense head-mounted displays (soldier and pilot HMDs)
size_2026_usd: $45-270M (own estimate; central ~$115M). Below the $200M floor at the central case; not emerging (>$50M).
size_2030_usd: $0.35-2.0B (own estimate; central ~$0.8B). $1B+ is reached in the upper ~40% of scenarios (own judgement).
volume_vs_price: Strongly volume-led. Waveguide pieces grow from 1.6-3.9M (2026) to 20-65M (2030), a ~70-110% unit CAGR driven by more display glasses and the shift from monocular to binocular. Blended ASP falls ~15-25%/yr: geometric $50-120 -> $20-45 and diffractive glass $15-40 -> $8-20 per piece, as yields rise and Chinese suppliers compete on price. Wider FOV, full-colour multilayer stacks and a SiC premium partly offset the decline. Current pricing on geometric parts reflects yield-limited supply, not demand-shock shortage pricing, so that premium will erode as SCHOTT and Quanta yields improve. The volume growth is durable; the ASP path is the main risk.
math: TOP-DOWN 2026 (own estimate): display-waveguide glasses 1.2-3.0M units = Meta Ray-Ban Display 0.4-1.0M + China waveguide-display brands (Rokid, RayNeo, INMO, Even, Meizu, Quark/Xiaomi display SKUs) 0.6-1.5M + Snap Specs / Android XR display glasses / Vuzix / enterprise 0.2-0.5M. Eyes per unit ~1.3 (Meta monocular; China mostly binocular) -> 1.6-3.9M pieces. Geometric: 0.5-1.4M pieces x $50-120 = $25-170M. Diffractive: 1.1-2.5M x $15-40 = $17-100M. Total $45-270M; central 0.9M x $75 + 1.7M x $25 = ~$110-115M. TOP-DOWN 2030: 12-35M display-waveguide glasses x 1.6-1.9 eyes = 20-65M pieces (central ~34M). Geometric share 35-55% (central 14M x $30 = $0.42B); diffractive glass 40-60% (central 17M x $14 = $0.24B); SiC 0-10% (central 2M x $60 = $0.12B). Central ~$0.78B, range $0.35-2.0B. CAGR central = (0.78/0.115)^(1/4) - 1 = ~61%. CROSS-CHECK (own estimate, unverified): 0.4-1.0M Ray-Ban Display units in 2026 imply ~$30-120M waveguide revenue at SCHOTT/Lumus. In the full optical engine (waveguide + light engine, ~$200M in 2026, central), waveguides are ~55% of the value.
catalyst_timing: 2026: Ray-Ban Display capacity ramp and the deferred international rollout; Android XR display glasses (Google with Samsung, Warby Parker, Gentle Monster) and Snap consumer Specs, both slated for 2026; China launch cycles around 618 and Double-11. 2027: rumoured binocular Ray-Ban Display successor and Meta's wider-FOV AR glasses; Apple glasses entry (display-less first, per press reports, unverified). 2028-2030: binocular full-colour becomes mainstream; first SiC/wide-FOV consumer volumes.
key_suppliers: Geometric reflective: Lumus (private, Israel; IP/design licensor); SCHOTT AG (private, Germany, Carl Zeiss Foundation-owned; Meta Ray-Ban Display manufacturing partner; est. >60-80% of 2026 geometric volume, own estimate, unverified); Quanta Computer (2382.TW; Lumus licensee/manufacturer); Chinese array-waveguide makers incl. Lochn Optics (private) and Crystal-Optech (002273.SZ; program unverified). Diffractive: Snap/WaveOptics (SNAP, captive); Dispelix (private, Finland); DigiLens (private, US); Vuzix (VUZI; Quanta-backed); Magic Leap (private; Google partner); Applied Materials (AMAT; waveguide fab program); Goertek Optical (002241.SZ); Sunny Optical (2382.HK); Goolton (private); North Ocean Photonics (private); Lingxi AR (private); Mojie (private; etched/SiC). High-index glass: SCHOTT, HOYA (7741.T), Ohara (5218.T), AGC (5201.T), Corning (GLW), CDGM (private); wafer processing: Lante Optics (688127.SS). All shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Geometric reflective is TIGHT. In practice there is one at-scale producer (SCHOTT), with Quanta qualifying. The process is complex: dozens of coated partial-mirror layers, stack bonding, angled slicing and flatness polishing, with low yields reported (third-party commentary, unverified). Meta paused the early-2026 international rollout citing limited inventory (reported, recalled). New lines take 12-24 months to build and qualify (own estimate). Diffractive glass is LOOSE: dozens of Chinese suppliers run nanoimprint lines, capacity is added easily with EVG/Canon NIL tools, and price competition is visible (Chinese press, unverified in-session). High-index glass wafers: moderate; a handful of qualified melters.
substitution_risk: High and two-sided. (1) Combiner switching inside the niche: if Meta's 2027+ glasses move from reflective to diffractive or SiC, geometric share collapses, and the reverse can happen. (2) Out-of-niche substitutes: polymer/plastic waveguides (lighter, cheaper, lower ASP), holographic/volume-HOE and liquid-crystal polarization-grating combiners, birdbath optics for tethered viewers, and display-less AI glasses, which have zero waveguide content and may capture most AI-glasses demand.
cyclicality_risk: Consumer-hardware hype cycles (Google Glass 2013, HoloLens, Magic Leap). Subsidy-driven Chinese demand and dozens of venture-funded Chinese diffractive startups make overcapacity and price wars likely by 2027-2028. Double ordering is low today because supply is limited, but could appear in 2027 if OEMs over-book SCHOTT/Quanta reflective capacity ahead of binocular launches. Concentrated demand (Meta is ~30-50% of 2026 pieces, own estimate) means one programme slip moves the whole niche.
faster_sub_niche: Geometric reflective (Lumus-type) waveguides are likely faster in REVENUE in 2026-2028 (own estimate 50-90% CAGR): they carry Meta's volume, prices are supported by yield-limited supply, and binocular successors double content per unit. Diffractive SRG on glass grows faster in UNITS but has steeper ASP erosion from Chinese price competition (revenue CAGR ~35-70%). SiC diffractive is the fastest from ~2028 but is too early (2026 <$20M). The split depends almost entirely on Meta's 2027 combiner choice, so the parent niche is kept intact.

name: MicroLED-on-silicon microdisplays for waveguide AR/AI glasses (monochrome now, full colour from 2027-28)
definition: IN: microLED-on-CMOS microdisplay panels (<=~0.3 in diagonal, <=5 um pitch) used as the light source in waveguide glasses, including the projection lens when sold as a projector module. Covers monochrome (green) panels and full-colour versions: X-cube combined three-panel, monolithic RGB, QD colour conversion and nanowire. OUT: microLED for TVs, watches and automotive; LCoS; micro-OLED; laser-beam scanning.
value_chain_path: Consumer AI devices -> AI smart glasses -> waveguide display glasses -> per-eye microdisplay light engine -> microLED-on-silicon microdisplay (mono -> full colour)
size_2026_usd: $20-100M (own estimate; central ~$45M). Borderline EMERGING (central just under $50M); JBD est. ~60-80% share (own estimate, unverified).
volume_vs_price: Volume-led. MicroLED eyes grow from ~0.9-2.5M (2026) to ~6-39M (2030; central ~15M), a ~75-100% unit CAGR as binocular Chinese glasses scale and Western OEMs adopt microLED for power and brightness. The blended ASP per eye is roughly flat to -10%/yr: monochrome panel+lens $12-30 falls to $6-12, but the mix shifts to full colour ($60-120/eye in 2026 -> $20-40 in 2030), which lifts content per eye. This is not shortage pricing, but monochrome panels will commoditize as Chinese entrants (Raysolve, Sitan and others) qualify.
math: 2026 (own estimate): Chinese binocular waveguide glasses 0.4-1.0M units x 2 eyes = 0.8-2.0M, plus Vuzix/Even Realities/others 0.1-0.5M -> ~0.9-2.5M monochrome eyes x $15-30 = $14-75M. Full colour (RayNeo X3 Pro-class, X-cube) 0.05-0.2M eyes x $60-120 = $3-24M. Total ~$17-99M; central 1.5M x $22 + 0.1M x $90 = ~$42-45M. 2030: 20-65M display eyes (central 34M) x microLED share 30-60% (central 45% -> ~15M eyes) x blended $15-30 (central $25: 60% full colour at ~$35 + 40% mono at ~$10) = central ~$0.38-0.4B, range $0.15-1.2B. CAGR central = (0.4/0.045)^(1/4) - 1 = ~73%.
catalyst_timing: 2026: Chinese binocular launches (Rokid, RayNeo, INMO, Even G2, Meizu) and Android XR display glasses (light-engine choice unverified). 2027-2028: full-colour microLED readiness (efficient red at <5 um pitch) is the gating milestone. Meta (Orion lineage and in-house Plessey) and Google (Raxium) are the likeliest Western adopters. 2029-2030: monolithic full colour cuts the size and cost of the X-cube approach.
key_suppliers: JBD / Jade Bird Display (private, Shanghai; dominant merchant monochrome supplier; IPO plans unverified); Aledia (private, France; GaN nanowire); Porotech (private, UK); Raxium (Google captive, GOOGL); Plessey (Meta captive, META); Raysolve (private, China); Sitan (private, China); Saphlux (private; QD colour conversion); Mojo Vision (private); Q-Pixel (private); PlayNitride (6854.TWO; mostly larger panels). Module/optics: Sunny (2382.HK), Goertek (002241.SZ), Young Optics (3504.TW). Shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Monochrome is moderately tight: effectively one high-volume merchant supplier (JBD), with OEM qualification taking 12-24 months, epitaxy-to-CMOS hybrid bonding and pixel-level repair/yield as constraints. Chinese second sources are emerging. Full colour is very tight and immature: red efficiency at small pitch, colour uniformity and X-cube alignment cost limit supply. Whoever cracks monolithic full colour will hold real pricing power in 2028-2030.
substitution_risk: LCoS (the full-colour incumbent today, used in Meta Ray-Ban Display) could hold the binocular full-colour slot through 2029 if microLED full colour slips. Micro-OLED works in reflective waveguides at lower brightness. Laser-beam scanning is a niche option. Captive supply (Meta Plessey, Google Raxium) could shrink the merchant addressable share in the West.
cyclicality_risk: Demand is concentrated in Chinese brands that are sensitive to consumer subsidies and venture funding. Monochrome capacity additions by several Chinese microLED startups risk a price collapse by 2027-2028. Western adoption is binary on one or two programmes.
faster_sub_niche: Full-colour microLED microdisplays (X-cube now, monolithic RGB later): 2026 <$20M (emerging) growing 100%+ CAGR if Meta, Google or Apple adopt them in 2027-2029 binocular glasses. Monochrome green grows ~40-60% in units with falling ASP.

name: LCoS microdisplay light engines for waveguide AI glasses (panel + LED illumination + PBS/projection optics)
definition: IN: field-sequential-colour LCoS panels (front-lit or PBS-illuminated) plus LED illumination and projection optics, sold per eye into waveguide glasses. OUT: LCoS for projectors, automotive HUDs and telecom wavelength-selective switches; microLED and micro-OLED engines; waveguides.
value_chain_path: Consumer AI devices -> AI smart glasses -> waveguide display glasses -> per-eye microdisplay light engine -> full-colour LCoS projector
size_2026_usd: $15-70M (own estimate; central ~$35M); panel-only value ~$7-25M. EMERGING (<$50M central).
volume_vs_price: Volume-led through 2028 on Meta Ray-Ban Display, Snap Specs and Lumus-based reference designs: eyes grow from ~0.45-1.3M (2026) to ~5-20M (2030). ASP per engine falls ~10-15%/yr ($30-55 -> $15-25) as front-lit integration (e.g. Himax) removes PBS optics. After 2028, growth depends on whether microLED full colour displaces LCoS.
math: 2026 (own estimate): Meta Ray-Ban Display 0.4-1.0M eyes + Snap Specs / Android XR / enterprise 0.05-0.3M = 0.45-1.3M eyes x $30-55 per engine (panel $8-15 + LEDs/PBS/lens $20-40) = $14-70M; central 0.85M x $40 = ~$34M. 2030: 20-65M display eyes (central 34M) x LCoS share 25-45% (central 35% = ~12M) x $15-25 = central ~$0.24B, range $0.1-0.5B. CAGR central = (0.24/0.034)^(1/4) - 1 = ~63%.
catalyst_timing: 2026: Ray-Ban Display ramp and international rollout; Snap consumer Specs (2026). 2027: Meta binocular successor (light-engine choice is the key unknown). 2028+: risk of displacement by full-colour microLED.
key_suppliers: OmniVision (Will Semiconductor, 603501.SS; LCoS product line; reported but UNVERIFIED as the Ray-Ban Display panel supplier); Himax Technologies (HIMX; front-lit LCoS plus WLO optics); Raontech (Korea, KOSDAQ; LCoS); Snap (SNAP; captive via Compound Photonics, acquired 2022); Jasper Display (private, Taiwan); Holoeye (private). Engine/optics: Avegant (private; reference designs), Young Optics (3504.TW), Sunny (2382.HK), Goertek (002241.SZ). Shares unverified.
supply_tightness: Moderate. LCoS backplanes are made on mature CMOS nodes with ample foundry capacity, and the LC/cell assembly know-how is held by a handful of firms. The real constraint is miniaturized, high-efficiency illumination optics and engine assembly yield, not the panel. Pricing power is limited.
substitution_risk: High after 2028. Full-colour microLED (better power, contrast and size) is the expected successor for binocular all-day glasses, and micro-OLED competes in reflective designs. LCoS keeps a cost and brightness edge for full colour until monolithic microLED matures.
cyclicality_risk: Single-customer concentration (Meta ~50-75% of 2026 eyes, own estimate). A design loss at Meta's 2027 refresh would cut the 2030 value roughly in half.
faster_sub_niche: Front-lit (PBS-free) LCoS modules, the Himax-type integrated front-light, are the faster slice because they shrink engine volume enough for binocular frames. Otherwise none: LCoS is the slower sibling of microLED (Candidate 2) over 2026-2030.
